title: Insulting Coworkers By Offering Help

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never insult your co-workers directly.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Instead, undermine their confidence by pretending to be helpful.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let me know if you need help fixing the grammar in your slide deck.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What?

setting: Office, with Dogbert standing on a conference table
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, stands on a table and teaches that you should never insult coworkers directly. He advises undermining their confidence by pretending to be helpful. In the final panel, a coworker demonstrates this by offering to fix the grammar in Alice's slide deck, and Alice reacts with irritation.
punchline: The offer of help is really a passive-aggressive insult implying Alice's slides are full of grammar errors, and her annoyed "What?" shows the tactic works.
summary: A consulting dog explains how to disguise a put-down as generosity, and a coworker promptly puts the lesson into practice.

title: Meeting Attendees Announce Their Handicaps

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you all for coming. I'm hoping we can make a lot of progress in the next hour.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I didn't get any sleep last night, so don't expect much from me.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: I'm so hungry I can barely think.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: I might be a bit distracted today because my wife told me she wants to leave me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't stay for the whole meeting. I have another thing in a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Man in blue shirt
transcript.text: I'm only here to sabotage your project because I can't abide the success of others.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't all of you leave now and I'll make all the decisions myself.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How'd the team meeting go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Better than I expected.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting, then a hallway
situation: Dilbert opens a team meeting hoping to make progress, but each attendee in turn offers an excuse for contributing little: lack of sleep, hunger, marital trouble, a scheduling conflict, even open intent to sabotage. Dilbert suggests they all leave so he can decide everything himself, and afterwards tells a coworker the meeting went better than expected.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic invitation for everyone to leave actually works, so the meeting becomes a success precisely because the team disperses and he gets to work alone.
summary: A string of unhelpful colleagues each announce why they can't contribute, and the one who finally clears the room finds that outcome a pleasant surprise.

title: Doing Right Gets You Punished

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hypothetically, if my boss told me to do something stupid, should I do it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You should do what you know is right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, good.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And then your boss should punish you for doing it.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker with two tufts of hair, who is holding up his hands in a calm, sage-like manner, whether he should follow a hypothetical stupid order from his boss. The coworker first gives lofty advice to do what is right, then adds that the boss should punish Dilbert for obeying that ethical instinct.
punchline: Following your conscience against a boss's bad order sounds noble, but the coworker cynically points out that management will punish you for it either way.
summary: A seemingly wise piece of ethical advice turns out to come with a built-in penalty from the boss.

title: Home Security Drone Neutralizes Package Thief

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Uh-oh. My home security system is showing a thief stealing a package from my front door.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Activating particle beam defense.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: The threat has been neutralized.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you say "neutralized," does that mean...

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Activating crime scene cleanup drone.

setting: Office break room or conference table
situation: Tina watches her phone and sees a thief stealing a package from her front door via her home security system. She remotely activates a particle beam defense and announces the threat is neutralized. When Dilbert nervously asks what that means, she activates a crime scene cleanup drone, implying the thief was killed.
punchline: Tina's casual, deadly overreaction to package theft is revealed when she deploys a cleanup drone, showing the thief was vaporized over a stolen package.
summary: A coworker uses her smart home's lethal defenses on a porch thief and calmly sends a cleanup drone afterward, leaving her colleague horrified.

title: Dogbert Refs the Meeting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, the meeting referee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That reminds me of a story.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tweeet!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fifteen-yard penalty for a time-wasting story!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll make it quick.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Red card!

situation: Dogbert wears a referee uniform and acts as a meeting referee. When the Boss begins to launch into a story, Dogbert blows a whistle and assesses a fifteen-yard penalty. The Boss promises to be brief, and Dogbert immediately shows him a red card.
punchline: Even the promise of a quick story is treated as a flagrant foul, since meeting-wasting anecdotes are so predictably long that they deserve ejection from the meeting.
summary: A dog in a referee outfit polices a manager's rambling by throwing penalty flags at him, ejecting him before he can even begin.

title: Boss Misreads Jargon-Filled Project Update

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you for that two-hour summary of your project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't understand any of the jargon you used, but based on the context, I believe you are saying the software will be done soon.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I didn't say anything about software.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I guess neither of us did our best work today.

situation: The Boss thanks a coworker for a two-hour project summary, then admits he understood none of the jargon. He guesses from context that she said the software will be done soon. She replies that she never mentioned software, and he shrugs that neither of them did well.
punchline: The Boss's confident guess about what he heard is completely wrong, yet he treats the failure as a shared one rather than his own for not listening or understanding.
summary: After sitting through a long technical briefing he did not follow, a manager confidently guesses its message, gets it wrong, and spreads the blame evenly.

title: Phone Addict Asks Permission To Scroll

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My digital devices have reduced my attention span so much I can barely concentrate on work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a dopamine hit every four seconds or I look for something else to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you mind terribly if I play with my phone while you drone on and on?

situation: Dilbert stands beside a seated female coworker and complains that his digital devices have wrecked his attention span. He explains that he needs constant stimulation every few seconds. He then politely asks if he can use his phone while she keeps talking to him.
punchline: Dilbert dresses up his phone addiction as a medical-sounding limitation and then uses it as an excuse to ignore his coworker, insulting her by calling her speech droning.
summary: A man blames his shrunken attention span on gadgets, then asks permission to tune out his coworker by scrolling on his phone.

title: Demonize Critics Instead of Fixing

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I recently learned that everything we have been doing is stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does that mean we'll be changing what we do?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let's see how far we can get by demonizing our critics first.

setting: Office hallway or break area, with coffee cups in hand
situation: A coworker with a spiky hairstyle tells Dilbert over coffee that he has just realized everything they have been doing is stupid. Dilbert asks whether that means they will change course. The coworker instead proposes attacking and demonizing their critics before considering any change.
punchline: Rather than fix a known mistake, the organization's first instinct is to smear the people who pointed it out.
summary: Upon admitting their whole approach is flawed, a colleague opts to discredit detractors rather than alter anything.

title: Boss Promises Blockchain in Two Days

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I go with you to the customer meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm worried you might promise something we can't deliver.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't be ridiculous!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been having customer meetings without engineers for years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know. And they all turn into disasters.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You worry too much!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything will be fine!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Can you replace our data centers with blockchain?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give us two days.

setting: Office hallway, then a customer meeting room
situation: Dilbert asks to join the Boss at a customer meeting because he fears the Boss will overpromise. The Boss dismisses the concern, even though Dilbert points out that his solo meetings always end in disaster. At the meeting, a customer asks for an enormous, unrealistic IT overhaul and the Boss casually agrees to deliver it in two days.
punchline: The Boss proves Dilbert's fear right by instantly committing to an absurdly impossible deadline for replacing data centers with blockchain.
summary: Brushing off an engineer's warning, a manager walks into a client meeting and immediately commits his team to an impossible technical miracle.

title: Bumper Sticker Regulatory Advice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Government regulations prevent us from marketing our products the way we want. What should we do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll consult my bundle of bumper stickers for some guidance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Question authority."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did you get so smart?

situation: The boss complains to Dilbert that government regulations stop the company from marketing its products the way it wants and asks what to do. Dilbert pulls out a bundle of bumper stickers and reads one aloud as his guidance. The boss is impressed by the slogan and asks how Dilbert got so smart.
punchline: Dilbert's advice is just a cliche bumper sticker slogan, yet the boss treats it as profound wisdom, and the slogan itself ironically urges defiance of the very authority regulating the company.
summary: Asked how to get around marketing restrictions, Dilbert offers a slogan from a bumper sticker and is praised as a genius.

title: Both Sides Sound Right

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We tried that plan already and it didn't work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop living in the past.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop refusing to learn from experience.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... Why do we both sound right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know. It's freaking me out a little.

situation: Dilbert and the Pointy-Haired Boss debate a proposed plan. The boss says it has already been tried and failed, and Dilbert replies that he should stop living in the past. Each then throws a contradictory but plausible-sounding cliche at the other, and they realize both arguments seem valid.
punchline: Business cliches can be flipped to argue opposite positions equally convincingly, which exposes how empty such slogans are as reasoning.
summary: Two coworkers trade opposing platitudes about past failures and are unsettled to find that both of them sound correct.

title: Horror Novel About Cubicle Monster

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm writing a horror novel.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's about a horned monster who puts people in boxes and makes them do meaningless work while insulting them.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That sounds great.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The monster is also very dumb.

situation: Alice sits at her desk and tells a coworker holding a coffee cup that she is writing a horror novel. The monster she describes puts people in boxes, assigns meaningless work and insults them. When the coworker says it sounds great, she adds that the monster is also very dumb.
punchline: The 'horror monster' is a thinly veiled description of the Boss, and the horror is simply ordinary office life under incompetent management.
summary: A cubicle worker pitches a scary book whose villain is obviously her own clueless, insulting supervisor.

title: Engineering Obsolescence Into Perfect Product

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've designed our new product to work flawlessly for up to ten years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one will need an upgrade. That's no good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Add some code to slow it down and make it unreliable after two years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But make sure the device doesn't slow down until we have an upgrade to sell.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then draft an apology I can put in a press release when we get caught.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have turned my engineering success into the darkest day of my career.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not even close to being true.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your darkest day will be when the press figures out what we did and I fire you for it.

situation: Dilbert proudly presents a new device he engineered to run flawlessly for ten years. The Boss objects that nobody would need an upgrade, so he orders Dilbert to secretly code in slowdowns and unreliability after two years, plus a ready-made apology for when they get caught. Dilbert laments that his success has become his darkest day, and the Boss says it will get worse when he fires Dilbert as the scapegoat.
punchline: The Boss not only orders deliberate sabotage of a great product but also plans to blame and fire Dilbert when the scheme is exposed.
summary: A well-built gadget is deliberately crippled by management to force upgrade sales, with the engineer lined up to take the fall.

title: Shred Documents, But Copy First

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Company policy says we must shred all proprietary documents.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But make copies first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should we shred the copies too?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do I have to do all the thinking around here?

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss announces that company policy requires shredding all proprietary documents, then immediately adds that everyone should make copies first. Dilbert asks whether the copies should be shredded as well, and the Boss responds with irritation that he is the only one expected to think.
punchline: The Boss's instruction to copy documents before shredding them defeats the purpose of the policy, and when Dilbert points out the obvious flaw, the Boss indignantly blames him for not thinking.
summary: A manager orders documents destroyed but wants duplicates kept, then gets defensive when an employee questions the logic.

title: Millennial Fever Brings Existential Doubt

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got millennial fever from talking to a millennial.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I see my job as a meaningless series of empty tasks.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: What do you expect me to do about that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was hoping for some praise.

situation: Dilbert tells Ratbert he has caught 'millennial fever' after talking to a millennial, and now sees his job as a meaningless series of empty tasks. Ratbert asks what he is supposed to do about it. Dilbert reveals he was hoping Ratbert would give him some praise.
punchline: Dilbert's mock-serious complaint about losing his sense of purpose is really a stereotypical millennial need for praise and validation, which he is now seeking from Ratbert.
summary: After chatting with a young coworker, Dilbert suddenly doubts the value of his work and angles for a pat on the back.

title: Harazzmat Suits for Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need you to wear this harazzmat suit when you meet with Tina.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina will also be wearing a harazzmat suit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The suits will prevent you from trying to harass each other.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You won't be able to speak directly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A radio inside the suit will transmit your words to our human resources department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he must wear a protective 'harazzmat' suit when meeting with Tina. The suits prevent direct speech, with a radio sending their words through Human Resources to be scrubbed of inappropriate content. Dilbert, in the suit, asks whether the Boss wears one when he talks to Tina privately.
punchline: The Boss doesn't wear a suit when speaking to Tina privately, but she wears three of them, implying she goes to great lengths to protect herself from his unwanted advances.
summary: A manager forces an employee into a bulky protective suit to stop harassment, then unwittingly reveals that the real offender is himself.

title: Leaked Strategy and Weak Password

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to find out who leaked our strategy to our competition.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Is your email password still 123?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop changing the subject.

setting: Office, at a desk with a laptop
situation: The Boss tells a seated coworker that they must find out who leaked the company's strategy to a competitor. The coworker, with a large mass of curly hair, asks if his email password is still 123. The Boss, not seeing the connection, accuses the coworker of changing the subject.
punchline: The Boss's absurdly weak password is the obvious cause of the leak, but he is too oblivious to realize the question is directly relevant.
summary: A manager hunting for the source of a corporate leak brushes off the one question that would solve the mystery.

title: Agile Data Center Without Plans

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I put together a plan for our data center project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't need a plan. We're an agile company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's better to move fast and fix our mistakes as we go.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're thinking of software, where the cost of mistakes is low. This is a construction project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That data center will be full of software, will it not?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't be afraid of change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I rapidly make a plan and tell you I didn't?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that agile enough for you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll need to Google that.

situation: Dilbert presents a plan for the company's data center project, but the Boss rejects it because the company is 'agile' and should just fix mistakes as it goes. Dilbert points out that building a data center is construction, where mistakes are costly, and the Boss twists the argument by noting the building will contain software. Dilbert finally offers to secretly make a plan and deny it, leaving the Boss confused.
punchline: The Boss misuses 'agile' as an excuse to avoid any planning, and when Dilbert offers a sneaky workaround, the Boss is too clueless to even understand it without searching online.
summary: A manager waves away a construction plan by invoking agile buzzwords, so the engineer offers to plan covertly and pretend otherwise.

title: Disguises Instead of Fixing Data Breach

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our customers are complaining because we let hackers get their personal data.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So we've decided to change the name of the company and wear disguises until it all blows over.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take a mustache from the bag and pass it around.

situation: The Boss tells his employees at a meeting that customers are angry about a data breach. His solution is not to fix security but to rename the company and have everyone wear disguises until the controversy fades. He then tells the staff to take a fake mustache from a bag and pass it around.
punchline: Management responds to a serious data breach by hiding from the blame with silly disguises and a new company name rather than fixing anything.
summary: Faced with angry customers after a security breach, the boss decides the company should simply hide behind fake mustaches and a new name.

title: Car Problem Is Really Starbucks

transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. I had a car problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What kind of car problem?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't get in it soon enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds like a "you" problem.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then my stupid car took me to Starbucks.

situation: Wally arrives late to meet the Boss, holding a coffee cup, and blames a vague 'car problem.' When the Boss asks what kind, Wally admits he simply didn't get in the car early enough, and the Boss points out that this is Wally's own fault. Wally then shifts blame to the car itself for taking him to Starbucks.
punchline: Wally treats his own lateness and coffee stop as the fault of his car, absurdly blaming an inanimate object for his choices.
summary: A tardy employee clutching a fresh coffee blames his vehicle for both his delay and his detour.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that everyone says he hates the new product test plan. Dilbert replies that he actually likes it, but the coworker dismisses this because so many people believe otherwise. Dilbert points out he is the authority on his own opinion, and the coworker shrugs it off as his word against everyone else's.
punchline: The coworker treats rumor and consensus as more reliable than a person's own statement about what he thinks, absurdly siding with the crowd over the one person who actually knows.
summary: A colleague insists the office gossip about Dilbert's opinion outweighs Dilbert's own account of it.

title: Joyless Dance Team-Building Event

transcript.text: This year's team-building event will be a dance. No alcohol will be served.

transcript.text: The event is for employees only, and you're not allowed to touch each other.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Have a great time.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How?

situation: The Boss announces to his employees that this year's team-building event will be a dance. He then strips it of every enjoyable element: no alcohol, no guests, and no physical contact between attendees. The last panel shows the office building from outside, with the staff's incredulous voices asking how they are supposed to have a good time.
punchline: A dance with no alcohol, no outside guests and no touching is a contradiction in terms, so the wish for the employees to have a great time is absurd.
summary: Management plans a dance for staff but bans drinks, dates and any contact, then expects everyone to enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know who keeps turning up the thermostat, but it's too hot to think.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert lists a long series of complaints to the Boss about how his co-workers and the office environment keep him from working: noisy phone calls, foot traffic, food smells, dumb questions and a hot thermostat. The Boss responds by offering to threaten to fire him, and Dilbert agrees to try it.
punchline: Dilbert's excuses are so exhaustive that the Boss offers a threat of firing as a motivator, and Dilbert cheerfully accepts while admitting he'll just be pretending to work.
summary: After a litany of grievances about why office distractions prevent him from getting anything done, an employee accepts his manager's offer of a firing threat while openly planning to fake his productivity.

title: Wellness Initiative Meets Birthday Cake

punchline: Management announces a wellness program and unhealthy cake in the same breath, and dismisses the obvious contradiction by telling employees to just mentally separate the two.
summary: A manager's wellness campaign collides with free birthday cake, and his answer to the hypocrisy is to simply ignore it.

situation: Dilbert tells Carol he has spent three days in virtual reality with no human contact, and that real people now feel disappointing by comparison. Carol asks whether that includes her, and Dilbert responds that being put on the spot like this is a problem he never has in virtual reality.
punchline: Dilbert's reply shows he finds real people, including Carol, awkward and disappointing next to a virtual world where nobody ever challenges him, and he can't even manage a polite answer.
summary: After days immersed in a simulated world, Dilbert finds actual coworkers a letdown and cannot even smooth over the insult when one calls him on it.

punchline: Faced with the choice between a decent apology and dishonest weaseling, the embarrassed coworker eagerly picks the dishonest route, showing how people double down rather than admit error.
summary: A gloating colleague publicly ridicules Dilbert, only to be undone by fresh evidence and then shamelessly angle for the dishonorable way out.

title: Team Confesses Phone Addiction Honestly

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I accomplished nothing this week because I'm addicted to apps on my phone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What about the rest of you losers?

situation: At a meeting, Alice admits she got nothing done because she is hooked on phone apps. A coworker says he hasn't slept in three days due to playing Fortnite. The Boss asks what the rest of the group's excuse is, and Dilbert shushes him because he is secretly listening to a podcast through one earbud.
punchline: Everyone in the meeting is distracted by their devices, and Dilbert proves it by ignoring the boss to keep listening to a podcast.
summary: A meeting turns into a roll call of smartphone and gaming distractions, capped by someone secretly tuning out with an earbud.

title: Boss's Vague Performance Review Praise

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've seen a lot of employees in my day, and you are definitely one of them.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Are you saying generic things because you don't know what my job is or how well I performed?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And... you speak truth to power.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Please stop.

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss gives an employee his performance review using empty, meaningless statements. The employee, Ted, asks whether the boss is being generic because he doesn't actually know Ted's job or how well he did it. The Boss responds with another vague line praising Ted for speaking truth to power, and Ted asks him to stop.
punchline: The Boss's feedback is so generic that he can't even recognize Ted's pointed question as proof that he has no idea what Ted does, and instead turns it into another empty compliment.
summary: A manager who knows nothing about an employee's work offers hollow platitudes in a review and cheerfully praises the employee for calling out that very emptiness.

title: Hiring Criminals Who Haven't Been Caught

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The job market is so competitive that we can't even find ex-cons who want to work here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So we're hiring active criminals who haven't yet been caught.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Say hello to Paul.

transcript.speaker: Paul
transcript.text: I hear our data center has a lot of copper wire.

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of the office building in the middle panel
situation: The Boss explains to Dilbert that the tight job market means the company can't even attract ex-convicts, so it has started hiring criminals who haven't been caught yet. He then introduces a new hire, Paul, a sunglasses-wearing man carrying bolt cutters, who announces his interest in the data center's copper wire.
punchline: The company's desperate hiring has brought in an active thief who openly plans to steal the copper wire from the data center.
summary: A manager brags about recruiting not-yet-caught criminals, and the new hire immediately eyes the company's valuables.

title: Patient Ignores Smartphone Addiction Diagnosis

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You've got a bad case of smartphone syndrome.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: One hundred percent of your mental and physical problems are caused by using your phone too much.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I don't feel as if I'm getting through to you.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: She's still talking. LOL.

situation: A doctor wearing a stethoscope diagnoses a patient with smartphone syndrome and explains that all of her health problems come from overusing her phone. The patient, shown mostly from behind, never responds. In the last panel she is hunched over her phone, texting someone about the doctor's lecture.
punchline: The patient is so absorbed in her phone that she is mocking the doctor's warning in a text message while the doctor delivers it, which proves the diagnosis.
summary: A physician warns a patient about phone overuse, only to find the patient is busy messaging a friend about the lecture.

title: Bringing Down Everyone's Average

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Warren Buffett says you should spend time with people who are better than you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why would people who are better than me be dumb enough to spend time with me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well... I assume you have to find people who are better than you, but not smart enough to avoid you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because, obviously, you'd be bringing down the average of anyone who was better than you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Which reminds me, I need to cut this meeting short to keep my average up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we can continue the meeting without him.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That would only be good for you. I need to find better people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The meeting went downhill from there.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Can you wrap this up? You're bringing down my average.

setting: Conference room, with a final panel in Dilbert's living room
situation: During a meeting, Asok relays Warren Buffett's advice to spend time with people who are better than you and wonders why such people would tolerate him. Alice and Dilbert explain that he would lower their averages, and the others then use that logic to cut the meeting short and exclude him. In the last panel Dilbert recounts this to Dogbert, who uses the same reasoning to rush him.
punchline: The advice to associate with better people backfires when everyone applies it to each other, since each person is the worse company in someone else's eyes and gets excluded.
summary: A famous investor's tip about befriending superior people turns into a round of polite exclusion once everyone realizes they are someone else's weak link.

title: Pepper Boaster Learns Painful Lesson

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried a habanero pepper last night. It almost burned off my face.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can eat the hottest peppers in the world and not even break a sweat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm glad you said that, because I have with me the hottest peppers in the world.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Pffft. Easy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Gulp.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Foom!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will you admit you were wrong?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You don't see any sweat, do you?

situation: Dilbert mentions a habanero nearly burned his face off, and a coworker brags he can eat the hottest peppers in the world without sweating. Dilbert produces the world's hottest peppers, the coworker eats one, and his head bursts into flames. Even as a skull, he insists there is no sweat.
punchline: The boastful coworker is so determined to win the argument that he claims victory even after his head has been incinerated, since technically he isn't sweating.
summary: A braggart who tops a story about spicy food gets his comeuppance when he swallows an impossibly hot pepper and his head goes up in flames.

title: Dilbert Asks Out an Android

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like to have a drink after work?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I don't drink.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about lunch?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I also don't eat. Do you see the pattern yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're an android?

situation: Dilbert stands beside a seated female coworker at her computer and asks her out for a drink after work. She says she doesn't drink, so he suggests lunch, and she says she doesn't eat either and asks if he sees the pattern. Dilbert's only conclusion is that she must be an android.
punchline: Dilbert completely misses the obvious hint that she's not interested and instead reaches the absurd conclusion that she's a robot.
summary: A coworker politely stonewalls an invitation with excuses, but the clueless engineer decides she must be a machine rather than uninterested.

title: Boss Profits From Worthless Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've noticed that 20% of my employees do 80% of the work around here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I need to keep all of the worthless employees because my pay is based on how many people report to me.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Doesn't their incompetence bother you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not since I found a way to get paid for it.

situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the red cat sitting on a desk, that only a fifth of his staff does most of the work. He explains he can't get rid of the unproductive ones because his compensation depends on his headcount. Catbert asks if their incompetence bothers him, and he says it no longer does since it earns him money.
punchline: The Boss's pay structure rewards him for keeping incompetent employees, so he has a financial incentive to tolerate poor performance.
summary: A manager admits he keeps useless staff on the payroll because the more people report to him, the more he earns.

title: No Budget For Whiny Employees

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a more ergonomic office chair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me check the budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm... Nope. We don't have a budget for making whiny employees happy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My current chair hurts my back.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's no picnic for the chair either.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a more ergonomic office chair because his current one hurts his back. The boss pretends to check the budget on his phone, then refuses by calling Dilbert a whiny employee. When Dilbert explains the back pain, the boss callously jokes that sitting on Dilbert is hard on the chair too.
punchline: The boss dismisses a legitimate health complaint by sarcastically implying that Dilbert's weight is the real problem, showing he cares more about insulting employees than spending money on them.
summary: A manager brushes off a worker's request for better seating by mocking him and suggesting the furniture is the one suffering.

title: Boss Blames Employees' Mental Problems

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm worried that all of my employees might have mental problems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They exhibited anger issues when I told them to work all weekend for no extra pay.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Did they say you're the cause of their mental problems?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't listen to crazy people.

setting: Office, with Catbert sitting on a desk and the Boss standing holding a coffee cup
situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the evil HR director, that he is worried his employees all have mental problems because they got angry when he ordered them to work all weekend without extra pay. Catbert asks whether the employees blamed him for their condition, and the Boss dismisses the idea by saying he doesn't listen to crazy people.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious and self-serving that he treats his employees' reasonable anger at unpaid weekend work as mental illness, and dismisses any complaint about himself by labeling the complainers crazy.
summary: A clueless manager diagnoses his furious staff as mentally unwell after demanding free weekend labor, then shrugs off any blame by refusing to listen to them.

title: Boss Praises Easy Management Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking of getting a degree in business and moving onto the management track.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it fun being a boss?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's the best!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I haven't done anything hard since the day I got this job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I mostly just criticize idiots all day long.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's as if the company is paying me to do my hobby.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Speaking of pay, my salary is about triple your pay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there any downside?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had a lot of guilt at first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must have been awful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, it was the longest ten minutes of my life.

setting: Office meeting table, with a panel showing the company building exterior
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he is considering a business degree and a move into management, and asks whether being a boss is fun. The Boss gleefully explains that the job is effortless, consists of criticizing idiots, pays triple Dilbert's salary, and only caused him guilt briefly.
punchline: The Boss's guilt about being overpaid for an easy job lasted only ten minutes, showing how little conscience or effort management requires.
summary: A manager cheerfully tells an aspiring employee that his well-paid supervisory role is easy, enjoyable, and barely troubled his conscience.

title: Your Face Said No Invitation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why didn't you invite me to the meeting?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I could tell by your face that you didn't want to be invited.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I DID want to be invited.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Tell that to your lying face.

situation: Dilbert confronts a seated coworker about not being invited to a meeting. The coworker claims he could read from Dilbert's face that he didn't want to attend. When Dilbert insists he did want to be invited, the coworker blames Dilbert's face for lying.
punchline: The coworker treats Dilbert's facial expression as more truthful than Dilbert's own words, using a made-up excuse to justify excluding him.
summary: A man excuses leaving a colleague out of a meeting by claiming his expression secretly signalled disinterest, then dismisses the colleague's protest as his face lying.

title: Motivational Speaker Inspires Everyone to Quit

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The motivational speaker you hired was great!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We all decided to quit our jobs and become motivational speakers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He was supposed to make you work harder here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You wanted him to motivate us to be dumb?

situation: Alice tells the Boss that the motivational speaker he hired was fantastic, then reveals that she and her coworkers have all decided to quit and become motivational speakers themselves. The Boss protests that the speaker was supposed to make them work harder at the company, and Alice responds that he can't have wanted them motivated to be dumb.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies that quitting stable jobs to become motivational speakers is the only sensible outcome of motivation, and that the Boss is the one who wanted employees to act against their own interests.
summary: A pep talk meant to boost productivity instead convinces the whole staff to leave and take up the speaker's own line of work.

title: Treadmill Desks Meet Hamster Wheel

transcript.text: All of your employees are fat and unhealthy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's why you should replace your outdated cubicles with treadmill desks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My company makes a treadmill desk that requires no electricity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if the employees don't like it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They already hate everything about their jobs. There's no real downside.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good point.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I know.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll send you one of our demo units so you can test it out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I finally feel as if I'm getting somewhere.

setting: The Boss's office, ending with a giant hamster wheel
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss his employees are unhealthy and pitches treadmill desks that need no electricity. When the Boss worries employees won't like them, Dogbert points out they already hate their jobs. The Boss agrees to test a demo unit, which turns out to be a giant hamster wheel.
punchline: The 'electricity-free treadmill desk' is really a hamster wheel, and the Boss happily runs in it, feeling like he's making progress while going nowhere.
summary: A scheming dog sells a gullible executive a human-powered exercise gadget that leaves him sprinting in place and calling it progress.

title: Two Liars Bond Over Dating Profiles

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't look like your photos on the dating app.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Your profile said you like to go to the gym. So I guess we're both huge liars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we can build on that.

setting: Social gathering or bar where Dilbert and a woman hold drinks on a first date
situation: Dilbert meets a woman he matched with on a dating app and tells her she looks different from her photos. She replies that his profile claimed he likes the gym, so they have both been dishonest. Dilbert suggests that their shared dishonesty could be a foundation for a relationship.
punchline: Dilbert treats mutual lying as a promising basis for a relationship, a sarcastic jab at how dishonest online dating profiles are.
summary: Two people on a first date discover they both padded their dating profiles and decide that shared dishonesty is a fine place to start.

title: Self-Driving Car Bug Gray Area

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our self-driving car went off a cliff with Ted in it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you tweak the software to make that happen?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, that was a bug.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Was it a known bug?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now we're getting into a gray area.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that the company's self-driving car drove off a cliff with Ted inside. Asked whether he tweaked the software to cause it, Dilbert says it was just a bug. When asked if it was a known bug, Dilbert admits that question gets into a gray area.
punchline: Dilbert insinuates that the engineers may have known about the fatal bug and shipped the car anyway, making the death ethically murky and possibly deliberate.
summary: An engineer calmly disclaims responsibility for a fatal autonomous-vehicle crash, until asked whether the flaw was already known.

title: Spending Company Money, Nobody Cares

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This price is too high.

transcript.speaker: Man in blue jacket
transcript.text: Why do you care?

transcript.speaker: Man in blue jacket
transcript.text: You're spending the company's money, not your own. And the company doesn't care if you live or die.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me a minute to think of why that doesn't make sense.

transcript.speaker: Man in blue jacket
transcript.text: Take as long as you need.

setting: Office desk during a purchasing negotiation
situation: Dilbert holds a quote and complains that the price is too high. The man across the desk, who appears to be the seller, asks why he cares and points out that it is the company's money and the company doesn't care about him. Dilbert asks for a moment to find the flaw in that argument, and the seller generously agrees.
punchline: The seller's argument that employees shouldn't care about company spending is so cynically plausible that Dilbert can't immediately refute it, implying the company really doesn't value its employees.
summary: A vendor talks a skeptical buyer out of haggling by reminding him that his employer doesn't care about him, and the buyer struggles to disagree.

title: Crumbs Cause Crosstalk On Protocols

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Wally, can you help me with a computer problem?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: People usually don't ask me for help.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Why is that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll find out.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I can't log in to the server.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll need to ask you a few questions.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you ever eaten food near your computer?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Um... Yes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's your problem.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your crumbs are causing crosstalk on the protocols.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Is this why no one asks you for help?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's in the top ten.

situation: Carol asks Wally for help because she can't log in to the server. Wally warns her that people rarely ask him for help, then blames her problem on eating near her computer and claims her crumbs are disrupting the network protocols. Carol realizes this nonsense is why nobody asks him for help.
punchline: Wally gives a ridiculous, technobabble-sounding diagnosis blaming crumbs for crosstalk on protocols, which confirms exactly why people avoid asking him for help.
summary: A coworker seeking tech support gets a bogus explanation from Wally that proves why he is usually avoided.

title: Ninjas Can't Scare the Unafraid

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why aren't you worried about the Elbonian ninjas who are reportedly coming here to kill you in your sleep?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the best way to die. I won't care about anything after I'm gone, so this is the ideal scenario for me.

transcript.speaker: Ninja
transcript.text: He's ruining everything with his cheery attitude.

transcript.speaker: Ninja
transcript.text: Let's see how he likes another thirty years in a cubicle.

setting: Office break area, then a muddy Elbonian village
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert why he isn't afraid of Elbonian ninjas supposedly coming to kill him in his sleep. Dilbert replies that dying in his sleep is the ideal way to go. The ninjas, lurking nearby and then back in Elbonia, are annoyed that he isn't scared and decide to make him suffer longer instead.
punchline: Dilbert's cubicle life is so bleak that being assassinated sounds like a relief, so the ninjas conclude that sparing him for thirty more years of office work is the worse punishment.
summary: A man unfazed by assassins gets a grimmer fate planned for him when the would-be killers decide that more years of office drudgery will do more harm than death.

title: Instinct Says Mating, Colleague Runs

transcript.text: It's mostly about mating.

situation: A coworker holding a sheet of paper says he must choose between two good options and will rely on his instinct. Dilbert asks what his instinct tells him, and the coworker admits it is mostly about mating. A third coworker in a yellow shirt responds by telling everyone to run.
punchline: Relying on gut instinct is a bad idea when human instinct is mostly driven by the urge to mate, which makes the instinct-guided decision-maker a creepy hazard to those around him.
summary: A man planning to trust his gut learns that his gut is basically obsessed with romance, so his colleague urges everyone to flee.

title: Boss Blames Dilbert For Own Mistake

transcript.text: This is exactly why I say bad things about you behind your back!

transcript.text: Your tardiness and sloth cannot be rewarded.

Dilbert calmly points out that he delivered the draft the same day it was requested, and that the Boss is holding it in his hand. The Boss, after a silent pause reading the paper, says he will return once he figures out how to blame Dilbert anyway.

summary: A manager berates an employee for a missing report, only to discover he has had it all along, and still hunts for a reason to assign blame.

title: Old Ned Orders Coffee From Engineer

punchline: Ned thinks treating a female senior engineer like a coffee gofer is keeping up with the times, but it is actually outdated and sexist behavior that he refuses to acknowledge.
summary: A self-styled up-to-date older man demands that a senior engineer bring him coffee, and brushes off her objection.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: Dilbert quizzes his boss on object-oriented programming concepts, and when the boss admits he doesn't know them, Dilbert asks how he can manage someone who does. The boss, who is looking at his phone, turns the question around and asks Dilbert if he knows the difference between managing and bullying. When Dilbert says no, the boss declares the problem solved.
punchline: The boss resolves the challenge to his authority by exploiting Dilbert's ignorance of the line between managing and bullying, implying he will simply bully the engineer instead of understanding the work.
summary: A manager answers an engineer's challenge about his technical ignorance by suggesting that intimidation can replace expertise.

title: Jargon Overload Leaves Meeting Confused

situation: A presenter wraps up a meeting and asks if anyone has questions. Dilbert admits he understood none of the jargon used for the past hour. When the presenter asks why he didn't speak up earlier, Dilbert replies that speaking up is only worthwhile for people who still have hope.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that he has long since given up hope that raising concerns in meetings would change anything or make the speaker communicate clearly.
summary: After an hour of impenetrable buzzwords, a weary engineer explains that voicing confusion is something only the optimistic bother to do.

title: Two Ways To Help: Both Bad

punchline: Both of the coworker's options for 'help' are exploitative and insulting, showing she has no interest in genuine collaboration and is happy to use him or sabotage him.
summary: An offer of assistance gets Dilbert a choice between being a doormat and being slandered to management.

punchline: Asok is fearless around Dilbert because he considers him physically weak, implying Dilbert couldn't harm anyone, while Alice's ferocity makes her genuinely frightening.
summary: A junior engineer explains he fears the aggressive coworker but not Dilbert because Dilbert can barely carry office supplies.

title: Giving 110% Meets Absent Team

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, can I get 50% effort from any of you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Conference room, with an exterior office building shown in the middle panel
situation: The boss tells the team that the project will only succeed if everyone gives 110%. Team members respond that they will be absent, undergoing surgery, or have already given notice. The boss lowers his demand to 50% effort, and Dilbert replies that he can give only the extra 10% the boss imagines exists.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that the '110%' the boss demands is an impossible fiction, so the only thing he can offer is that nonexistent extra 10%.
summary: A manager's demand for more than total effort collapses when his staff reveal they are leaving, away, or going under the knife.

title: Support Now, Stab Me Later

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your idea is great, but I plan to oppose it because I feel diminished by the success of others.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could support it now and then stab me in the back later.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's two great ideas you've had today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert his idea is great but says he will oppose it anyway because he feels diminished by other people's success. Dilbert offers a compromise: support the idea now and betray him later. The coworker is delighted and says that is Dilbert's second great idea of the day.
punchline: Dilbert's cynical suggestion to be backstabbed later is itself praised as a great idea, showing how normalized treachery and petty envy are in office politics.
summary: A jealous colleague admits he will sabotage a good idea out of insecurity, and Dilbert's deadpan compromise earns him another compliment.

title: Ricky Lowers Intelligence Bar for AI

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recommend adding Ricky to our artificial intelligence project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He lowers the bar on what constitutes human intelligence, so it will be easier for us to achieve the artificial kind.

transcript.speaker: Ricky
transcript.text: I would be honored to work on the project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Okay, I see what you mean.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that he recommends adding Ricky to their artificial intelligence project. He then explains it's because Ricky's low intelligence makes the bar for human intelligence easier to beat. Ricky, oblivious to the insult, says he would be honored to join, and the coworker concludes he understands the reasoning.
punchline: Dilbert recommends Ricky not for his skills but because his lack of intelligence makes it easier for artificial intelligence to match or surpass human intelligence, and Ricky is too dim to notice the insult.
summary: A colleague gets invited onto a high-tech project as a deliberate way of making the goal easier to hit, and he gratefully accepts without catching on.

title: Lie On The Survey

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're trying to get on "Best Places to Work" list.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you agree to lie on the survey, maybe we can attract some good employees to make this a best place to work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep your eye on the prize.

setting: Office, with a view of the office building exterior in the middle panel
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally that the company wants to land on a 'Best Places to Work' list. He asks the employees to lie on the employee survey, reasoning that the resulting ranking will attract good talent who will then make it a genuinely good workplace. Dilbert reacts with confusion while the Boss tells him to focus on the goal.
punchline: The company plans to fake its way onto a best-workplace list through dishonest survey answers, with the backwards logic that the lie will later become true once talented people are fooled into joining.
summary: Management asks staff to fib on a workplace-satisfaction questionnaire so the firm can earn a reputation it hasn't yet deserved.

title: Wally's Training Is Career Sabotage

transcript.text: You'll need to figure out how much of what he says is real training and how much is career sabotage.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Career sabotage?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Employees don't like competition.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only the top 20% get bonuses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They'll do what they can to keep you out of that group.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: I assume you're exaggerating.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll see.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Has anyone told you about no-pants Fridays?

setting: Office conference room and break area
situation: The Boss tells a new employee that Wally will train him, but warns that coworkers may deliberately give bad advice to protect their own bonuses, since only the top 20% get paid one. When the new hire doubts this, a coworker immediately walks up and asks if anyone has told him about 'no-pants Fridays.'
punchline: The boss's warning about sabotage is instantly proven true when a coworker tries to trick the newbie with a fake, humiliating office tradition.
summary: A manager cautions a newcomer that colleagues will undermine him to protect their bonuses, and a prankster promptly confirms it with an absurd lie about Friday dress code.

title: Denial Slogan Sounds Like Admission

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it too late to rethink our new marketing slogan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When we say, "We're not a bunch of morons," it kinda sounds to my ears as if we are.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: But it says we're NOT.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you're NOT a rat-faced waste of oxygen.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: Thank you.

setting: Office, at the marketing manager's desk
situation: Dilbert asks a marketing employee whether the company's new slogan, "We're not a bunch of morons," can still be changed, because denying the insult makes it sound like an admission. The employee insists the slogan literally says they are not morons. Dilbert demonstrates the problem by telling him he is NOT a rat-faced waste of oxygen, and the employee innocently thanks him.
punchline: The marketing manager falls for the very effect Dilbert is warning about: he politely thanks Dilbert for an insult phrased as a denial, proving that negating an insult still plants it.
summary: Dilbert shows a marketing employee why a slogan that denies an insult still plants it by insulting him in the same negated form, and the man responds with thanks.

title: Blaming Boss for No Artificial Deadline

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You've been promising me you'd finish the web page for the last six months.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is your fault for not giving me an artificial deadline.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay, I need it by end of day.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And miss my dental appointment???

situation: Alice confronts Wally about a web page he has repeatedly promised to finish over the past six months. Wally claims it's her fault for never imposing an artificial deadline. When Alice immediately gives him one, he objects that it would make him miss his dental appointment.
punchline: Wally blames Alice for the lack of a deadline, but when she gives him one he instantly produces an excuse, showing he never intended to finish the work.
summary: A chronically unproductive coworker faults his colleague for not pressuring him, then balks the moment she does.

title: Covering Tracks After Failed Pivot

transcript.speaker: Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Later, I'll change the project name to cover my tracks.

transcript.text: What about your sunk costs?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Gone like footprints in the sands of time.

setting: Office hallway or break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: Wally explains to Dilbert that when his project began failing, he quietly switched to an entirely different idea while keeping the original project name. He plans to rename it later so nobody can trace the switch. When Dilbert asks about the sunk costs, Wally dismisses them poetically.
punchline: Wally treats the money and effort wasted on the failed project as something that will simply vanish from memory, so he can escape accountability by rebranding and hoping everyone forgets.
summary: A cunning employee hides a failed project by secretly swapping in a new idea under the old name and then renaming it, trusting that the wasted investment will fade from everyone's memory.

title: Wi-Fi Typo Slide Deck Insult

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's "Wi-Fi."

situation: The Boss holds a printout of Dilbert's slide deck and lectures him that a typo has destroyed his credibility and made the presentation sloppy. He then warns Dilbert not to mention his wife in the slides. Dilbert calmly points out that the word was actually "Wi-Fi."
punchline: The Boss, while berating Dilbert for a typo, himself misreads "Wi-Fi" as "wife," showing he is the sloppy and ignorant one.
summary: A manager scolds an employee over a spelling mistake in his slides, only to reveal his own misunderstanding of a technical term.

title: Insurance Against Humorous Death Headlines

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You don't want the headlines to read "Pointy-haired idiot mauled to death by the king of the jungle."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So instead, the moment you die, my agents rush in to create a narrative for the media.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In this case, we might spin the story as "Local man teaches zoo how to reduce food costs."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are the policies affordable?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, if you waive coverage for mascot-related deaths.

situation: Dogbert, acting as an insurance salesman, pitches the Boss a policy that protects his reputation if he dies in a humiliating way. He describes a scenario where the Boss is mauled by lions at the zoo while retrieving sunglasses, and explains his agents would spin the story for the media. The Boss asks about affordability.
punchline: Dogbert offers cheap rates only if the Boss waives coverage for mascot-related deaths, implying Dogbert plans to have him killed by a mascot, so the policy is a scam he will cause himself.
summary: A scheming dog sells his gullible boss reputation insurance against a ridiculous death, then reveals a loophole that suggests he's planning one.

title: Software Upgrade Needs More Aspiration

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's just a software upgrade.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I want the audience to feel it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They can feel the handouts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's like you're not even trying to understand!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Genius is often misunderstood.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know what else is misunderstood?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Super-genius?

setting: Office, at a desk during a one-on-one review
situation: The Boss reviews Dilbert's slide deck and demands it be made more 'aspirational' so the audience can feel it, even though it's only about a software upgrade. Dilbert replies literally, the Boss accuses him of not trying to understand, and then claims he is a misunderstood genius. Dilbert hints that something else is also misunderstood, and the Boss answers with a flattering guess.
punchline: The Boss is so convinced of his own brilliance that he hears Dilbert's setup for an insult (that he's simply confused or incompetent) and completes it with 'super-genius', missing the point entirely.
summary: A manager demanding an emotionally moving presentation for a dull software update brushes off criticism by calling himself a misunderstood genius, then walks right into the insult.

title: Insulting the Boss Without Him Noticing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think you just invented my new favorite game.

transcript.text: Working for you is like boiling an ocean.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you!

setting: Office hallway and the boss's office
situation: Dilbert tells Wally that he insulted the boss's presentation using technical jargon and the boss took it as praise. Wally, delighted, decides to play the same game and walks into the boss's office to tell him that working for him is like boiling an ocean. The boss again thanks him, oblivious to the insult.
punchline: The boss is so clueless that he mistakes jargon-laden insults, like boiling an ocean (a hopeless, futile task), for compliments.
summary: After learning that a technical put-down passed as flattery with their boss, a coworker tries his own insult and gets thanked for it too.

title: Invisible Drone, Fake Cloaking Demo

transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.text: I'll demonstrate it flying as soon as I finish the noise cancellation.

setting: Conference room during a product demonstration
situation: An engineer presents two drones, claiming one is a standard model and the other uses his invented cloaking technology. Because the cloaked drone is invisible, his empty left hand earns gasps of amazement from the audience. summary: A showman presents an empty hand as a cloaked invention and wins instant praise from his gullible bosses.

title: Childless Dilbert Refuses Chocolate Fundraiser

Dilbert declines, pointing out that as a childless person his taxes already help pay for the coworker's kid's education. The coworker admits to counting on social awkwardness to get a sale, and Dilbert replies that the coworker actually owes him money.
punchline: Dilbert turns the guilt-trip sales pitch around by arguing that, since childless taxpayers already fund schools, the parent is the one in his debt.
summary: A parent's attempt to guilt a colleague into buying fundraiser candy backfires when the childless target claims he's already paid his share and then some.

title: Estimating Ted's Completion Time Range

transcript.text: When will I get the test data?

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: Just give me a range.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert when he will receive the test data, and Dilbert says Ted is working on it. When pressed for an estimate of Ted's completion time, Dilbert says he can't know because he isn't Ted. The Boss asks for a range, and Dilbert supplies an absurdly wide one.
punchline: Dilbert technically gives the requested range, but one so wide (one day to seven hundred years) that it is useless, mocking the managerial habit of demanding estimates for work no one can predict.
summary: A manager who demands a delivery estimate for someone else's work gets an answer that is technically responsive and completely worthless.

title: Dogbert's Grim Life Advice

transcript.text: How do I find meaning in my life?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Customer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What answer gets me the best review on Yelp?!

setting: Dogbert's life advice booth, with a desk and a $100 sign
situation: A customer pays $100 for life advice and asks Dogbert how to find meaning in life. Dogbert bluntly replies that nothing has meaning and the best one can do is delay a lonely, painful death. When the customer reinterprets this as a call to look after his health, Dogbert quickly adopts that answer.
punchline: Dogbert drops the nihilism the moment he realizes that the customer's more cheerful interpretation is the one that will earn him a better Yelp review.
summary: A paying client gets a bleak answer about life's emptiness, then watches the advisor pivot to whatever will earn the most flattering online rating.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: Catbert accuses Dilbert of deleting Alice's files from the server, claiming multiple sources told him.
