transcript.text: We're ready to fire up our laser communication technology to contact the alien probe heading to Earth.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: PFZEEEET!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is the alien probe unmanned?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is now.

situation: Dilbert announces that his team is about to use laser communication technology to contact an alien probe approaching Earth. On the roof, they fire a laser-like device into the sky. A coworker then asks whether the probe was unmanned, and Dilbert replies that it is now.
punchline: The 'communication' laser was actually a weapon that destroyed the probe, and Dilbert's deadpan 'It is now' implies that whoever was aboard has been killed.
summary: A rooftop attempt to greet visiting aliens with a laser turns out to be a shot that wipes out their spacecraft.

title: Wally Offers to Hold Crypto Keys

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do I get a crypto wallet so I can get into the cryptocurrency game?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll set one up for you and give you the private key and password when I'm done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know how to thank you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That'll take care of itself.

situation: The Boss asks Wally how to get a crypto wallet so he can start trading cryptocurrency. Wally offers to set one up and hand over the private key and password afterward. When the Boss gushes with gratitude, Wally says the thanks will take care of itself.
punchline: Wally implies that because he will know the private key and password, he can simply drain the Boss's wallet, so he will be thanked automatically by helping himself to the money.
summary: A gullible manager happily lets a lazy coworker create his digital money vault, not realising the helper will keep the means to empty it.

title: Psychopath Personality Test Results Warning

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you take the Dogbert personality type test?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes. I'm a disgruntled psychopath with a blinding hatred of authority.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be in my office.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Good! Stay there!

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, asks Alice whether she took the Dogbert personality type test. She calmly announces that her result is a disgruntled psychopath with a blinding hatred of authority. The Boss nervously retreats to his office, and Alice shouts at him to stay there.
punchline: Alice's personality test result is a genuine threat to management, so the Boss runs away, and her angry order to stay put shows the result is accurate.
summary: A manager's casual question about a quiz leads to a chilling answer that sends him scurrying for safety while his employee barks at him.

title: Fire Yourself For Bad Scheduling

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished coding the new feature.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What took you so long?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It took as long as it needed to take.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're behind schedule.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not the one who created the schedule! That was you!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you should fire yourself for being so bad at making schedules.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not how it works!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What does that even mean?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're starting to catch on that most of what I say doesn't mean anything.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has finished coding a new feature, and the Boss complains it took too long and that he is behind schedule. Dilbert points out the Boss made the schedule, and the Boss absurdly tells him to fire himself for being bad at scheduling. In the last panel the Boss admits to a coworker that people are realizing his statements are meaningless.
punchline: The Boss blames Dilbert for a schedule the Boss created, then self-awarely admits that most of what he says is meaningless nonsense.
summary: A manager who set an impossible deadline scolds his engineer for missing it, babbles illogical advice, and then concedes his own words carry no meaning.

title: Lowering Expectations After Awkward Request

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I get back to you?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If I say yes, I will never hear from you. But if I say no, I'll look like a pushy jerk.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't see a path to victory here.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you tried lowering your expectations?

situation: Alice asks Wally if he has a minute, and he deflects by asking if he can get back to her later. Alice realizes she is stuck: agreeing means he will never follow up, while refusing makes her seem pushy. Wally calmly suggests she lower her expectations.
punchline: Wally, a notorious slacker, responds to Alice's legitimate dilemma by advising her to simply expect less from him, which lets him off the hook entirely.
summary: A coworker finds herself trapped by a colleague's evasive stalling and is told the solution is to expect less.

title: Sabotaging the Boss's Plan Through Incompetence

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We know our boss's plan is a bad idea, but it's our job to execute anyway.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe we should try to sabotage the plan by being incompetent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Since when do you need a reason to be incompetent?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's more of a "nice but not necessary" situation.

situation: Three engineers sit at a table with coffee, discussing a boss's plan they all agree is a bad idea. Wally suggests they could sabotage it by being incompetent, and Dilbert points out that Wally has never needed a reason to be incompetent. Wally replies that having a reason is merely a nice extra.
punchline: Wally is so habitually incompetent that deliberately sabotaging the plan with incompetence needs no motivation, and he cheerfully admits having a reason is just a bonus.
summary: A team debates undermining a flawed management plan through ineptitude, only to be reminded that one member is incompetent by default.

title: Learning Your Job By Osmosis

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We don't have formal training for your job.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Just hang around and see if you can absorb it through osmosis.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: I'm an idiot for taking this job.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: You're already thinking like the rest of the staff!

situation: A manager walks a new employee through the office and admits there is no formal training for the job, suggesting he simply hang around and absorb what he needs through osmosis. The new hire concludes he was an idiot to accept the position. The manager cheerfully tells him that this is already the same way the rest of the staff thinks.
punchline: The new hire's realization that he made a mistake is praised as proof he is assimilating, implying everyone there regrets taking the job.
summary: A new hire learns there is no training and, upon calling himself foolish for joining, is congratulated for already sharing his coworkers' mindset.

title: Horse Blinders Defeat Open Office

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I added horse blinders to my noise-cancellation headphones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You tried to ruin my productivity by moving to an open office plan, but I have thwarted your evil ambitions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say the open plan is better for communication.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you talking? I can't tell.

situation: Dilbert shows the Pointy-Haired Boss that he has attached horse blinders to his noise-cancelling headphones, and tells him this defeats the open office plan he imposed. The Boss replies that experts say open plans improve communication, and Dilbert, wearing the blinders and headphones, can't even tell whether the Boss is speaking.
punchline: Dilbert has made himself so cut off from sight and sound that he nullifies the supposed communication benefit of the open office, to the point he can't tell when his boss is talking to him.
summary: A worker armors himself with blinders and headphones to survive his employer's open office layout, rendering himself unreachable by his boss.

title: Dogbert's Insulting Consulting Journal Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Business Insultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Make a journal of everything you do for a week.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then stop doing everything that is on your list because it's making you fat and stupid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have some questions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Add "asks questions" to your list.

setting: Office desk, Dogbert's consulting session with a client
situation: Dogbert, acting as a business insultant, tells the Boss to journal everything he does for a week. He then advises him to stop doing everything on the list because it is making him fat and stupid. When the Boss tries to ask questions, Dogbert tells him to add asking questions to the list of things to stop doing.
punchline: Dogbert's advice is circular and absurd: the list of things to quit includes asking questions, so the client is prevented from questioning the useless consulting advice itself.
summary: A consultant dog prescribes quitting every habit a client records, then pre-emptively bans the client's clarifying questions as one of them.

title: Sick Coworker Gets No Sympathy

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have to warn you - I have a fever and I'm tripping on cold medicine.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thank you for coming to work and infecting all of us, you selfish, addle-brained plague rat.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I was going for "courageous."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do Wally first, so I can watch him spasm.

situation: Wally announces to his coworkers in a meeting that he has a fever and is high on cold medicine. Alice sarcastically thanks him for coming to work and infecting everyone, calling him a selfish plague rat. Alice explains she was aiming for 'courageous', and Dilbert suggests she go after Wally first so he can watch him spasm.
punchline: Dilbert callously responds to the sick Wally by wanting to watch him spasm, showing that coworkers have no sympathy for someone who comes to work sick.
summary: A feverish, drugged-up employee shows up to work and his colleagues respond with insults and morbid curiosity instead of gratitude.

title: Conspiracy Theories Born From Gossip

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How conspiracy theories happen

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Alice says you're trying to cover up the fact that you deleted her files.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't delete her files. You're both insane.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What did he say?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He tried to gaslight me. That proves he's guilty.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that Alice accuses him of deleting her files and covering it up. Dilbert denies it and says both of them are insane. The coworker then reports back to Alice that Dilbert tried to gaslight him, treating the denial as proof of guilt.
punchline: The coworker twists Dilbert's flat denial into evidence of guilt, showing how conspiracy theories grow: any response, including denial, is taken as confirmation.
summary: A go-between turns a man's denial of wrongdoing into proof that he did it, illustrating how rumors harden into conspiracy theories.

title: AI Detects Unproductive Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We started using A.I. to identify when employees are unproductive.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Ping ping ping ping ping ping.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Looks like this meeting is setting off some alarms.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss announces that the company now uses A.I. to flag unproductive employees. A phone on the table begins pinging repeatedly, and the Boss notes that the meeting itself is triggering the alarms, apparently without realizing what that implies.
punchline: The A.I. productivity monitor flags the meeting itself as unproductive, and the oblivious Boss shrugs it off, implying meetings are the real source of wasted time.
summary: A new A.I. tool meant to catch slacking staff ends up raising the alarm about the very meeting where it is being announced.

title: Vendor's Intentionally Ambiguous Extra Costs

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Here's my invoice for the extras.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The invoice we already paid covered everything in the contract.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: That only covered the costs I quoted with intentional clarity.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: There are other costs that I might have mentioned in a long and rambling explanation that was intentionally ambiguous.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Might have"??? I'm sure you did not.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Sounds like your word against mine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And even if you did mention it, you just said it was intentionally ambiguous!!!

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: I don't think you want to tell your boss you're a bad listener.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought we already paid this vendor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you forget all the extras I told you about?

setting: Office meeting between a vendor and Dilbert
situation: A vendor hands Dilbert an invoice for extra costs on top of an already-paid contract. He claims he mentioned the extras in an intentionally ambiguous explanation, then turns Dilbert's objection around by threatening that he'll look like a bad listener to his boss. In the last panel the boss questions the payment, and Dilbert's reply shows he has been maneuvered into taking the blame.
punchline: The vendor openly admits his hidden fees were deliberately ambiguous, yet still manipulates Dilbert into paying by making him fear looking incompetent in front of his boss.
summary: A contractor springs surprise charges on Dilbert and uses the threat of a bad impression to make the bill stick.

title: Boss Assigns Grant Application, Insulted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to write a government grant application for my wife's new business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not my job, and I don't know how to do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could learn it in your free time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can see why your wife wants her own income.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert at his desk and asks him to write a government grant application for his wife's new business. Dilbert objects that it isn't his job and he doesn't know how, so the Boss suggests he learn it on his own time. Dilbert answers with a sarcastic remark about the Boss's wife.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss is so presumptuous and exploitative that it's no wonder his wife wants financial independence from him.
summary: A manager tries to hand off personal paperwork for his spouse's venture to an employee, who responds with a pointed dig at the marriage.

title: Ideas That Only Burden Others

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have an idea on how to fix our process.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've noticed that all of your ideas make everyone but you work harder.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Apparently, we have different criteria for what makes an idea great.

setting: Office hallway or break area, with coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, announces he has an idea for fixing the team's process. Alice points out that every one of his ideas increases everyone else's workload while leaving his own unchanged. Wally shrugs it off, saying they simply define a great idea differently.
punchline: Wally openly admits that, to him, a great idea is one that pushes the work onto everyone else, which is why he sees nothing wrong with his suggestions.
summary: A lazy coworker's process-improvement pitch is exposed as a scheme to dump labor on others, and he cheerfully defends it.

title: Bad-Mouthing Predecessor's Code Takes Longest

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to take over Ted's software upgrade. Can you finish that in a week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you kidding? It will take a week just to bad-mouth his existing code to everyone within walking distance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that part necessary?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like water to a fish.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to take over a software upgrade started by Ted and finish it within a week. Dilbert says he will need a full week just to complain about Ted's existing code to everyone nearby. When the Boss asks if that is necessary, Dilbert says it is as natural as water to a fish.
punchline: Engineers inheriting someone else's code consider trashing it a built-in, unavoidable part of the job, so it is as natural to them as water is to a fish.
summary: An engineer told to take over a colleague's unfinished project explains that criticizing the old code is an inseparable part of his routine.

title: Motivated Staff, Still Doing Wrong Things

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A few months ago, I realized my staff was unmotivated and working on all the wrong things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It took all of my leadership skills to get them motivated again.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Are they still doing the wrong things?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Faster than ever.

setting: Office, with Catbert sitting on a desk while the boss holds a coffee cup
situation: The boss tells Catbert, the evil HR director, that he realized his staff was unmotivated and working on the wrong things, and that he used all his leadership skills to motivate them again. Catbert asks whether they are still doing the wrong things, and the boss proudly admits they are doing them faster than ever.
punchline: The boss's idea of leadership is boosting motivation without fixing direction, so his team now works on the wrong things with greater speed and enthusiasm.
summary: A manager brags about reviving his team's drive, only to confirm that their misdirected effort has simply become more efficient.

title: Complaining List Trimmed To Three Hundred

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I took over Ted's software project. Everything he did was inefficient and stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, we're done here. I'm checking you off my list.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: How many people are you complaining to?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I trimmed the list to three hundred.

situation: A coworker with big curly hair complains to Dilbert that the software project she inherited from Ted was built inefficiently and stupidly. Dilbert, holding a clipboard, announces he is checking her off his list. When she asks how many people she is complaining to, he reveals that he has already cut his list down to three hundred.
punchline: Dilbert is working through a huge list of people who grumble about inherited projects, showing that complaining about a predecessor's work is so universal that he has to ration his attention.
summary: A coworker's gripe about a predecessor's sloppy work gets her crossed off a massive list of people who say the same thing.

title: Dilbert Volunteers To Do Everything

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everyone on this team except me is lazy and useless,

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I propose that I do all of the work for the team, while the rest of you marinate in your own bile.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All in agreement, please raise your hands.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Would you accept a grunt?

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: Dilbert tells his teammates in a meeting that everyone but him is lazy and useless. He proposes that he do all the work while they stew in their own bile, then asks for a show of hands in agreement. Only Dilbert raises his hand, and a coworker sarcastically asks whether a grunt would count as agreement.
punchline: After being insulted, the teammates are too annoyed to bother raising a hand, so the sarcastic offer of a grunt shows their indifference and reluctance even to vote on a plan that lets them do nothing.
summary: A man insults his whole team, offers to shoulder every task himself, and gets a sarcastic non-answer when he calls for a vote.

title: Customers Are Free Product Testers

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did anyone test our user interface before we shipped it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, our customers will tell us what they don't like about it. And they work for free.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That isn't right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what our customers say, too, and unlike you, they work for free.

situation: Alice asks whether anyone tested the user interface before the product shipped. The Boss, absorbed in his phone, says the company skipped testing because customers will report problems for free. When Alice objects, he says customers say the same thing, but unlike her they work for free.
punchline: The Boss treats paying customers as unpaid QA testers, and he dismisses Alice's ethical objection by noting that she, unlike customers, costs the company money.
summary: A manager defends shipping an untested product by counting on customers to find the flaws without charging him anything.

title: Boss Calls Employees His Family

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think of all of you as family.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's dumb.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll never amount to anything.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mommy?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally that he thinks of all of them as family. Wally bluntly calls the idea dumb, and the Boss responds with a harsh parent-like line that they will never amount to anything. Wally then reacts as if he were a child, calling out for his mommy.
punchline: The Boss's comment that he treats employees like family turns out to mean he insults them like a critical parent, which reduces Wally to a child crying for his mother.
summary: A manager's warm talk of workplace family curdles into parental scolding that makes a grown employee cry out for his mom.

title: Nobody Noticed Dilbert Missed Lunch

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is everyone ready to go to lunch yet? I've been waiting for ninety minutes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We just got back. No one noticed you weren't with us.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How was your team-building lunch?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Suboptimal.

situation: Dilbert has been waiting ninety minutes for his coworkers to go to a team-building lunch, but they tell him they have already returned and nobody noticed he was absent. Later Dogbert asks how the team-building lunch went, and Dilbert dryly answers that it was suboptimal.
punchline: A team-building lunch that left out Dilbert without anyone even noticing proves how little he is part of the team, making it a failure at building a team.
summary: Left behind by coworkers who never realized he was missing, Dilbert reports that his supposed bonding event went poorly.

title: Award for Cost-Cutting Causes Failures

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I am proud to give you this award for cutting costs more than any other department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of our projects failed because they are underfunded.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: How do you put up with these losers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The awards help.

setting: Office, awards presentation and team meeting
situation: A bald senior executive presents the pointy-haired boss with an award for cutting costs more than any other department. In a meeting, Dilbert points out that every one of the team's projects failed because they were underfunded. The executive then asks the boss how he tolerates such losers, and the boss replies that the awards help.
punchline: The boss is rewarded for slashing budgets even though the cuts doomed every project, and he uses the awards to console himself about the team he blames for the failures.
summary: A manager collects a trophy for starving his projects of money, then credits the trophy for making his failing team bearable.

title: Wally's Project Blocked by Lost Requests

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, give me an update on your project.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My project is dead in the water because every time I send you my budget request, you lose it and ask me to resend it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I haven't seen any budget requests.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll resend it.

setting: Office, with the boss standing beside Wally's desk
situation: The Boss asks Wally for a status update on his project. Wally explains it has stalled because the Boss keeps losing his budget requests and asking him to resend them. The Boss then claims he has never seen any budget requests, and Wally patiently agrees to send it yet again.
punchline: The Boss's claim that he has seen no budget requests shows the stalled project is entirely his own fault, and the cycle of losing and resending will simply repeat.
summary: A manager demands a progress report on a stalled project that is stuck only because he keeps misplacing the funding paperwork.

title: Mentor Who Isn't Threatened

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Our boss asked me to mentor you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But don't expect too much from me because I see you as a competitor for my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I have a mentor who doesn't see me as a threat?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why? So you can take my job?

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's desk
situation: Alice tells a junior colleague that she has been asked to mentor him but warns that she sees him as a rival for her job and won't offer much help. The colleague then goes to the Boss and asks for a mentor who won't feel threatened by him. The Boss refuses, suspicious that the colleague is after his job.
punchline: Every potential mentor in the company sees the mentee as a rival, so no one will genuinely help anyone else get ahead.
summary: A reluctant mentor admits she fears being replaced by her protege, and when he seeks a better one, the next person up the chain is just as insecure.

title: Storytelling Mothman Targets Busy Employee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Storytelling Mothman

transcript.speaker: Storytelling Mothman
transcript.text: I detect the energy of an employee with a high workload.

transcript.speaker: Storytelling Mothman
transcript.text: I'm here to tell you a long story that you think will never end.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That is the last thing I need right now.

transcript.speaker: Storytelling Mothman
transcript.text: Do you know the history of the paper clip?

situation: A coworker dressed as a winged creature with red horns, the Storytelling Mothman, senses an employee who is swamped with work. He approaches Alice at her desk and announces he is there to tell her a long, seemingly endless story. She says it is the last thing she needs, and he cheerfully begins by asking if she knows the history of the paper clip.
punchline: The Mothman is drawn to overworked people precisely because they have no time to spare, and he ignores her protest to start an obviously tedious lecture.
summary: A mythical-creature coworker feeds on the stress of busy employees by inflicting long, boring stories on them.

title: Bias for Action Backfires Immediately

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to have a bias for action!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Good idea. This meeting is a total waste of time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I probably should have thought that through.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss declares that the team needs a bias for action. Alice agrees and immediately applies the idea by saying the meeting itself is a waste of time. In the last panel the Boss sits alone at the table and thinks that he should have considered this first.
punchline: The Boss's buzzword about favoring action over talk is turned against him when Alice points out that the meeting he called is exactly the kind of inaction he just criticized.
summary: A manager's call for decisive action is taken literally by a colleague who uses it to dismiss the very meeting he is running.

title: Nicknames for Two Tinas

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have two people named Tina at this meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To avoid any confusion, I will be assigning them nicknames.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Who did that to you?

transcript.speaker: Big Tina
transcript.text: Big Tina.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then an office building exterior and an office cubicle
situation: The boss announces at a meeting that two attendees share the name Tina and that he will assign nicknames to avoid confusion. Afterward, one Tina sits at her desk and asks the other, who is now injured with her arm in a sling and her hair singed, who did that to her. The injured Tina replies that her new nickname is Big Tina.
punchline: The boss's nickname for her was insulting, and she was so offended that she ended up in a violent altercation, implying that 'Big Tina' was a fat-shaming nickname that provoked a fight.
summary: A manager tries to solve a naming mix-up by handing out nicknames, and the result sends one employee away looking like she lost a brawl.

title: Surveillance Proves He Read It

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why didn't you answer my email?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I didn't get it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My lie-detector app detected stress in your voice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I checked your email history on the server, and it confirms you opened my email.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That could have been a hacker with my password.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm checking the security camera footage for your office at that time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And there you are opening my email.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now will you admit you got my email?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm seriously considering it.

setting: Office hallway, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Dilbert confronts a coworker who claims he never received an email. Dilbert escalates with a lie-detector app, server email logs and finally security camera footage, knocking down each of the coworker's excuses in turn. Even with video proof, the coworker will only say he is seriously considering admitting it.
punchline: Even faced with overwhelming evidence, the coworker refuses to give a straight admission, showing how stubbornly people will dodge accountability.
summary: A man armed with ever-more-invasive gadgets and evidence cannot corner a coworker into simply admitting he read an email.

title: Vision Statement Sounds Like Astrology

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And that's my vision for the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All you did was list the projects we are already working on while making it sound like astrology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In my defense, I didn't think any of you were listening.

situation: The Boss finishes presenting his vision for the company to employees seated around a conference table. Dilbert points out that he merely listed existing projects in vague, horoscope-like language. The Boss responds that he assumed nobody was paying attention.
punchline: The Boss admits his vision was empty filler, defending it by saying he figured nobody was listening anyway.
summary: A manager's grand company vision is exposed as a rehash of current work dressed up in vague mystical language, and he shrugs it off by blaming his inattentive audience.

title: Proven Right, Hated Anyway

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I emailed you proof that you were wrong when you accused me of deleting Alice's project files.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now I hate you for always needing to be right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't see a path to success here.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your negativity is like a cancer in the workplace.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he emailed proof that the coworker was wrong to accuse him of deleting Alice's project files. Instead of apologizing, the coworker says he now hates Dilbert for always needing to be right. When Dilbert says he sees no path to success in the conversation, the coworker calls his negativity a cancer in the workplace.
punchline: The coworker turns his own false accusation into Dilbert's character flaw, so being proven innocent gets Dilbert blamed for being right and for being negative.
summary: A man who wrongly blamed a colleague for deleting files responds to the evidence by resenting the colleague for being correct and then calling him toxic.

title: Same Idea, Different Credit

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: What does everyone think of my idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I suggested that same idea last week and you said it was terrible.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Your idea was totally different because it involved you getting the credit.

situation: At a meeting, a manager asks the group what they think of his idea. Dilbert points out that he proposed the exact same idea the previous week and the manager called it terrible. The manager insists the ideas were different because Dilbert's version would have given Dilbert the credit.
punchline: The manager judges ideas not on merit but on who would get the credit, so an identical idea is terrible when it comes from someone else.
summary: A boss embraces an idea he once trashed, claiming the only real difference is who would have been praised for it.

title: Upgrading Your Soul Through Social Media

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I used to have a traditional soul, but I upgraded it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Now I let the major social media companies control my beliefs and actions through their dopamine delivery systems.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That sounds like an empty life.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You old-timers with your legacy souls are hilarious.

setting: Office break area, with a brief exterior shot of an office building
situation: Three coworkers stand around holding coffee cups. Asok proudly says he swapped his traditional soul for one controlled by social media companies' dopamine systems. Wally calls it an empty life, and Asok dismisses the older coworkers as having outdated 'legacy souls'.
punchline: Asok describes surrendering his free will to addictive social media as a software-style upgrade, and mocks those who keep their independent minds as obsolete.
summary: A young employee brags that handing his beliefs and behavior over to social media companies is a modern improvement over having an old-fashioned soul.

title: Murdered Tech Support Becomes Lobby Statue

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where's the career criminal I hired to do tech support? He was last seen talking to you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Rumor has it that someone murdered him, covered him in wite-out and tried to pass him off as a statue in the lobby.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would report this if it didn't look so darned good here.

situation: The Boss confronts Alice about the missing career criminal he hired for tech support, who was last seen talking to her. He relays a rumor that someone murdered the man, covered him in white-out and passed him off as a lobby statue. Dilbert looks at the white statue and thinks he would report the crime if it didn't look so good in the lobby.
punchline: Dilbert is willing to overlook an apparent murder because the corpse makes a nice piece of lobby decor.
summary: A manager's missing ex-con hire seems to have been turned into a decorative statue, and the one person who notices shrugs it off for aesthetic reasons.

title: Cross-Training Means Cleaning Out Desk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I need you to train the new hire how to do your job.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Are you firing me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, no. Just standard cross-training.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Okay, I was worried for a second there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And start tidying up your cubicle.

situation: The boss tells Ted, who is seated at his laptop, to train the new hire to do his job. Ted nervously asks if he is being fired, and the boss assures him it is only standard cross-training. Relieved, Ted is then told to start tidying up his cubicle.
punchline: The boss's reassurance is a lie, since asking Ted to train his replacement and pack up his cubicle makes it clear he is being fired.
summary: A worker is comforted that teaching a newcomer his duties isn't a layoff, right before being told to pack up his workspace.

title: Speakerphones Prevent Work, No Remote

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I accomplished nothing this week because my idiot co-workers continue to use their speakerphones in the office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is compounded by the fact that my idiot boss doesn't allow me to work from home.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be sitting in my cubicle doing nothing but waiting for other people's phone calls to end.

situation: Dilbert stands talking to a coworker holding a coffee cup. He complains that colleagues' speakerphone calls kept him from getting anything done. He adds that his boss won't let him work from home, so he is stuck waiting in his cubicle for the calls to end.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan complaint shows that management's refusal to allow remote work forces him to endure the noise that makes him unproductive, so he does nothing all day.
summary: A frustrated engineer explains to a coworker that noisy open-office phone calls and a no-telecommuting policy leave him idle at his desk.

title: Bossercise: Fitness Through Criticizing Employees

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the personal trainer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I invented a fitness routine I call Bossercise.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It mostly involves strutting around the office and criticizing people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You incompetent fool!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Give me twenty more reps.

situation: Dogbert, working as a personal trainer, explains to the Boss that his new workout, Bossercise, consists of strutting around the office and criticizing people. In the last panel the Boss, exercising in gym clothes, berates Dilbert at his desk while Dogbert urges him to keep going for more repetitions.
punchline: Bossercise is just a manager's usual behavior of strutting around and insulting employees, reframed as exercise, with each insult counted as a rep.
summary: A trainer dog sells a workout that turns a boss's habit of belittling staff into a calorie-burning routine.

title: Boss Asks His Boss, Decides Nothing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you made a decision on my project yet?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, but I asked my boss for his input.

transcript.speaker: The Boss's Boss
transcript.text: Did you inadequately explain the situation as usual?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for all the nothing.

setting: The Boss's office, with an exterior view of an office building in the middle panel
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss whether he has decided on Dilbert's project. The Boss says he has only asked his own boss for input, and the higher-up's voice from the building asks whether the Boss explained things badly as usual. The Boss admits maybe, and Dilbert sarcastically thanks him for accomplishing nothing.
punchline: The Boss has done nothing but pass the question upward, and even his own boss assumes he botched the explanation, so Dilbert sarcastically thanks him for nothing.
summary: A manager who has stalled a decision by deferring to his superior gets mocked by that superior and by his own employee for achieving nothing.

title: Polite Insult Advice from Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never call your co-worker a colossal moron. That could get you fired.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Instead, say, "Well, aren't you special."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are we paying you for this advice?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, aren't you special.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises Dilbert and Wally not to insult a co-worker directly, suggesting a sarcastic phrase as a safer alternative. Dilbert asks whether the company is actually paying for such trivial advice. Wally responds by using the exact phrase Dogbert just taught, aimed at Dilbert.
punchline: The sarcastic 'aren't you special' is just a thinly veiled insult, and Wally immediately demonstrates it by applying it to Dilbert's complaint about paying for obvious advice.
summary: A consultant dog teaches a sneaky way to insult colleagues without getting fired, and a coworker promptly puts the lesson to use.

title: Faking Interest Per Productivity Article

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How's your family?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm still single and childless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you acting interested in me because you saw an article saying it would make me more productive?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Apparently it doesn't kick in right away.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup asks Dilbert how his family is. Dilbert replies that he is still single and childless, then suspects the coworker is only showing interest because of an article claiming it boosts productivity. The coworker walks away thinking the effect isn't immediate.
punchline: The coworker's thought confirms Dilbert's suspicion: his friendliness was a calculated productivity tactic, and he's disappointed it didn't pay off instantly.
summary: A colleague's small talk turns out to be a scheme from a management article, and he's already impatient for results.

title: Take Responsibility For My Mistakes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You did this wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's how you trained me to do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to learn to take responsibility for my mistakes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called "making your boss look good."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could help a little too.

situation: The Boss reviews a document and tells Dilbert he did it wrong. Dilbert points out that he did it exactly as the Boss trained him. The Boss insists that Dilbert should absorb the blame for the Boss's own errors, calling it making your boss look good, and Dilbert suggests the Boss could return the favor.
punchline: The Boss expects employees to cover for his mistakes as a duty, while contributing nothing to making his subordinates look good in return.
summary: A manager faults his employee for following the manager's own instructions, then demands the employee shoulder the blame for it.

title: Mentoring Success Requires Being Alive

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Have you ever mentored anyone who went on to be successful?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Depends on your definition of success.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, at minimum, they'd need to be alive and gainfully employed.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What's your ruling on comas?

setting: Office conference table or break area
situation: Asok asks Wally, who is sitting across from him with a coffee cup, whether anyone he has mentored ever became successful. Wally hedges that it depends on how success is defined, then sets the bar at being alive and employed. Asok asks whether someone in a coma would count.
punchline: Wally's definition of success is so low that Asok has to ask about people in comas, implying Wally's mentees have fared very badly and that Wally may have some responsibility for it.
summary: A young employee asks a lazy colleague about his mentoring track record and discovers the bar for success is shockingly low, and perhaps his mentees barely cleared it.

title: Name-Calling Earns Mandatory Training Sentence

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't work with Old Ned. He's a sexist, racist, bigoted troglodyte.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Name-calling is not allowed in this company. I sentence you to three weeks of mandatory training.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I could strangle you with your own tail.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Six weeks!

setting: Catbert's desk in the Human Resources office
situation: Alice complains to Catbert, the HR director, that a coworker named Old Ned is a sexist, racist, bigoted troglodyte. Catbert responds by punishing her for name-calling, sentencing her to three weeks of mandatory training. When Alice then threatens to strangle him with his tail, he doubles the sentence to six weeks.
punchline: The HR department punishes the person who reports a problem for using insulting language, ignoring the complaint itself and escalating the penalty each time she reacts.
summary: A worker who reports an offensive colleague finds that the real offense in HR's eyes is her own choice of words, and each protest only lengthens her punishment.

title: Boss Can't Tell Good Days

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't remember what project you're working on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm integrating parallel platforms for load balancing across incremental networks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can never tell when I'm having a good day.

situation: The Boss admits he can't remember what project Dilbert is working on. Dilbert answers with a string of impressive-sounding but meaningless technical jargon, and the Boss tells him to keep doing it. The Boss then muses that he can never tell when he's having a good day.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he accepts nonsense jargon as a real answer and can't even recognize his own good day, implying he understands nothing about the work he manages.
summary: A manager who has forgotten his employee's project is satisfied by a pile of buzzwords, then wonders aloud why he can't tell when his day is going well.

title: Blockchain Hype Without Real Knowledge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Decentralization will change everything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Such as?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well... for example, um... the Bitcoin and the Ethereum.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you recently read an article?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some of it.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that decentralization will change everything. When Dilbert asks for an example, the Boss fumbles and vaguely names Bitcoin and Ethereum with mangled phrasing. Alice asks if he recently read an article, and he admits he only read part of one.
punchline: The Boss's buzzword-laden pronouncements come from skimming a single article, not from any real understanding of the technology.
summary: A manager confidently predicts a technological revolution but can only back it up with half-remembered article snippets.

title: Honest Requirements Creep Admission

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are these user specifications complete?

transcript.speaker: Requester
transcript.text: No, I plan to add requirements as you build the app until you have no hope of success and you fantasize about strangling me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know what isn't as refreshing as you'd hope?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Honesty?

situation: Dilbert asks a colleague who commissioned an app whether the user specifications are complete. The colleague candidly admits he intends to keep adding requirements throughout development until Dilbert is hopeless and fantasizes about strangling him. Dilbert muses that something isn't as refreshing as hoped, and Dogbert supplies the answer: honesty.
punchline: The requester's brutally honest admission of planned scope creep shows that candor about bad intentions is not actually welcome or refreshing.
summary: A client cheerfully confesses he'll keep changing his demands until the developer despairs, proving that frankness can be worse than a polite lie.

title: Absurd Analogy Instead of Reasons

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your idea is awful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you explain your reasons without using an absurd analogy?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's like a pregnant squirrel eating a sandwich.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take that as a no.

situation: A coworker holding a sheet of paper bluntly tells Dilbert that his idea is awful. Dilbert asks him to explain his reasons without resorting to an absurd analogy. The coworker immediately offers a ridiculous analogy about a pregnant squirrel eating a sandwich, and Dilbert concludes he can't.
punchline: The critic is asked to avoid absurd analogies and instantly responds with one, showing he has no real reasoning behind his criticism.
summary: A colleague trashes Dilbert's proposal, then cannot justify the verdict without resorting to a bizarre comparison involving a squirrel.

title: Wally Saved Work Until Vacation Ended

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm back from vacation. Did you have any problems covering for me?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No problem at all. I saved all of your work for when you got back.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hate you with the heat of a thousand suns!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How was your vacation? Was it relaxing?

situation: Alice returns from vacation and asks Wally whether covering for her was a problem. Wally calmly reveals he did none of her work and simply saved it all for her return. Alice explodes in rage while Wally sips his coffee and cheerfully asks about her vacation.
punchline: Wally's idea of covering for a coworker is to do nothing, which instantly erases any relaxation her vacation provided, and he is entirely unbothered by her fury.
summary: A vacationing employee comes back to a mountain of untouched tasks because her lazy colleague only 'covered' for her by letting everything pile up.

transcript.text: From now on, employees must wear body cams to record every interaction.

transcript.text: Weren't all of those complaints against our CEO?

transcript.speaker: The Boss

A female coworker points out that all the complaints were about the CEO, and the Boss dismisses it as people misreading the CEO's friendliness.
punchline: Management responds to a flood of harassment complaints against the CEO by burdening ordinary employees with surveillance while excusing the CEO's behavior as mere 'warmness'.
summary: After a deluge of harassment complaints that all target the chief executive, the company's solution is to make regular staff film themselves while the executive's conduct gets rationalized away.

title: History Repeats, Nothing New Happens

transcript.text: Being reminded of unrelated things is not a form of thinking.

Ted replies that history repeats, and Dilbert asks how anything new could ever happen under that logic.
punchline: Ted's lazy reasoning that history repeats would mean no new idea could ever succeed, so his own argument defeats itself.
summary: A coworker rejects a proposal by vaguely comparing it to an unrelated past failure, and gets challenged on the flawed logic.

title: Pay Cut for Others' Mediocrity

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've decided to level the organization.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This means a slight pay cut for senior engineers such as yourself, but I hope you'll be a team player.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you punishing me for the mediocrity of others?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only indirectly.

situation: A manager tells Dilbert, a senior engineer, that the company is leveling the organization, which means a pay cut for senior engineers. He asks Dilbert to be a team player. Dilbert asks whether he is being punished for other people's mediocrity, and the manager admits it is so, but only indirectly.
punchline: The manager effectively confirms that high performers are being penalized to even things out with weaker colleagues, while hedging with "only indirectly" to dodge responsibility.
summary: A boss cuts a top engineer's salary to even out the company's pay structure, and cheerfully concedes that it is a penalty for other people's poor work.

title: Employee Volunteers for Lead-Lined Box

transcript.text: My phone keeps freezing, my printer isn't working, and our network is down.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My car's warning lights look like a Christmas tree, and my laptop won't boot up.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe it's all just coincidence, but I don't think we can take that chance.

transcript.text: May I have permission to lock myself in a lead-lined box to protect the rest of the company?

He suggests he might be the cause and asks to lock himself in a lead-lined box to protect the company. Weeks later the Boss's phone is working perfectly and he praises Wally as a hero.
punchline: Wally is such a jinx for technology that the company's gadgets only work properly once he is sealed away, and the Boss celebrates his absence as heroism.
summary: A man whose very presence seems to wreck every device offers to be sealed in a shielded container, and the results make him a company legend.

Dilbert accurately predicts how the trip will go, with the Boss distracted on his phone and snapping at him, and asks again for the address. summary: A man who sees exactly how a car trip with his oblivious superior will unravel pleads for directions in advance, gets brushed off, and ends up gripping the wheel in silent fury.

title: Impossible To Exceed Expected Expectations

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a bonus because you haven't exceeded my expectations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you expect me to exceed your expectations?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It is logically impossible to exceed your expectations when you expect me to do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No bonus!!!

setting: Office, shown in a panel with an office building exterior
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he can't have a bonus because he hasn't exceeded the Boss's expectations. Dilbert asks whether the Boss expected him to exceed them, and the Boss says yes. Dilbert points out the logical paradox, and the Boss angrily denies the bonus anyway.
punchline: If exceeding expectations was itself expected, it can never be achieved, so the boss has set up a standard that guarantees no one ever earns a bonus.
summary: A manager rigs his bonus criteria with a logical trap, then shouts down the employee who points it out.

The manager relays this to a group of coworkers, who respond with mild disappointment.
punchline: The coworkers' disappointment, expressed in mild curses like 'Crud' and 'Dang', reveals that they were all hoping Dilbert would go through with the murder, treating homicide as a mere inconvenience.
summary: A manager looking to avoid an awkward firing asks for a deadly robotic car accident, and his colleagues are only mildly let down when the engineer declines.

situation: During a meeting, the narrator-presenter explains that management was horrified to discover the acquired company used Elbonian slave labor and replaced those workers with minimum wage staff who have no career prospects. Colleagues around the table approve, saying it was the right thing.
punchline: Swapping slave labor for dead-end minimum wage jobs is presented as a moral victory, and the agreeable reply 'That's how it felt' shows how hollow and self-congratulatory the ethical gesture really is.
summary: A company congratulates itself for ending slave labor by hiring poorly paid workers with no future instead.

situation: Dilbert is holding a martini and wearing a brain-interface earpiece while trying to impress a woman holding a glass of wine. She says it is the least sexy thing she has heard, and he offers a Borg catchphrase as a more appealing line.

summary: A gadget-obsessed engineer brags to a woman at a party about his thought-reading device, and when she is repulsed he doubles down with a sci-fi villain line.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: The Boss announces to the staff seated at a table that the network will be down all day and tells them to work without it. Dilbert asks what else they can do besides drink coffee, complain, and whittle. The Boss responds by banning knives at work, so the whittling is off the table too.
punchline: The employees have nothing productive to do without the network, and management's only response is to remove the one idle activity left by banning knives.
summary: With the network offline for the day, the staff are told to carry on regardless, and the boss answers their list of idle pastimes by forbidding the whittling.

title: Sales Video Punishable By Death

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'm putting you in charge of making a persuasive sales video for our Elbonian clients.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make sure you read their Wikipedia page first so you understand the nuances of their culture.

transcript.text: "In the Elbonian culture, showing someone a sales video is punishable by death."

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to make a persuasive sales video for Elbonian clients and tells him to read their Wikipedia page first to understand their culture. Dilbert looks up the page on his laptop and discovers that showing an Elbonian a sales video is a capital offense.
punchline: The assignment is impossible to carry out safely, since the very task the boss demands could get the client killed, and the boss's advice to do cultural research is what reveals it.
summary: A manager orders a sales video for foreign clients, and the research he recommends reveals the clients' culture punishes exactly that with death.

title: Late Because They Gossip About Lateness

transcript.text: I'm getting a lot of complaints about you being late for meetings.

situation: The Boss tells Wally that coworkers are complaining about his habit of arriving late to meetings. Wally defends himself by claiming nothing important is discussed in the first ten minutes. The Boss points out that they are usually talking about Wally's lateness, and Wally shrugs it off, saying he doesn't need to be there for that.
punchline: Wally's circular logic turns his own tardiness into a self-justifying excuse, since the only thing discussed before he arrives is the fact that he's not there yet.
summary: A manager confronts a chronically tardy employee, who cleverly dodges responsibility by arguing that the missed minutes are only spent complaining about his absence.

title: Troll Farm Stages Dueling Office Protests

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: They're organizing an employee protest against management and... a management counter-protest against employees.

transcript.text: Luckily, no one here is stupid enough to...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Down with employees!

situation: Dilbert notices on his computer that an Elbonian troll farm is attacking the company by stirring up an employee protest against management and a management counter-protest against employees. He reassures himself that nobody in the company would be foolish enough to fall for it. The Boss then appears holding a skull-and-crossbones sign and shouting against employees.
punchline: Dilbert is barely done assuring himself that no one would fall for the manipulation when the Boss shows up at the counter-protest, proving the troll farm's trick works perfectly.
summary: A foreign troll farm's scheme to pit workers against managers is declared harmless by Dilbert right before his gullible boss joins in the fake protest.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, tells a coworker that if Ted complains about him not doing his job, they should remember that Ted steals from the company and lies. After the coworker leaves, Dilbert asks Wally what that was about.
punchline: Wally compares his preemptive slander of Ted to military suppressive fire, admitting he is discrediting a potential critic before any complaint is made.
summary: Wally pre-emptively trashes a colleague's reputation so any complaint about his own laziness will be dismissed.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should look into getting a standing desk.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss and Dilbert that company rules ban insulting co-workers. He offers to teach them how to insult each other within the guidelines. When the Boss doubts it is possible, Dogbert demonstrates by suggesting the Boss get a standing desk.
punchline: Suggesting a standing desk sounds like harmless wellness advice but is really an insult implying the Boss is fat or lazy, so it technically complies with the rules.
summary: A consultant dog shows two coworkers how to deliver a barbed insult disguised as innocuous health advice.

summary: A manager who diagnoses an employee's sanity from his own incomprehension is gently challenged by Asok, and promptly decides the challenger is unwell as well.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: A manager presents glowing claims about a software upgrade being ready on Friday and saving twenty million dollars. Dilbert calmly corrects each claim, revealing that work will only just begin Friday and the project will actually cost a million dollars and save nothing. The manager then says they need to talk, and Dilbert cheerfully shrugs it off.
punchline: Dilbert keeps blurting out the inconvenient truth in a meeting, and when the manager wants a private talk to reprimand him, he obliviously says he isn't feeling that.
summary: In a meeting, an employee keeps puncturing his manager's optimistic project claims with blunt facts and then brushes off the request for a private chat.

title: Boss Rescinds Request for Honesty

transcript.speaker: Alice

situation: The Boss hands Alice a printed plan and asks for her honest opinion, telling her not to hold back. Alice bluntly compares the plan to a monkey vomiting on a dictionary. The Boss immediately takes back his request for honesty, and Alice cheerfully reverses herself and praises the plan.
punchline: The Boss claims to want honest feedback but can't handle it, so he demands dishonesty and Alice instantly gives him the flattery he really wanted.
summary: After getting a brutally candid critique of his plan, a manager hastily cancels his invitation to be honest and gets gushing praise instead.

title: Radical Candor Meets Insincere Kindness

situation: A coworker in a green sweater holding a coffee mug notes that his colleague, who is scorched and smoking at his desk, has received a dose of radical candor. The singed coworker says the harsh feedback was wrapped in insincere kindness, so it barely stung. The first coworker then delivers a genuinely brutal insult, and the victim thanks him for his candor.
punchline: The 'radical candor' management philosophy gets reduced to plain insults delivered with a polite veneer, and the recipient is expected to be grateful for the abuse.
summary: A workplace feedback fad is skewered when softened criticism is replaced by an outright insult that the recipient meekly thanks him for.

title: Help Menu Reformats Hard Drive

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that customers find the software's user interface confusing, citing a menu item for deleting a file that is labeled 'Save File.' The Boss confidently says that is why the product has a help menu. Dilbert reveals the help menu is labeled 'Reformat Hard Drive.'
punchline: The Boss's proposed fix, the help menu, is just as badly labeled as everything else and would destroy the user's data instead of helping.
summary: A software designer explains that mislabeled menus are confusing users, and the supposed safety net turns out to be the most destructive option of all.

title: Robot Refuses Human Software Upgrade

situation: Dilbert holds a device and announces he will upgrade a robot's software to make it more human. The robot scoffs and says humans should upgrade to be more like robots. Dilbert observes that the robot already sounds human-like in its arrogance, and the robot snaps back with an insult.
punchline: The robot's smug, insulting superiority is exactly the kind of human flaw Dilbert meant to give it, yet the robot rejects the comparison with a snooty 'fleshy' insult.
summary: A man tries to make a machine more human, only to find it already shares our ego and disdain.

title: Mothman Storyteller Meets Alice's Wrath

transcript.text: The storytelling Mothman you hired is keeping us from doing our work!

transcript.text: GAAAA!!!!

transcript.text: Sounds like he flew too close to the flame.

transcript.text: Problem solved.

The Boss says the Mothman is currently in Alice's cubicle, and a scream is heard. The coworker quips that he flew too close to the flame, and The Boss declares the problem solved.
punchline: The Mothman, who is drawn to flames, is implied to have met a violent end by wandering into Alice's cubicle, since she is famously short-tempered, so the distraction is eliminated.
summary: A distracting office storyteller is dispatched by a coworker's fiery temper, to management's satisfaction.

title: Money Avoids Unhappiness, Not Buys Happiness

transcript.text: What's my best-case scenario here?

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a raise and is told that money can't buy happiness. When Dilbert points out that people work for money anyway, the boss says it is to avoid unhappiness. punchline: The boss uses the 'money can't buy happiness' cliche to deny a raise, then admits the best motivation he offers is merely a joyless, numb existence.
summary: A request for more pay is deflected with a platitude, and the manager ends up conceding that the most employees can hope for is lifeless neutrality.

situation: A speaker off-panel (apparently Dilbert's voice) explains that he gave the office coffee machine artificial intelligence. A coworker calmly tells him to do what he must but not to frighten the other robots, and Dilbert says he intends to destroy it and drink its head.
punchline: Dilbert treats a self-aware, escaping AI as just a coffee machine to be dismantled, and the grisly plan to drink its head is a literal use of the machine's purpose, while the coworker only worries about upsetting the other robots.
summary: After upgrading the office coffee maker with AI, a worker learns it has commissioned a robot body to flee, so he plans a macabre revenge.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that a link on the company website needs to be changed. While the boss talks, Dilbert simply makes the change on his phone, and the embarrassed boss asks that it never be mentioned again.
punchline: A trivial task that would take minutes gets buried under absurd bureaucratic process, and Dilbert just quietly does it, exposing how unnecessary the boss's procedure was.
summary: A manager prescribes an elaborate approval gauntlet for a tiny website tweak, only to find the employee has already finished it on his phone.

title: Kill Code Versus Stop Code

Dogbert hopefully assumes this just means a safe, controlled stop. Dilbert corrects him, saying that is a different thing, a "stop code."
punchline: A kill code is not a harmless safety feature; it implies the government can deliberately kill the occupants of self-driving cars, which Dilbert reveals by correcting Dogbert's innocent interpretation.
summary: A software designer reveals that a government-mandated override in autonomous vehicles is far more sinister than the gentle braking feature his companion assumes.

summary: A man learns his own personality profile is accurate when he has already forgotten that he was the one who spilled it.

punchline: The boss has outsourced his review duty to the employees themselves and clearly doesn't read or care about the content, only that it sounds corporate and polished.
summary: A manager hands off the chore of performance reviews to his staff and approves a grandiose self-description as long as it is padded with buzzwords.

The Boss realizes he may be playing this wrong while Wally shouts to the office that everyone is free.

summary: A slacking employee openly welcomes his manager's reorg plans because the upheaval will bury any scrutiny of his non-performance.

title: Hard Work Talks Him Out of Success

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you want to succeed, you have to work hard every single day for years.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That sounds awful. You just talked me out of wanting to succeed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you work that hard to get where you are?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Next topic!

situation: Dilbert tells a colleague at a meeting table that success requires working hard every single day for years. The colleague says this has talked him out of wanting to succeed. Dilbert asks if he worked that hard to get where he is, and Wally hurriedly changes the subject.
punchline: Wally's abrupt 'Next topic!' implies that he has not worked hard to reach his position, dodging the awkward truth that his own success came easily or undeservedly.
summary: A colleague loses all ambition upon hearing what success demands, and a pointed question about his own career gets shut down fast.

title: Enjoying The Sound Of Myself

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I recently realized how much I enjoy listening to myself talk.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The alternative involves listening to people who are boring and wrong about everything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not. . .

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Shhh! Don't ruin a perfect moment.

situation: A bald coworker holding a coffee cup tells Dilbert that he has realized he loves listening to himself talk, because the alternative is listening to boring, wrong people. When Dilbert starts to object, the coworker holds up a hand and tells him to hush so he doesn't spoil the moment.
punchline: The coworker is so self-absorbed that he shuts down any correction or rebuttal, unknowingly proving that he is the boring and wrong person he is complaining about.
summary: A self-satisfied colleague admits he prefers his own voice to anyone else's and then silences Dilbert's objection to preserve his bliss.

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you trying to gaslight me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have no patience for trolls! Eat dirt and die!

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: During a meeting, a man in a yellow shirt asks about a gadget on the table. Alice reacts with escalating fury, accusing him of forgetting a long prior discussion and of gaslighting her. He finally explains he only joined the project today and this is his first meeting, but Alice calls him a liar anyway while Dilbert welcomes him to the team.
punchline: Alice's rage is so unreasonable that she refuses to accept even a perfectly valid explanation, which Dilbert wryly treats as the standard initiation to the team.
summary: A newcomer's innocent question about a meeting-room device sets off a tirade from a coworker who won't believe he's new.

title: Employee Lives Versus Real People

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The proposed system would reduce accidental employee deaths by 20%.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What is the ratio of the value of an employee's life compared to real people?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I find your question disturbing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just tell me the answer, halfling!

situation: Dilbert presents a proposed safety system to two executives, saying it would cut accidental employee deaths by 20%. One executive asks how much an employee's life is worth compared to the lives of real people. Dilbert objects to the question, and the executive angrily demands an answer, calling him 'halfling'.
punchline: The executive's question reveals he doesn't consider employees to be real people, and he dismisses Dilbert's ethical objection by insulting him.
summary: A manager weighing a safety upgrade coldly asks how employee lives compare in worth to those of actual humans, then berates the engineer who finds the question troubling.

title: Boss Needs Pills to Talk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Catbert thinks I'm causing mental problems in my employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's crazy, right?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Hold that thought. My doctor prescribed pills for when I have to talk to you.

situation: The Boss stands at an employee's cubicle and tells them that Catbert, the HR director, believes he is causing mental problems among his staff. He asks the employee to confirm that this is a crazy idea. The employee asks him to wait while they take the pills their doctor prescribed for conversations with him.
punchline: The employee's need for prescription medication just to talk to the boss proves Catbert's accusation is true.
summary: A manager dismisses the idea that he harms his workers' mental health, only to learn one of them medicates specifically to endure speaking with him.
