transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why they pay me.

setting: Office cubicle area and conference room, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert an assignment due Friday. Dilbert complains it will consume all his free time and turn his life into a death march, and the Boss says that's why the company pays him. When the Boss tries to rephrase, he makes it worse by admitting he only cares about his bonus, and Dilbert calls him a heartless monster.
punchline: The Boss takes being called a cold, heartless monster as proof he is earning his management pay, since the company rewards him for exploiting employees.
summary: A manager dumps a life-consuming deadline on an employee, then cheerfully admits that callousness is exactly what his compensation rewards.

title: Which Part Of The Apology Is True

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Hackers got our customer data. Write a press release saying we are sorry and it will never happen again.

transcript.speaker: Writer
transcript.text: Is any of that true?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Part of it is.

transcript.speaker: Writer
transcript.text: Which part?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Hackers got our customer data.

situation: The boss orders a subordinate writing a press release to say the company is sorry about a customer data breach and that it will never happen again. The writer asks whether any of that is true, and the boss admits only part of it is. When asked which part, he says only the fact that hackers got the customer data is true.
punchline: The boss admits the only true fact is the breach itself, meaning the apology and the promise it will never happen again are insincere PR fiction.
summary: Told to draft a contrite statement after a security breach, an employee learns that the only honest part of the message is the admission that the company was hacked.

title: Dogbert Dumps Frozen Customers Away

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Being the owner of a cryogenic investment firm is a lot of work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So instead of keeping my customers' brains frozen, I decided to toss them in the river and hope no one notices.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The best kind of customers are the ones who can't write bad Yelp! reviews.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert on the couch and Dogbert on a side table
situation: Dogbert, who runs a cryogenic investment firm, tells Dilbert that the job is a lot of work. He explains that he got around the effort by throwing his customers' brains into the river instead of keeping them frozen. Dilbert sits quietly with a coffee while Dogbert wraps up with his reasoning.
punchline: Dogbert's fraud is justified by the fact that dead, discarded customers can never complain or leave negative online reviews.
summary: A dog entrepreneur cuts corners on brain preservation by dumping his clients in a river and celebrates that they can't post complaints.

title: Catbert Test Twice Astrology's Reliability

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All job applicants must take the Catbert personality test to see how well they will fit into our culture.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Studies show the test is twice as reliable as using astrology alone.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Astrology has zero reliability.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're not a good fit.

situation: Catbert, the human resources director, sits behind a desk and tells a job applicant that all candidates must take his personality test to assess culture fit. He boasts that the test is twice as reliable as astrology. The applicant points out that astrology has zero reliability, and Catbert promptly declares him a poor fit.
punchline: Twice zero is still zero, so the test is worthless, and Catbert punishes the applicant for pointing out the flaw in his logic.
summary: An HR cat brags about a hiring quiz that beats astrology, then rejects the candidate who notes that this is not saying much.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a negotiation trainer, is hired by the Boss to begin lessons on Monday. Dogbert casually offers a vague window of Monday to Wednesday. When the Boss objects that Monday was paid for, Dogbert claims his no-show will itself be a valuable lesson.
punchline: Dogbert reframes his unreliability and breach of the agreement as part of the training, a negotiation tactic that leaves the Boss with no leverage.
summary: A hired consultant dodges a firm start date and then spins his absence as the very education the client is buying.

situation: A new employee asks the Pointy-Haired Boss to give him a tour and introduce him to his coworkers. The boss refuses, since he'd have to admit he doesn't know most of their names. When the new hire asks if the boss at least knows his own name, the boss stalls and offers a useless guess.
punchline: The boss is so clueless about his staff that he can't name the new hire he just met, and his tentative guess that the name 'starts with a letter' is no help at all.
summary: A newcomer wants a guided office tour, but his manager is too embarrassed by his ignorance of staff names to oblige, and he fails to recall even the newcomer's.

title: Complaining About Workload Backfires

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm doing the job of three people and it isn't fair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good point. Alice is doing the job of seven people. I'll give you two of her jobs to balance it out.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So... is complaining better than hiding?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No... you were right.

situation: Asok complains to the Boss that he is doing the work of three people and it is unfair. The Boss agrees but then notes that Alice does even more, and offloads two of her jobs onto Asok to 'balance it out.' Wally, who avoids work by hiding, asks if complaining is better, and Asok admits Wally was right.
punchline: Complaining about an excessive workload only gets you more work, so Wally's strategy of hiding from management turns out to be the smarter one.
summary: An overworked employee protests his load and is rewarded with extra tasks, proving that keeping a low profile beats speaking up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert about things he supposedly said regarding the project's budget, feasibility and timeline. Dilbert, absorbed in his phone, flatly denies ever saying any of it, no matter what is put to him. The coworker mistakes this for victory and later brags to another colleague that he owned Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert wins the argument by simply denying everything while ignoring the other person for his phone, yet the coworker is so oblivious that he believes he was the one who won.
summary: By staring at his phone and denying every accusation, Dilbert leaves a coworker so flustered that the man sincerely believes he came out on top.

situation: The Boss asks Wally to write his own job description, and Wally suspects it is so a replacement can be hired. Wally types up a string of meaningless technical buzzwords and hands it over. summary: A worker defends his position by describing it in such nonsensical technobabble that nobody would dare to replace him.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to write his own performance review so the Boss can just sign it. The Boss then says he will sign it for Dilbert too and sees no reason for Dilbert to be involved. He finally instructs Dilbert to include a note about insubordination, and Dilbert calmly agrees while staring at his phone.
punchline: The Boss is so detached that he orders his employee to write a review accusing himself of insubordination, without noticing the contradiction or the irony of delegating his own management duty.
summary: A lazy manager hands off the task of writing a staff evaluation to the very employee being reviewed, then asks him to include a negative mark against himself.

situation: An interviewer tells a job candidate that the company only hires people with experience. The candidate asks how anyone is supposed to gain experience if nobody hires inexperienced people. The interviewer replies that they do hire liars, and the candidate instantly claims to have tons of experience.
punchline: The interviewer admits the company rewards dishonesty, and the candidate immediately proves he qualifies by lying about his experience.
summary: A job seeker stuck in the experience catch-22 is told that fibbing is the way in, and he promptly takes the hint.

punchline: The manager fished for a departed employee so he could safely pin his project's delay on someone who can no longer defend himself.
summary: A manager checks for a freshly fired colleague before reporting, then conveniently makes him the scapegoat for a late project.

He explains that the trick is to wrap an insult in a compliment, then demonstrates on Alice by praising her for dressing for function over appearance. Alice thanks him before starting to realize she has been insulted.
punchline: Dogbert's example compliment is really a dig at Alice's fashion sense, and she needs a moment to realize the 'compliment' was an insult.
summary: A scheming dog coaches on backhanded flattery and immediately tests it on a coworker, who takes a beat to catch on.

punchline: The manager is so easily satisfied by a bumper-sticker cliché that Dilbert can admit to bypassing permission and face no consequences, showing how little real accountability exists.
summary: Dilbert dodges blame for an unauthorized server change by quoting a bumper sticker, and his gullible manager simply agrees.

Dogbert bluntly interprets the story as proof that the co-worker is a natural leader and Dilbert is a wimp. When Dilbert says he wanted empathy, Dogbert quips that he is looking in the wrong place.

summary: A man grumbling about being bossed around by someone he tried to help gets zero comfort from his unsympathetic dog.

title: Dogbert Judges the Thermostat War

situation: Dogbert, dressed as a judge on a bench, presides over 'Temperature Court' to settle a dispute between two coworkers, one who is freezing and one who is overheated. situation: In a meeting, Alice complains that the office is so cold her hands turned to ice, while Dilbert, sweating, says it is so hot he can't concentrate. The Boss asks whether the two are even the same species, and Dilbert answers that it's a gray area because they could not mate.

summary: Two coworkers blame opposite office temperatures for their lack of productivity, prompting their boss to wonder whether they are even the same kind of creature.

title: Wi-Fi Slide Insults Boss's Wife

punchline: The Boss unintentionally confirms the insult by conceding that his wife, like the Wi-Fi, is spotty, which suggests he knows the comparison is apt.
summary: A furious boss wants a slide-deck author sacked for slighting his spouse, only to concede that the offending description fits her as well as it fits the wireless network.

title: Leading Around the Clock From Bed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll all need to work around the clock to meet the launch schedule.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be leading you every step of the way!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now, don't hate me because I can lead you while I'm home asleep. That's not my fault.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team that everyone must work around the clock to hit the launch schedule. He claims he will lead them every step of the way, then admits he can do that while he is at home asleep. Dilbert and Wally sit silently as he defends himself.
punchline: The Boss's promise of round-the-clock leadership is hollow, since he plans to sleep at home while his team works through the night, and he insists the unfairness isn't his fault.
summary: A manager demanding nonstop work from his staff cheerfully admits his leadership will happen while he is sleeping.

title: Coworkers Aren't Dumber, Just Known

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it my imagination, or are my co-workers getting dumber every day?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: They aren't getting dumber.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're just getting to know them better.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It looks the same.

situation: Dilbert stands beside a desk where Catbert sits and asks whether his coworkers are getting dumber each day. Catbert calmly explains that they are not changing at all and that Dilbert is simply learning more about them. He adds that from the outside it looks identical.
punchline: Catbert implies that Dilbert's coworkers were always this dumb, and his growing familiarity just reveals it, so the decline is an illusion.
summary: A puzzled engineer wonders if his colleagues are declining in intelligence, and a cynical cat assures him they were always like this.

title: Thorough Review Leaves Blank Pages

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I reviewed your draft and deleted the stuff that was wrong.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: These pages are blank.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You asked me to be thorough.

situation: Dilbert returns a draft document to a coworker after reviewing it and removing everything incorrect. The coworker looks at the pages and discovers they are completely empty. Dilbert calmly explains that he was just being thorough as requested.
punchline: By deleting everything that was wrong, Dilbert implies the entire draft was incorrect, delivering a deadpan insult disguised as diligent editing.
summary: A reviewer proves so exhaustive in removing errors that the author's manuscript comes back as nothing but empty sheets.

title: Insult Coworkers Using Anonymous Rumors

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never insult your co-workers directly. The company would fire you for that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Instead, say you heard a rumor but you can't divulge your source.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That feels wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Someone told me you're dating your pillow.

setting: Office, in a consulting session at a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises a young employee not to insult coworkers directly because he could be fired. He suggests instead claiming to have heard a rumor from an undisclosed source. When the employee says this feels wrong, Dogbert demonstrates by using the technique on him.
punchline: Dogbert shows how the rumor loophole works by insulting his client with a made-up rumor that he is dating his pillow, implying he is lonely and pathetic.
summary: A canine consultant teaches a tactic for slipping insults past HR and promptly tests it on his unsuspecting client.

title: Elbonia Spares Dilbert, Sentences Him to Work

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Elbonia called off its plan to kill you for your culturally offensive sales video.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They decided it was more cruel to keep you alive and working here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're monsters!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Get back in your cubicle.

setting: Office hallway and exterior of the office building
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that Elbonia has dropped its plan to kill him over a culturally offensive sales video he made. Instead, they concluded that forcing him to keep working at the company is a crueler punishment. Dilbert reacts with horror and is ordered back to his cubicle.
punchline: Dilbert's life is spared, but the punishment is worse: being made to continue working at his own miserable job, which the Elbonians consider more cruel than death.
summary: A foreign government's chosen revenge on an employee turns out to be simply making him keep his desk job.

title: Midnight Emails Won't Get You Noticed

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I keep working hard, but no one notices.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's why I send out department-wide emails at around midnight every night.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I didn't know you work at home every night.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do I need to speak slower here?

situation: Asok complains to Wally that his hard work goes unnoticed. Wally explains his own strategy: sending department-wide emails around midnight every night to look dedicated. Asok misses the point and takes it literally, assuming Wally works from home each night.
punchline: Wally's midnight emails are a fake-diligence trick to appear hard-working, and Asok's literal-minded reply leads Wally to sarcastically ask whether he needs to speak more slowly.
summary: A frustrated young employee gets a lesson in faking dedication from a colleague, but fails to grasp the trick.

title: Fired Employee Threatens With Archived Messages

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, your performance is terrible. You're fired.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you aware that every message you have ever sent using company devices is archived on a network you assigned me to maintain?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that a threat?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I also archive your web searches.

setting: Office, in front of Wally's desk
situation: The Boss tells Wally he is fired for poor performance. Wally calmly points out that he maintains the network where all of the Boss's company messages are archived. When the Boss asks if that is a threat, Wally adds that he also archives the Boss's web searches.
punchline: Wally turns his IT access into implied blackmail, and the Boss's worry shows that his messages and web searches contain things he does not want revealed.
summary: A manager tries to dismiss a lazy employee who quietly reminds him that he controls the records of the manager's digital life.

title: Defective Inspirational Poster Theory

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The inspirational poster I put in the break room isn't working.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I asked around and no one is soaring with the eagles.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Is the poster defective?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the only explanation that makes sense.

situation: The Boss complains to Catbert, the HR director, that the inspirational poster he hung in the break room has had no effect. He says he asked employees and nobody feels like they are soaring with the eagles. Catbert suggests the poster might be defective, and the Boss agrees that is the only logical explanation.
punchline: The Boss assumes a motivational poster is faulty rather than considering that posters cannot actually motivate employees or that his workers are unhappy for other reasons.
summary: A manager blames a faulty motivational poster when his staff fail to feel uplifted by it.

title: Dilbert Complains, Therapist Blames Him

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today a dozen people got angry at me because they believed I was privately thinking the opposite of what I was saying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why can't people just listen to my words???

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: Have you tried not being boring?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whenever I tell you I have one problem, I leave with two.

setting: A living room or therapy-style setting with a blue couch
situation: Dilbert stands in front of a small ghost perched on a couch and vents about a dozen people getting angry because they assumed he secretly meant the opposite of what he said. When he wonders why people can't just take his words at face value, the ghost offers the blunt suggestion that he try not being boring. Dilbert grumbles that every time he presents one problem, he walks away with two.
punchline: Seeking advice for one problem, Dilbert gets an insult from the ghost that gives him a second problem, making the 'counselor' worse than useless.
summary: After complaining that people misread his true intentions, Dilbert gets a rude diagnosis from a ghostly confidant that only adds to his troubles.

title: Stolen Idea, Monkey With Drinking Problem

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Hey! Someone stole my product idea!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To be fair, your idea would have been obvious to a monkey with a drinking problem.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But a monkey couldn't build this product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Neither can you. Let's call it a tie.

situation: Asok, holding a handheld device, complains to Dilbert that someone stole his product idea. Dilbert replies that the idea was so obvious that even a drunken monkey could have thought of it. When Asok protests that a monkey couldn't actually build the product, Dilbert points out that Asok can't build it either and declares it a tie.
punchline: Dilbert insults Asok twice over, implying his idea was trivially obvious and that he lacks the skill to build it, then dismisses the dispute as a draw.
summary: A colleague griping about idea theft gets a deadpan reality check that both his idea and his abilities are unimpressive.

title: Fine Lines Between Optimism and Death

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed there's a fine line between optimism and idiocy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's also a fine line between cynicism and realism.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just lost my will to live.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's a fine line between dead and working.

setting: Outdoors, standing on a grassy slope while holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert and Wally stand outside with their coffee cups, trading observations about fine lines between opposing concepts. Dilbert muses on optimism versus idiocy, and Wally responds with cynicism versus realism. When Dilbert admits he has lost his will to live, Wally sips his coffee and says there's a fine line between being dead and working.
punchline: Wally implies that working is practically the same as being dead, since a worker with no will to live is indistinguishable from a corpse.
summary: Two coworkers swap philosophical quips over coffee until one despairs and the other jokes that employment and death are nearly the same thing.

title: Hired for Avoiding Her Children

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you enjoy spending time with your children?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: No, they're boring and needy.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: They can't even hold a conversation. If I'm being honest, I prefer working long hours so I see less of them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Perfect. You're hired.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I mean, I love them, but I don't like them.

situation: During a job interview, the boss asks a female candidate whether she enjoys spending time with her children. She candidly says they are boring and needy and that she prefers working long hours to see less of them. The boss immediately hires her, and she awkwardly adds that she loves them but doesn't like them.
punchline: The boss treats a candidate's dislike of her own family time as the ideal qualification because it means she will gladly work endless overtime.
summary: A manager hires an applicant on the spot once she admits she would rather stay late at the office than go home to her kids.

title: Half a Potted Plant Excitement

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Something exciting happened at work today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We reconfigured the cubicles, and now I have a partial view of a potted plant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're happy about seeing half of a potted plant?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call it bringing the outdoors in.

setting: Dilbert's living room at home, with Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dilbert comes home and tells Dogbert that something exciting happened at work. It turns out the cubicles were reconfigured and he can now see part of a potted plant from his desk. Dogbert incredulously questions his excitement, and Dilbert spins it as bringing nature indoors.
punchline: Dilbert's office life is so dreary that glimpsing half of a potted plant counts as an exciting event, which he proudly reframes as bringing the outdoors in.
summary: A cubicle shuffle gives Dilbert a glimpse of a houseplant, and he treats it like a thrilling connection to nature.

title: Quitting Over Dehumanizing Workplace, Then Named

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: This workplace is dehumanizing! I can no longer work in this environment!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I refuse to allow any more assaults on my dignity.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I quit!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And your name is...?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I mean after this one.

situation: An employee storms into the boss's office, complaining that the workplace is dehumanizing and loudly announces he quits to defend his dignity. The boss calmly asks the man's name, revealing he has no idea who the employee is. The employee, stung, adds that he means no more insults after this one.
punchline: The boss's failure to even know the quitting employee's name proves the workplace really is dehumanizing, and the employee gets one more assault on his dignity right after quitting over them.
summary: A worker dramatically resigns over lost dignity only to be met with a boss who doesn't know who he is.

title: Missing Files Spark Office Conspiracy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How conspiracy theories start

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't find my spreadsheet files.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I saw Dilbert going into the server room.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That doesn't mean any. . .

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Carol said he was mad about something you said.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued. . .

situation: A woman with big curly hair complains that she can't find her spreadsheet files. A coworker holding a coffee cup points out that Dilbert was seen going into the server room. When she tries to dismiss the idea, he adds hearsay from Carol that Dilbert was angry about something she said, building a case against Dilbert.
punchline: A simple missing-file problem snowballs into an accusation against Dilbert through coincidence and secondhand gossip, showing how conspiracy theories get started.
summary: One person's misplaced files quickly turn into suspicion of a colleague as office gossip piles up circumstantial clues.

title: Fake Receipts Make Chocolate Capitalist

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm selling chocolate bars to raise money for my kid's school.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds like communism. I'm out.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll give you a fake receipt so you can expense it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now it sounds like capitalism. I'm in.

situation: A coworker holding a phone tells the Boss she is selling chocolate bars to raise money for her kid's school. The Boss waves her off, calling it communism. When she offers a fake receipt so he can expense the purchase, he immediately agrees, calling it capitalism.
punchline: The Boss only supports a charity fundraiser when he can cheat the company expense system, revealing his idea of capitalism is really expense fraud.
summary: A manager rejects a school fundraiser until he learns he can pad his expense account with a phony receipt.

title: Email Trail Proves Consistent Opinion

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green
transcript.text: You said you hated this idea last week, but now you say you like it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green
transcript.text: How do you explain your flip-flopping?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I always liked the idea. Nothing changed.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green
transcript.text: Hahaha! Nice try! You're back-pedaling because I busted you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my email trail from the first moment the idea came up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you can plainly see, I have liked the idea from the start.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green
transcript.text: Why is it so hard for you to admit you were wrong?

situation: A coworker accuses Dilbert of flip-flopping, claiming he hated an idea last week but now likes it. Dilbert denies changing his mind, and when the coworker gloats that he caught him back-pedaling, Dilbert produces an email trail proving he always supported the idea. The coworker ignores the evidence and asks why Dilbert can't admit he was wrong.
punchline: Even with documented proof he is right, Dilbert is met with a person who refuses to accept evidence and simply repeats the accusation.
summary: Dilbert shows written proof that he never changed his stance, yet his accuser dismisses it and demands an admission of error anyway.

title: Breaking the Law, Then Witnesses

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your plan doesn't sound legal. I'm not comfortable with it.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We break the law all the time. It hasn't been a problem yet.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Do you feel better now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your position on killing all witnesses?

situation: Dilbert sits across from a manager holding a paper and objects that the manager's plan seems illegal. The manager breezily replies that the company breaks the law constantly with no consequences, then asks if Dilbert feels better. Dilbert responds by asking about the company's stance on killing all witnesses.
punchline: After hearing that the company routinely breaks the law without consequence, Dilbert darkly jokes about murdering witnesses, implying the company's lawlessness could escalate to anything.
summary: A worker's legal qualms are brushed aside with a cheerful admission of habitual lawbreaking, prompting him to ask whether murder is also on the table.

title: Mentor's Cynical Success Strategy Ranking

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Can you mentor me on how to be successful?

transcript.speaker: Older Mentor
transcript.text: Your best strategy is a combination of lying and being related to rich people.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What is the second-best strategy?

transcript.speaker: Older Mentor
transcript.text: Crime is second. Winning a lottery is third.

situation: Asok, a young employee, asks an older bald coworker with glasses to mentor him on becoming successful. The mentor cynically says lying and being related to rich people is the best approach. When Asok asks for the runner-up, the mentor lists crime second and winning the lottery third.
punchline: The mentor's ranked list of success strategies implies that hard work and merit don't make the top three, and that success mostly comes from dishonesty, privilege or luck.
summary: A hopeful young worker seeks career wisdom and gets a bleak countdown of the real routes to getting ahead.

title: Blackmailing the Boss Over a Bug

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: I found a critical bug in our software that could make our product worthless in a week.

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: If you give me a huge raise, I won't tell anyone about the problem until you sell all of your company stock.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Deal!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two weeks later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why haven't I heard about the bug yet?

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: You didn't ask me if I knew how to fix it.

situation: A bald programmer in a green shirt tells the Boss he has found a critical bug that could make the product worthless. He demands a huge raise and promises to keep quiet until the Boss sells all his company stock. Two weeks later the Boss asks why nobody has reported the bug, and the programmer says the Boss never asked if he knew how to fix it.
punchline: The programmer exploited the Boss's greed and willingness to commit insider trading, then reveals he never intended to fix the bug and only technically told the truth.
summary: An employee gets a raise by delaying news of a product-killing flaw while his boss cashes out his shares, then shrugs off responsibility with a technicality.

title: One Hour, Zero Work Done

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have one hour to get some work done before my meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I can't concentrate when I'm hungry, so I need a snack.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This snack is making me thirsty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The label on this shirt is bugging me. I need to cut it off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A quick trip to the restroom and then I can get down to work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ugh. I have fifteen messages since I left my desk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now it's too close to my meeting to start a new task.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How's work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How would I know?

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and office, then his home
situation: Dilbert has one hour before a meeting and resolves to get work done, but he is derailed one small need at a time: a snack, thirst, an itchy shirt label, a restroom trip and a pile of messages. By the time he is free, it is too close to his meeting to start anything. At home, Dogbert asks how work is going and Dilbert admits he has no idea.
punchline: Dilbert spent the whole hour on trivial distractions and never did any actual work, so he has no idea how work is going.
summary: A man with a free hour before a meeting lets a chain of tiny distractions swallow all of it, leaving him with nothing to report.

title: Conspiracy Theory Built From Coincidences

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How conspiracy theories happen

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think Dilbert is trying to ruin my career.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Carol said he was mad about something I said, and he was in the server room right before I lost my files.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This morning he said he "had work to do."

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: OMG. He already started the cover-up.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: Alice tells a coworker she believes Dilbert is sabotaging her career, citing hearsay from Carol and the fact that he was in the server room before she lost her files. She adds that he said he "had work to do" that morning. The coworker eagerly escalates her suspicion by declaring that this is already evidence of a cover-up.
punchline: Ordinary, innocent facts, like a person doing their job in the server room, get twisted into proof of guilt once someone is already looking for a conspiracy, and a listener's eager agreement makes it worse.
summary: A paranoid coworker stitches together hearsay and routine behavior into a case against Dilbert while her colleague gleefully fuels the suspicion.

title: Hesitation Proves Dilbert Is Lying

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is it true you are telling everyone the new product road map is stupid?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Nothing remotely like that has ever happened. Here's an email in which I say how good it is.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You hesitated in your answer. That means you're lying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Read the email!!!

situation: Alice confronts Dilbert, who is seated at his laptop, about a rumor that he has been calling the new product road map stupid. Dilbert pauses briefly, denies it, and holds up his phone to show an email praising the road map. Alice dismisses the evidence, insisting that his hesitation proves he is lying, and Dilbert shouts at her to read the email.
punchline: Alice treats a brief pause as proof of guilt and refuses to look at the actual evidence that would clear him, making it impossible for Dilbert to defend himself.
summary: An accusing coworker decides a moment of hesitation is a confession and ignores the written proof held right in front of her.

title: Security Tracks Thief Into Restroom

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Someone stole my purse out of my cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No problem. We have security video nearly everywhere and we can track every phone that has our internal company app on it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That is mildly disturbing.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Here's a live feed of the perp in the third stall of the men's restroom.

setting: Office cubicle area, beside Catbert's desk
situation: Alice reports to Catbert that her purse was stolen from her cubicle. Catbert, who handles security here, boasts about the company's pervasive security cameras and phone tracking via the internal app. When Alice says that's disturbing, Catbert cheerfully shows her a live video feed of the thief in a men's restroom stall.
punchline: Catbert's proof that the surveillance system works is a live video feed from inside a restroom stall, showing that the company's monitoring is invasive well beyond what is acceptable.
summary: A theft victim learns just how thoroughly the company watches its employees when the security cat casually shows her footage from a bathroom stall.

title: Career Criminal Handles Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know the job market is highly competitive, but was it really a good idea to hire a career criminal?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Relax. He's just doing internal tech support.

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Man
transcript.text: I'll need all of your passwords to update your software.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Have you met my fist of justice?

setting: Office meeting room and cubicle area
situation: Dilbert questions the Boss about hiring a career criminal during a competitive job market. The Boss dismisses the worry, saying the man only does internal tech support. The bearded, sunglasses-wearing man then asks Alice for all her passwords, and she threatens him with her fist.
punchline: The new hire's job requires collecting everyone's passwords, which is exactly what a career criminal would want, so Dilbert's concern is justified and Alice threatens violence.
summary: A shady new hire asking staff for their passwords proves the worry about his criminal past was warranted.

title: Monkeys Fired for Phone Play

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't feel my job is helping me reach my human potential.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We only pay you because monkeys are hard to train and robots are expensive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll just play with my phone and pretend to work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what got the monkey fired.

situation: Dilbert complains to his boss that his job isn't helping him reach his human potential. The boss bluntly replies that he is only employed because monkeys are hard to train and robots cost too much. When Dilbert threatens to just play on his phone and pretend to work, the boss notes that this is exactly what got the previous monkey fired.
punchline: The boss reveals that Dilbert is essentially a cheaper substitute for a monkey or robot, and that his threatened slacking is no better than the monkey's, which got it fired.
summary: A worker's complaint about unfulfilling work is met with a manager's insulting admission that he is merely the cheapest available option, outranking only a fired monkey.

title: Old Ned Discovers Working Women

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to work with Old Ned on this project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's a little bit old-fashioned, but don't let that get to you. He retires in six months.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've been asked to work with you.

transcript.speaker: Old Ned
transcript.text: Women have jobs now???

situation: The boss hands Alice a document and asks her to collaborate with an elderly colleague named Old Ned, warning that he is a bit old-fashioned but will retire in six months. When Alice introduces herself to Ned, he reacts with shock that women now hold jobs.
punchline: Old Ned's astonishment that women work reveals he is wildly out of touch, making the boss's 'a little bit old-fashioned' warning a huge understatement.
summary: A manager downplays a retiring coworker's outdated views, only for the man to be stunned that a woman is a colleague.

title: Alice's Sabotaging Mentor Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Alice the Mentor

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: One thing I can tell you about our boss is that he loves constructive criticism.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: I feel as if your advice is intended to make me fail because you see me as a threat to take your job.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And he loves it when you grab him by the hair and yell, "Handles!"

situation: Alice, acting as a mentor, tells a younger colleague that the boss loves constructive criticism. The mentee suspects her advice is meant to sabotage him because he could take her job. Alice doubles down by claiming the boss also loves being grabbed by the hair and yelled at with the word 'Handles!'
punchline: Alice confirms the mentee's suspicion by offering even more absurd and career-ending advice, openly sabotaging a rival she sees as a threat.
summary: A mentor feeds her protege increasingly ridiculous tips about how to behave around their boss, deliberately steering him toward disaster.

title: Ted Steals Credit, Gets Promoted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm promoting Ted for coming up with a genius idea to reduce our software expenses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was actually my idea. All Ted did was tell you it was his idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you put up with these bitter losers?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: The promotion helps.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he is promoting Ted for a clever idea to cut software costs. Dilbert objects that the idea was his and Ted merely claimed it. The Boss then asks Ted how he tolerates bitter losers like Dilbert, and Ted answers that the promotion makes it easier.
punchline: Ted openly admits he stole the credit by saying the promotion helps him ignore Dilbert's complaint, while the Boss rewards the theft and dismisses the real inventor as a sore loser.
summary: A manager rewards a coworker for an idea he took from someone else and brushes off the actual originator as merely bitter.

title: Jargon Makes Readers Feel Dumb

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project summary needs more jargon and acronyms.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The goal is to make ourselves look smart while making the readers feel dumb.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about clarity?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Clarity is not our friend on this one.

situation: A coworker holding Dilbert's project summary tells him it needs more jargon and acronyms. He explains the aim is to make the authors look smart and the readers feel dumb. When Dilbert asks about clarity, the coworker says clarity works against their purpose here.
punchline: The coworker openly admits that obscure jargon is used deliberately to impress and intimidate readers rather than to communicate, so clarity is treated as an obstacle.
summary: A colleague coaches Dilbert to bury his report in buzzwords so the authors seem brilliant and the audience feels foolish.

title: Exclamation Mark Reveals Fake Interest

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why did you send me a sarcastic email response?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then how do you explain this exclamation mark?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was pretending to be interested in what you said.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, okay. I like that.

situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert at his desk, accusing him of sending a sarcastic email reply. Dilbert denies it, so the coworker points to an exclamation mark in the message as evidence. Dilbert explains that he was only pretending to be interested, and the coworker happily accepts this.
punchline: Dilbert's excuse admits to insincere, faked enthusiasm, and the coworker is pleased by it, showing that workplace fakery is welcomed over honest sarcasm.
summary: A colleague demands to know why an email seemed sarcastic, and is perfectly content to learn the punctuation was just feigned interest.

title: The FYI Boss Redefines Leadership

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to be more of an "FYI boss."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll forward emails that already went to every employee and add a note saying, "FYI."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you call that managing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I call it leading.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a meeting table, the boss announces he will become an "FYI boss." He explains that he will forward emails everyone already received and just add "FYI" on top. Dilbert asks if that counts as managing, and the boss insists it is leading.
punchline: The boss rebrands his total lack of useful work as "leading," implying that pointless email forwarding is all management amounts to.
summary: A manager proudly plans to contribute nothing but redundant forwarded emails and dignifies this laziness with the label of leadership.

title: Wally's Valor Award For Napping

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The employee award for valor goes to Wally.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: During the false alarm, we noticed Wally was not with the other evacuees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He stayed behind to make sure everyone else got out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At least that's what he told us later.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, do you have any words of inspiration for the group?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Most of you are cowards. But imagine how good you would feel winning a non-monetary award for valor.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I ask all of you to think about how you can repay me for my selfless valor on your behalf.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you sleep through the fire alarm?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Most productive nap I've ever had.

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of the office building during an award presentation
situation: The Boss presents Wally with an employee valor award because he supposedly stayed inside during a false fire alarm to make sure everyone got out. Wally accepts by insulting his coworkers as cowards and asking them to repay him for his bravery. Afterward Dilbert asks if he actually slept through the alarm, and Wally admits it was a great nap.
punchline: Wally's 'heroism' was actually sleeping through the fire alarm, and he cheerfully exploits the award to get credit and favors from coworkers.
summary: A slacker is honored as a hero for a fire drill he simply napped through, and happily milks the glory.

title: The Frickin' Bottleneck Nickname

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I wish I had a cool nickname at work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You do. You're known as the "Frickin' Bottleneck."

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Who calls me that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bad people. I try to stop them.

setting: Office break area, with coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: Asok tells Dilbert he wishes he had a cool nickname at work. Dilbert replies that he already has one, 'the Frickin' Bottleneck.' When Asok asks who calls him that, Dilbert says bad people and claims he tries to stop them.
punchline: Dilbert pretends to defend Asok while casually confirming that the insulting nickname is common knowledge, so the supposed protection is no comfort at all.
summary: A coworker longing for a flattering nickname learns his actual office moniker is an insult about slowing everyone down.

title: Radical Candor Sends Colleagues to Therapy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new system of using "radical candor" is working out great.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been criticizing people all morning and only three of them went into therapy over it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I turn my candor to you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Die, monster!

situation: The Boss brags to Carol about his new management approach of radical candor, admitting that his criticism has already driven three employees into therapy. When he announces he will now direct his candor at Carol, she fends him off with a crucifix and calls him a monster.
punchline: The Boss proudly treats a trail of traumatized employees as a success, and Carol reacts to him as though he were a vampire or demon.
summary: A manager happily reports that his brutal honesty has only sent a few staffers to therapy, then turns on a coworker who greets him like a creature of the night.

title: Blockchain Dreams, Legacy Maintenance Reality

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to work on our blockchain project to keep my skills updated.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to be a team player and maintain our legacy systems until your technical skills become obsolete.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What kind of team is that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll be on the losing team.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss if he can work on the company's blockchain project so his skills stay current. The boss, absorbed in his phone, tells him to be a team player and keep maintaining the legacy systems until his skills are obsolete. When Dilbert asks what kind of team that is, the boss cheerfully admits it's the losing team.
punchline: The boss openly admits he is sacrificing Dilbert's career to keep old systems running, and he casually calls the assignment the losing team.
summary: A request for career-boosting new work is turned down in favor of dead-end maintenance, with the manager shamelessly acknowledging the downside.

title: Reasonable Doubt About Stolen Crypto

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I put five thousand dollars into the cryptocurrency wallet you created for me and it disappeared!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're the only other person who knew my password and private key.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's not true. I shared them with Dilbert to create reasonable doubt.

situation: The Boss confronts Wally, saying the $5,000 he put into a cryptocurrency wallet Wally created for him has vanished. He points out that Wally was the only other person who knew the password and private key. Wally casually replies that he shared them with Dilbert so there would be reasonable doubt about who took the money.
punchline: Wally essentially admits to the theft by revealing he planned ahead, deliberately dragging Dilbert in as a scapegoat to muddy the blame.
summary: A manager accuses a coworker of making his digital savings vanish, and the coworker's defense is that he pre-emptively spread the secret codes around to cast suspicion elsewhere.

title: A Blanket To Make Boss Look Good

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, always remember that a good employee makes her boss look good.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe I could toss a blanket over you when other people are around.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not talking about my physical appearance.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The blanket would also muffle the sound.

situation: The Boss lectures Alice that a good employee makes her boss look good. Alice sarcastically offers to throw a blanket over him whenever other people are around. When he protests that he wasn't talking about his appearance, she adds that the blanket would also muffle his voice.
punchline: Alice deadpans that the best way to make her boss look good is to hide him and silence him, implying his speech is as embarrassing as his looks.
summary: Told to make her manager look good, Alice proposes covering him up so nobody can see or hear him.

title: Directionally Accurate Financial Projections

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Are you confident in your financial projections?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: They're directionally accurate.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Your columns don't even add up.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Why is it so hard for you to give a compliment?

setting: Office desk or meeting table with coffee cups
situation: A manager holding a printed report asks a bald, bespectacled employee whether he is confident in his financial projections. He hedges that they are 'directionally accurate.' The manager points out the columns don't even add up, and the employee responds as if he has been denied a compliment.
punchline: The employee treats 'directionally accurate' as praiseworthy, deflecting from obviously broken math by complaining that the manager won't compliment him.
summary: An employee defends sloppy budget numbers with weaselly wording, then acts wounded when his boss notes the arithmetic doesn't even work.

title: Optimal Meeting Density Excuse

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: We've achieved optimal meeting density.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: We have so many meetings that I can avoid all of them by saying I have another meeting at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: While you're here, can you review my slide deck?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'd love to, but I have fifty slide decks ahead of you.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker boasts that there are so many meetings that he can skip any of them by claiming a scheduling conflict. His colleague then asks him to review a slide deck. He deflects with the same kind of excuse, saying he has fifty decks queued ahead of it.
punchline: The coworker who has mastered avoiding meetings with a fake conflict immediately uses a similar made-up backlog to dodge another task, showing that the excuse works for anything.
summary: A man gleefully explains how too many meetings let him dodge meetings, then uses a similarly bloated queue to avoid reviewing a colleague's presentation.

title: Offensive Sales Video For Elbonians

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my first cut at a sales video for our Elbonian market segment.

transcript.speaker: Tablet video
transcript.text: If you enjoy juggling cabbages while overdrinking, you'll love our products!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This sounds kind of racist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Inebriated cabbage-juggling is their national sport.

situation: Dilbert hands a coworker a tablet with his draft sales video aimed at the Elbonian market. The video's pitch invites viewers to juggle cabbages while overdrinking, and the coworker, Asok, points out it sounds racist. Dilbert defends it by claiming that drunken cabbage juggling really is the Elbonians' national sport.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses the charge of stereotyping by insisting the offensive stereotype is simply accurate, which is the very definition of the problem.
summary: A marketing draft built around an ethnic stereotype gets challenged, and its author defends it as plain cultural fact.

title: Dying in Your Sleep Is Good News

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The sales video you made for our Elbonian market is causing a public relations crisis.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Their government has ordered Elbonian ninjas to kill you in your sleep.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my sleep? That's the best way to die!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Stop confusing my bad news with your good news.

situation: Dilbert, carrying a coffee cup, walks with a coworker who tells him his sales video for the Elbonian market has caused a public relations crisis. The coworker adds that the Elbonian government has sent ninjas to kill him in his sleep. Dilbert cheerfully says that is the best way to die, which annoys the coworker.
punchline: Dilbert's upbeat reaction to a death threat undermines the coworker's attempt to deliver bad news, and the coworker complains that Dilbert's optimism is spoiling the delivery.
summary: A colleague warns Dilbert that assassins are coming for him over a botched video, but Dilbert sees a silver lining in the method of his demise.

title: Dilbert's Slide Deck Advice Misinterpreted

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could remove a few slides to make your deck shorter.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So you're saying I should give up on trying to be persuasive?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. I'm saying it would be more persuasive if it were shorter.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So you're saying that having zero slides would be the most persuasive of all?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. I'm saying you have more slides than you need.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So you're saying people don't need accurate information so long as they don't have lots of slides?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not saying anything like that!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did Dilbert have any suggestions?

transcript.speaker: Other Coworker
transcript.text: Just crazy ones.

situation: Dilbert gently suggests that a coworker cut a few slides from a presentation deck. The coworker keeps twisting each statement into an absurd extreme, until Dilbert is flustered and denies saying anything like it. In the last panel the coworker tells another colleague that Dilbert only had crazy suggestions.
punchline: The coworker deliberately exaggerates and misrepresents Dilbert's reasonable feedback, then blames Dilbert for the 'crazy' ideas the coworker invented.
summary: A man answers mild advice about trimming his presentation by escalating it into ridiculous claims, then complains that the adviser's ideas were nuts.

title: Troll Farm's Ineffective Nonsense Ad

transcript.text: How many views did it get?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a competitor has hired an Elbonian troll farm to damage the company's brand on social media. Dilbert checks his phone and reads out the troll farm's best attack ad, which is complete gibberish. When the Boss asks how many views it received, Dilbert says only seven, including his own.
punchline: The competitor's expensive troll farm produced an incoherent, broken-English ad that almost nobody saw, so the supposed brand attack is harmless.
summary: A feared social media smear campaign from an Elbonian troll farm turns out to be a garbled slogan seen by practically no one.

title: Become Smarter Before Asking Me

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.text: Then you won't need to ask me what to do next.

situation: A bearded coworker asks Alice what classes he should take to become an engineer. Alice, sitting at her laptop, tells him to take whatever class makes him fifty percent smarter. When he asks what comes next, she says that by then he won't need to ask her.
punchline: Alice's advice is a thinly veiled insult implying the coworker is not smart enough to figure out his own career path, and that she is tired of being asked.
summary: Alice answers a colleague's career question with a backhanded suggestion that he simply get smarter so he'll stop bothering her.

situation: The Boss talks on the phone with his doctor right next to Alice, who is already disgusted by the call. When she asks him to stop having medical conversations within earshot, he tells her to relax and then graphically describes his projectile boils and their milky contents. Alice yells that she hates him.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to reassure Alice only makes things far more disgusting, since his 'relax' explanation is a gross description of oozing boils.
summary: A boss's gross phone call with his doctor ends with a revolting description that sends his coworker into a rage.

title: Purchasing Rejected Form Over Typo

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I call that unknowable.

situation: A bald coworker in a green sweater, holding a coffee cup, complains to a colleague that purchasing rejected his request for a key system part over a form typo. He explains that he was not told for three months, so his product launch is now delayed by that amount. When asked if the part was finally ordered, he dodges the question.
punchline: The coworker blames purchasing for the delay but evades the obvious question, calling it 'unknowable', implying that he never fixed the typo or followed up and that the delay is partly his own fault.
summary: A man blames the purchasing department for a three-month launch delay, then dodges the question of whether the part was ever actually ordered.

situation: The Boss announces he is going off to do 'bossercizing,' a made-up workout routine. He explains it means walking around the office and yelling at underperforming employees. When a coworker asks whether the spittle is needed, he angrily sprays spit while shouting at her to stop questioning him.
punchline: The Boss's new fitness routine is just his usual abusive behavior, and he proves the spittle really is part of it by spraying it while yelling at the person who questions him.
summary: A manager rebrands his habit of stomping around and shouting at staff as a workout, and responds to a polite question by shouting and spitting at the questioner.

title: Unicorn Excuse for Never Being Wrong

transcript.text: Or are you an idiot for characterizing my reasonable idea as an absurd absolute?

transcript.text: Same reason you've never eaten a unicorn.

setting: Office, at a desk or meeting table with coffee cups
situation: A coworker in a green sweater calls Dilbert an idiot for thinking a software upgrade will fix every problem. Dilbert replies that the coworker is exaggerating his reasonable idea into an absurd absolute. When the coworker asks why Dilbert never admits he is wrong, Dilbert answers that it is for the same reason the coworker has never eaten a unicorn.
punchline: Dilbert implies that he never admits being wrong because, like unicorns, the situation simply does not exist, since he is never actually wrong.
summary: An argument over an overhyped software fix ends with Dilbert claiming that his never being wrong is as impossible as dining on a mythical beast.

transcript.text: What kind of manager has no faith in his employees?

transcript.text: You need to trust me to do what needs to be done.

transcript.text: You also need to trust your employees when they say they accomplished their goals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I see where this is going.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I was hoping you wouldn't.

situation: The Boss asks Wally whether he met his goals this quarter, and Wally enthusiastically claims it was his best quarter ever. When the Boss expresses surprise, Wally guilt-trips him for lacking faith in employees. When the Boss asks which goals were accomplished, Wally insists he must simply be trusted.
punchline: Wally exploits the idea of trust to avoid naming any actual accomplishments, making it clear he achieved nothing and is hoping the Boss won't notice.
summary: A slacker deflects his manager's request for proof of results by demanding blind trust in his claim of success.

title: Wally Promoted to Slow-Walker

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it too soon to ask for a raise?

situation: The Boss promotes Wally to a new role of slow-walker, explaining that he will be handed projects that could help the Boss's management rivals succeed, and his job is to stall them until they die. Wally proudly claims he has been preparing for this role all his life. When the Boss asks him to come to his office in ten minutes, Wally shows up two hours late and asks for a raise.
punchline: Wally's legendary laziness and slowness make him perfectly suited to the job, so he is already excellent at it and immediately wants to be rewarded for his lateness.
summary: A boss recruits his famously idle employee to sabotage rival managers' projects by dragging them out, and the employee proves his talent at once by turning up hours late and angling for more pay.

title: Naming the Coworker Who Doesn't Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What is the correct name for a co-worker who doesn't do any actual work?

transcript.text: I'm thinking "co-person," or possibly just "leech."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are we working right now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good point, co-person.

setting: Office hallway or break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, asks Dilbert what to call a coworker who does no actual work. Dilbert suggests "co-person" or "leech." Wally then points out that they are standing around drinking coffee instead of working, so Dilbert concedes and calls him "co-person."
punchline: Wally's question was really about himself, and Dilbert has to admit that the label for a non-working coworker applies to both of them at that moment.
summary: Two coffee-sipping colleagues debate what to call a slacker and then realise the term fits them while they chat.

title: Defending Against Accusations With Offense

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My new defense against every accusation is to be offended by the question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That works?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Depends how hard I sell it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why haven't you returned any of my emails?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How DARE you!

setting: Outside the office building, with coffee mugs in hand
situation: Wally tells Dilbert that his new strategy for dodging any accusation is to act offended that anyone would ask. Dilbert doubts it works, and Wally says it depends on how well he sells it. A coworker then asks why he has not answered her emails, and Wally responds with theatrical outrage.
punchline: Wally immediately demonstrates his tactic, using exaggerated indignation to deflect a perfectly reasonable question instead of giving an answer.
summary: A lazy employee boasts that feigned outrage defeats any complaint, then promptly deploys it on a colleague chasing him for replies.

title: Alien Annihilation, But Also Chair Safety

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If it got off a message to its home planet, your stupidity has doomed humanity to annihilation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Also, you didn't complete your mandatory training in chair safety.

situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert, who sits looking at his phone, because a laser communication prototype he built for NASA accidentally destroyed an approaching alien ship. The Boss warns that if the aliens sent a message home, humanity may be doomed. He then adds a complaint that Dilbert skipped mandatory chair safety training.
punchline: After accusing Dilbert of possibly dooming humanity, the boss treats a skipped chair safety training as an equally serious offense, showing how corporate compliance obsession trivializes even world-ending stakes.
summary: A manager berates an engineer for a possible alien apocalypse and then tacks on a reprimand about incomplete office furniture training.

transcript.text: That sounds risky.

situation: Asok asks Wally how he manages to stay happy while everyone else is stressed. Wally explains that he avoids arguments with idiots by pretending to agree with them so they leave him alone. When Asok says that sounds risky, Wally answers 'Yes, I agree,' applying the technique on Asok.
punchline: Wally demonstrates his tactic in real time by feigning agreement with Asok's objection, which also means he is brushing Asok off and ending the conversation.
summary: A stressed coworker wants to learn the secret to Wally's calm, and gets a live demonstration of it.

title: Hairs Grown On Company Time

transcript.text: No. I have to get a haircut.

transcript.text: You can't get a haircut on company time.

situation: The Boss asks Wally for a minute, but Wally says he has to leave for a haircut. The Boss objects that haircuts can't be taken on company time. Wally claims he is only trimming the hairs that grew while he was at work, and when challenged, says it is always hairs three and five.
punchline: Wally dodges work with an absurdly specific and unfalsifiable excuse, since no one can possibly verify which of his hairs grew on company time.
summary: Wally justifies skipping out for a haircut by insisting he'll only trim the strands that sprouted while he was on the clock.

title: Engineer's Weirdly Technical Presentation Feedback

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What did you think of my presentation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The signal-to-noise ratio was impressively low.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Engineers give weird compliments.

setting: Office, in a workplace conversation between Dilbert and The Boss
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert what he thought of his presentation. Dilbert replies in engineering jargon that the signal-to-noise ratio was impressively low. The Boss privately concludes it must have been a compliment, though it was actually a criticism.
punchline: A low signal-to-noise ratio means the presentation was mostly noise with little useful content, so Dilbert insulted it while The Boss, not understanding the jargon, mistook it for praise.
summary: A manager fishing for feedback misreads a technical insult as a quirky engineer's way of praising him.

title: Choosing Between Two Bad Options

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have only two choices, and both of them are bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So we'll do the only smart thing we can do in this situation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Choose the path that is least bad?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was going to say pick the path that hurts our enemies the most, but you're ruining it with your talking.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with an exterior building shot in the middle panel
situation: The Boss tells his team that they only have two choices and both are bad, then says he will announce the one smart thing to do. Dilbert guesses the obvious answer, choosing the least bad option. The Boss is annoyed because he was about to propose a different strategy: hurting their enemies the most.
punchline: The Boss's 'smart' strategy is spiteful revenge rather than minimizing harm to the company, and he blames Dilbert for spoiling his big reveal by stating the sensible answer first.
summary: A manager facing two lousy options plans to hurt his rivals as the clever move, but an employee's sensible guess steals his thunder.

title: Renaming the City-Killing Space Laser

transcript.text: It might help if we changed the project name from "City-Killing Laser in Space."

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: How about "Skylight"?

setting: Office or hallway, with both men holding coffee cups
situation: A manager tells a bald executive that his staff is threatening to quit over the company's military contracts. The executive suggests telling them the company only builds defensive weapons. The manager points out that the project is called "City-Killing Laser in Space," and the executive proposes the friendlier name "Skylight."
punchline: The executive thinks that giving an obviously offensive weapon a harmless-sounding name will solve the ethical objections, rather than changing what is actually being built.
summary: Faced with employees who object to building a weapon of mass destruction, leadership decides that a gentler brand name is a sufficient fix.

title: Maybe Your Ideas Are Just Obvious

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: And yet it was obvious.

situation: The Boss sits at a table staring at his phone and complains that people keep stealing his great ideas. Tina suggests he may only be coming up with obvious ideas. He admits he hadn't thought of that, and she remarks that the explanation was itself obvious.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he fails to see the obvious explanation for his ideas being 'stolen', and Tina notes that the insight he missed was itself obvious.
summary: A manager laments idea theft until a coworker points out his brilliance may simply be common sense he never noticed.

title: Insulting Salespeople Before Teaching Coding

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Classroom or training room at the office
situation: Dilbert stands in front of a class he has been asked to teach about coding and explains that programmers are hard to find. He then asks whether anyone in the room is smart or whether they all work in marketing and sales. One offended student speaks up, and Dilbert uses that reaction to identify the salespeople.
punchline: Dilbert's insulting question is really a trick to make the salespeople reveal themselves, since the one who gets offended outs himself as being in sales.
summary: Dilbert baits a roomful of trainees with a jab at sales staff and promptly picks out the one who takes the bait.

title: Robot Learns Human Behavior, Becomes Awful

transcript.text: Can you fix that bug?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some say climate change will get it done.

setting: Office, where two coworkers stand holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he built a robot that learns human behavior by watching people, and within a week it turned into a sexist, racist idiot. The Boss asks if Dilbert can fix that bug. Dilbert replies with a bleak joke that climate change might solve it.
punchline: The robot's awful behavior is not a bug but an accurate reflection of humans, so the only 'fix' Dilbert can imagine is humanity being wiped out by climate change.
summary: An engineer's people-watching robot quickly mirrors humanity's worst traits, and the only cure he can suggest is the end of the human race.

title: Doing Nothing Beats Doing Something

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're welcome.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'd be surprised how often doing nothing is as good as doing something.

setting: Office hallway with coffee cups in hand
situation: A coworker asks Wally if he remembers a task requested a month ago, and Wally says he doesn't. The coworker explains the circumstances changed and the task is no longer needed, so Wally takes credit as if his inaction was a favor. He then offers a smug piece of wisdom about doing nothing.
punchline: Wally's habitual laziness is retroactively justified, and he presents ignoring requests as a deliberate and effective strategy.
summary: A forgotten request turns out to be unnecessary, letting the work-averse Wally claim that ignoring tasks is a legitimate approach.

situation: Dilbert decides to start his day by writing a list of everything he needs to do. Eight hours later he realizes the list contains 347 urgent tasks and grows by about seven a day. He settles for crossing off the task of making the list and quitting for the day.
punchline: The only task Dilbert completes all day is writing the to-do list itself, and he counts that as his accomplishment since the backlog is hopelessly unmanageable.
summary: A worker spends a whole day listing his chores, discovers the pile is endless, and takes credit only for having made the list.

situation: The Boss consults Dogbert, billed as a mental health expert, and asks him to confirm that his employees have gone crazy. Dogbert agrees and says it is because they work for the Boss. The Boss then asks whether he himself is sane, and Dogbert says yes, because the Boss hired him.
punchline: Dogbert's reasoning is circular and self-serving: employees are insane for working for the Boss, while the Boss is declared sane only because he is paying Dogbert.
summary: A consultant plays psychiatrist and hands a manager a diagnosis in which the staff are crazy and the paying client is conveniently fine.

situation: An employee complains to Catbert, the HR director, that Alice called him a liar. Catbert asks what he was doing at the time, and he admits he was lying. When Catbert suggests discussing that, the employee smugly points out that he has checked and the company has no policy against lying.
punchline: The employee admits to lying yet feels untouchable because he has verified that company policy doesn't forbid it, so his complaint is both an admission and a loophole.
summary: A man reporting that a coworker accused him of lying cheerfully confesses to it, then shields himself by noting the rulebook never prohibits it.

title: Fire Them, Don't Pawn Problems

transcript.text: Everyone else on the team is lazy and useless, so I need you to do all of their work.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being added to the network upgrade project because the rest of the team is lazy and useless, and Dilbert must do all their work. Dilbert suggests the Boss simply fire the underperformers. The Boss reacts as if Dilbert is dumping his own problems on him.
punchline: The Boss dumps his team's performance problem on Dilbert, then accuses Dilbert of pawning off problems when he suggests the obvious management solution of firing them.
summary: A manager hands his employee the workload of a lazy team, then bristles when the employee proposes that the manager do his own job.

title: Too Many Problems Compared to What
