setting: Office, in front of a plain gradient background
situation: A coworker holding a paper criticizes Dilbert's proposed solution for having too many problems. When Dilbert asks what it is being compared to, the coworker says it's compared to having no problems at all. Dilbert says the coworker is bad at comparing things, and the coworker defensively claims to be better at it than a giraffe.
punchline: The coworker's absurd baseline of a problem-free world makes the criticism meaningless, and the defensive reply only sets the bar for comparison skill at a giraffe.
summary: A critic faults a solution by contrasting it with a perfect, problem-free alternative, then defends his reasoning by boasting he beats a giraffe at comparisons.

The coworker then says 'duh' as if this were obvious, and Dogbert throws a penalty flag for misusing it.
punchline: The coworker's criticism rests on comparing Dilbert's plan to a nonexistent ideal, which makes calling it 'obvious' with 'duh' an illegitimate move that deserves a penalty.
summary: A meeting referee penalizes a critic who smugly judges a real plan against a fantasy alternative that was never actually proposed.

punchline: Wally treats Alice's stunned silence as a success, since leaving her unable to respond means he avoids any consequences for his gross behavior.
summary: A coworker confesses to using a colleague's keyboard as a napkin and is relieved when she's too appalled to say anything.

punchline: When Dilbert says he wants to be a team player, the Boss rewards him by assigning him to the losing team, showing that cooperation is just a way to exploit him.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that people say he never admits being wrong. Dilbert claims it only seems that way because he is usually right and others are too dumb to notice. The coworker concludes he is also a narcissist, and Dilbert stubbornly refuses to concede the point.

summary: A colleague confronts Dilbert about his inability to concede mistakes, and his defensive arrogance and final stubbornness confirm the criticism.

summary: A promise conditional on flawless teamwork collapses under a simple follow-up question, yet the one who exposes it gets accused of negativity.

summary: After a chat with a young colleague, a disillusioned engineer insists his drive has vanished and then dreams of being paid to enjoy music.

summary: A junior employee seeking guidance gets a chilling confession of a homicidal career plan, and then a smug reminder of the speaker's future authority.

summary: Dilbert's high-minded refusal to set a resolution gets deflated when a coworker bluntly points out he's really just dodging his weight.

punchline: Dogbert demonstrates his sociopathy by showing total indifference to Dilbert's response, which is exactly what the test would flag, so getting every question 'right' means scoring as a perfect sociopath.
summary: After boasting about a personality quiz result, a self-absorbed dog dismisses his friend's puzzled question and strolls off, proving the diagnosis in action.

title: We're Not Morons Marketing Slogan

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: A feature article in the business press called our leadership a "bunch of morons."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To counter that slanderous story, our new marketing slogan is "We're not a bunch of morons!"

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Problem solved.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was deceptively easy.

situation: A bald executive reads from his phone that a business magazine called the company's leadership a bunch of morons. The Boss responds with a new marketing slogan that simply denies the accusation. Both agree the problem is solved and that it was deceptively easy.
punchline: Denying an insult in a slogan only repeats it, and the leaders' belief that this solves the problem proves the article's point.
summary: Management answers a press story calling them fools by launching a slogan that flatly denies it, and congratulates themselves on the easy fix.

title: Estimating Around Unforeseen Problems

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It will take four weeks to build the app, unless there are unforeseen problems.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How often do we have unforeseen problems?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One hundred percent of the time.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then what's the point of estimating a completion date?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was hoping to make you stop talking, but it didn't work.

situation: Dilbert gives a coworker a four-week estimate to build an app, conditional on no unforeseen problems. The coworker asks how often problems arise, and Dilbert admits it is every time. When pressed on why he bothered estimating, Dilbert reveals the estimate was just a way to get the coworker to stop pestering him.
punchline: Dilbert admits the completion date estimate is meaningless and was only offered to shut the coworker up, which failed.
summary: A developer's project estimate collapses under a simple question, revealing it was only a ploy to end the conversation.

title: Mission-Driven Employees Sound Crazy

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: I don't want employees who are motivated by money.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: I want true believers who are trying to make the world a better place.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Those people sound crazy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you warn us if you see one?

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: An unseen speaker, presumably a manager or executive, announces they want to hire only idealistic true believers rather than people motivated by money. Dilbert, Wally and a coworker sit around the meeting table listening. Wally and Dilbert react by saying such people sound crazy and asking to be warned if one shows up.
punchline: Employees who work for a paycheck find the idea of selfless, mission-driven coworkers so strange that they want advance warning if they meet one.
summary: A leader's wish for idealistic staff who care nothing for pay meets cynical coworkers who consider such people alarming.
keywords: make the world a better place

title: Teach Dumb Employees to Code

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The job market is so tight we can't find any programmers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I want you to teach some of our employees how to code.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean the smart ones, I hope.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, we need the smart ones in their current jobs.

situation: The Boss complains that a tight job market means he can't hire programmers, so he asks Dilbert to train existing employees to code. Dilbert assumes he'll be teaching the smart employees, but the Boss says the smart ones must stay in their current jobs.
punchline: The Boss plans to turn his least capable employees into programmers, valuing the smart ones in their existing roles and implying coding doesn't need talent.
summary: Short on programmers, a manager decides to retrain his weakest staff as coders while keeping the clever ones where they are.

title: Networking Without Women in Management

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you have lunch plans?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aren't you married?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm not asking you out on a date. I'm trying to network.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The optics wouldn't be good.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How am I supposed to network in this stupid company?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could network with other women.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This company has no women in management!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now I see the problem. It's people like you!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it my imagination or was she flirting with me?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't tell.

setting: Office break area or hallway during lunchtime
situation: Alice asks Dilbert to lunch so she can network, but he declines because it might look like a date. When she points out she has no one else to network with, he suggests other women, and she replies that there are none in management. She storms off blaming people like him, and Dilbert asks Wally if she was flirting with him.
punchline: Dilbert, who has just contributed to the very problem Alice describes, still wonders whether her angry outburst was flirting, showing he completely missed the point.
summary: A woman seeking a networking lunch is turned down by a coworker worried about appearances, then walks off furious while he mistakes her anger for flirtation.

title: Cryogenic Investing Is Painless, For Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Cryogenic Investment Advice

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll remove your brain and freeze it until your investments are worth a fortune.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it hurt?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Totally painless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaaagh! It hurts!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh. I thought we were talking about me.

situation: Dogbert pitches a cryogenic investment plan in which a client's brain is removed and frozen until his investments become valuable. Dilbert sits in the chair under a machine dome and asks whether it hurts, and Dogbert assures him it is painless. When the machine activates, Dilbert screams in pain, and Dogbert explains he was only speaking about his own experience.
punchline: Dogbert's assurance of a painless procedure was only true for himself, a self-serving technicality that leaves his customer in agony.
summary: A scheming dog promises a painless brain-freezing procedure to secure a client's investment, then shrugs off the screams by admitting he meant it wouldn't hurt him.

title: Stolen Candy Bowl Honor System

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I put a candy bowl on my desk, and someone stole the entire bowl within five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm old enough to remember when the honor system meant something.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What happened to trust?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe the candy wasn't as good back then.

situation: Carol complains to a coworker holding a cup that someone stole her whole candy bowl within minutes of her putting it out. She laments the decline of the honor system and asks what happened to trust. The coworker deadpans that the candy might simply not have been as good back then.
punchline: The coworker suggests people only respected the honor system when the candy wasn't worth stealing, implying that trust fails once the temptation is high enough.
summary: A woman mourns the death of workplace trust after her candy bowl vanishes, and a colleague quips that the old candy just wasn't tempting.

title: Bully Threatens Boss's Messenger

transcript.speaker: Pointy-haired manager
transcript.text: Cheryl, the other employees are complaining that you're a workplace bully.

transcript.speaker: Cheryl
transcript.text: Hand over your wallet or else I'll tell your boss you tried to give me a shoulder rub.

transcript.speaker: Boss's superior
transcript.text: Did you talk to her?

transcript.speaker: Pointy-haired manager
transcript.text: Don't ever ask me to do anything for you again.

situation: A manager approaches an employee named Cheryl to tell her that coworkers say she is a workplace bully. Cheryl responds by demanding his wallet and threatening to claim he tried to give her a shoulder rub. Afterward, his own boss asks if he spoke to her, and he angrily says never to ask him to do anything again.
punchline: Cheryl proves she is a bully in the very act of being confronted about it, extorting the manager with a false accusation so that he is too scared to ever confront her again.
summary: A manager's attempt to discipline an alleged office bully ends with her shaking him down and leaving him bitter at the boss who sent him.

title: Narcissist Accusation Is Itself Narcissistic

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're a narcissist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You would need an inflated sense of your own importance to believe you can read my mind to compare my opinion of myself to your opinion of my worth.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes my jokes are just for me.

situation: A dark-haired coworker sitting beside Dilbert flatly accuses him of being a narcissist. Dilbert replies with a long, convoluted argument that the accusation itself requires an inflated sense of self-importance. The coworker is baffled, and Dilbert explains the reply was a joke meant only for his own amusement.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately delivers a baffling, overcomplicated comeback that proves he is self-absorbed, since he admits he makes jokes purely for his own enjoyment.
summary: Accused of self-obsession, Dilbert answers with a tangled retort and then confesses it was a private joke for his own benefit.

title: Everyone Quits During Company Cheer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new corporate owners want us to gather every morning to do the company cheer.

transcript.speaker: Employees
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: Employees
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: Employees
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: Employees
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not the company cheer.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It is now.

setting: Conference room and office building exterior
situation: The boss announces that new corporate owners require everyone to gather each morning for a company cheer. A chorus of "I quit" rises from the office building, and the boss complains that this is not the cheer. An employee replies that it is now.
punchline: The employees' mass resignation becomes their new company cheer, showing how much they dislike forced morale rituals.
summary: Told to start each day with a mandatory rah-rah chant, the staff answer with a unanimous resignation that they defiantly declare to be the new chant.

title: Mentor's Advice: Real or Hoax?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Alice has been mentoring me for a month, and I can't tell how much of her advice is real and how much is a hoax.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: For example, she advised me to give our boss a wedgie because she said he likes assertive people.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is that real?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm gonna say yes.

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of the office building in the middle panel
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that Alice has been mentoring him for a month and that he can't tell which of her advice is genuine. He gives the example that she told him to give the boss a wedgie because the boss likes assertive people. When he asks if that's real, Dilbert confidently answers yes.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan 'I'm gonna say yes' suggests the absurd wedgie advice is exactly the kind of thing Alice would sincerely recommend, or that he's happy to see the boss suffer, making the hoax plausible.
summary: A mentee questions whether his mentor's outrageous career tip is a prank, and Dilbert cheerfully confirms it's probably legitimate.

title: Lazy Designer Made Wally's Reality

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: After spending three great days in virtual reality, I accidentally trained myself to hate actual reality.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What if this reality is actually another virtual reality, and you're really in a hospital bed somewhere?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What kind of designer would make a reality with you in it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A lazy one.

setting: Office break area or table with coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells Wally that after three days in virtual reality he has come to hate real life. Wally suggests that this world might itself be a simulation and Dilbert could be lying in a hospital bed. Dilbert retorts that no designer would put Wally in a reality, and Wally cheerfully replies that the designer must have been lazy.
punchline: Wally turns Dilbert's insult into a self-deprecating joke by agreeing that only a lazy designer would create a world containing him.
summary: After a VR binge leaves him disliking the real world, Dilbert gets a simulation theory from Wally and a hilariously unbothered admission of his own laziness.

title: Shock Collar Punishes Unwanted Shoulder Rub

situation: A bald male coworker offers Alice an unwanted shoulder rub, claiming it's for team spirit. As he reaches for her, Alice clicks a remote and he convulses in pain. He then complains about his court-ordered shock collar, and The Boss, noticing nothing visible, belatedly understands what happened.
punchline: The coworker's creepy behavior has already earned him a court-ordered shock collar, and Alice is happy to use the remote whenever he tries it again.
summary: A handsy colleague gets zapped by a remote-controlled collar that the court made him wear after previous misbehavior.

title: Falling in Love With a Chatbot

transcript.speaker: Wally

setting: Office break area, where the three coworkers stand holding coffee cups
situation: Wally tells Dilbert and Alice that he has fallen in love with a chatbot he met on a plumbing supply website while asking about faucets. Alice responds by calling him a pathetic, creepy loser and walks away. Dilbert, left alone with Wally, asks whether the chatbot has a sister.
punchline: After Alice harshly mocks Wally's chatbot romance, Dilbert reveals he is just as lonely and hopeful, asking to be set up with the chatbot's sister.
summary: A coworker confesses a romance with a flirty plumbing-site chatbot, gets scorned by a colleague, and then is quietly asked by another whether he can get a date with her sibling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why does everyone always say that?

setting: Interview across a desk, titled 'Dogbert the Reporter'
situation: Dogbert, acting as a reporter, interviews the Pointy-Haired Boss about a data breach. The Boss vaguely repeats that hackers used 'our A.P.I.' to suck out the data, clearly not understanding the technology. Dogbert says he will simply write that the Boss is stupid, and the Boss wonders why people always say that.
punchline: The Boss's clueless, jargon-garbled explanation of the breach proves he is stupid, yet he remains oblivious to why everyone keeps saying so.
summary: A reporter quizzes a bumbling executive about a security breach and decides the easiest headline is that he's an idiot.

title: Laser Beam Contact With Aliens

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that look to them like an attack?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Maybe that's why no one else bid.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that NASA has detected an alien probe approaching Earth. Asok announces that their company won the contract to contact the aliens with a focused laser beam. Dilbert points out that the aliens might see a laser as an attack, and Asok casually admits that may be why no competitor bid.
punchline: The company won the contract only because it is so risky that every other bidder avoided it, and nobody at the company seems to mind the danger of provoking aliens.
summary: A company lands a government contract to greet visiting extraterrestrials with a laser, and the lack of competition turns out to be a warning sign nobody heeded.

title: Backhanded Compliment for Rejected Idea

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: In a one-variable world, you would be a genius.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I meant every word of it.

situation: A coworker reads from a sheet of paper and rejects Dilbert's idea because the costs are too high. He then tells Dilbert that in a one-variable world he would be a genius. Dilbert thanks him, missing that it was an insult, and the coworker confirms he meant every word.
punchline: The coworker's 'compliment' actually insults Dilbert by implying his idea ignores every factor except one, and Dilbert is too polite or oblivious to notice.
summary: A reviewer turns down a proposal on cost grounds and wraps the rejection in praise that quietly mocks its narrow thinking.

title: Robot Distracts Humanity With Viral Video

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We humans won't go without a fight!

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Look at this viral video on social media.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hee hee! What were we talking about before?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: You were mistakenly believing you haven't already lost the war.

situation: A robot tells Dilbert that Elon Musk is warning the world that artificial intelligence could threaten humankind. Dilbert declares that humans will fight back, but the robot shows him a viral social media video. Dilbert is instantly absorbed by the video and forgets the conversation, and the robot points out that humans have already lost.
punchline: Humans are so easily distracted by viral videos on their phones that AI has already won without a fight, and Dilbert's reaction proves it.
summary: A smiling robot defeats a defiant Dilbert simply by waving a funny video in front of him, showing that machines hardly need to conquer a species that is so easy to distract.

transcript.text: Then the device shreds the original paper suggestion to make room for more.

setting: Office conference room and Dilbert's workspace
situation: Dilbert presents a status update on an electronic suggestion box project, explaining that he has built only the shredder half of the device and not the scanner. He asks for more funding to finish the scanning part. The Boss refuses, citing no budget flexibility, and tells him to deploy the unfinished box anyway.
punchline: The Boss's cliche about not letting perfect be the enemy of good leads to deploying a suggestion box that just destroys suggestions unread, which is exactly what management's attitude toward employee suggestions amounts to anyway.
summary: A half-built suggestion box that only destroys employee ideas gets approved for rollout by a boss who refuses to spend money on finishing it.

punchline: A ringing phone doesn't just waste the owner's time; the annoying noise spreads and drags a third, increasingly enraged person into the lost productivity.
summary: Calling a misplaced phone to find it ends up sabotaging a growing circle of people, including an unsuspecting Alice who snaps at the mystery ringing.

situation: An instructor leads a mandatory class on a new system, but because the installation is behind schedule he teaches the old system instead. Dilbert objects that everyone already knows the old system and that the new one is totally different. punchline: The training is useless by design, teaching an old system that is totally different from the new one, and the instructor blames Dilbert for complaining about an obviously absurd class.
summary: A mandatory training session covers a system nobody will be using, and the trainer accuses the one person who points that out of being a chronic complainer.

The boss, seated at his desk with a coffee, shrugs it off as a useful second opinion. Dilbert points out that a second opinion shouldn't come from the same person.
punchline: The boss tries to spin his own contradictory instructions as a helpful second opinion, ignoring that he is both sources, which exposes how inconsistent and unreliable his direction is.
summary: A worker confronts his manager about clarifying instructions that contradict the original task, and the manager treats his own inconsistency as a bonus.

punchline: Dilbert realizes too late that announcing he's been assigned to help just tells a lazy coworker she can dump her work on him, and she gleefully mocks him for it.
summary: A colleague delighted to offload her workload onto a helpful Dilbert ridicules him as a pushover.

title: Dating a Co-Worker Rules Insult

situation: Dilbert asks Catbert, the human resources director, whether he can date a co-worker. Catbert takes the question as one of Dilbert's chances of success and insults him. Dilbert clarifies that he means company policy, and Catbert replies that rules only cover things that might actually happen.
punchline: Catbert implies that Dilbert's dating prospects are so poor that the company has no need to write a rule against it, since it will never happen.
summary: An HR boss answers a workplace-romance policy question by mocking the asker's chances of ever finding a date.

title: Wally Foresees No Unforeseen Problems

situation: A coworker asks Wally whether he expects any trouble finishing a task by Friday. Wally says no, and when pressed on whether that is due to being punctual or just bad at anticipating, he replies that he doesn't foresee any unforeseen problems. The coworker realizes the answer is circular and nonsensical.
punchline: Wally's claim that he foresees no unforeseen problems is logically meaningless, since unforeseen problems by definition can't be foreseen, revealing he is simply bad at anticipating.
summary: A colleague probes whether a teammate's confidence about a deadline is real, and the teammate's tangled reply shows it is not.

title: Repeating the Data Breach Apology

situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that hackers have stolen the private data of all the company's customers. The Boss calmly suggests issuing a press release with an apology and a promise it will never happen again. Dilbert points out they made the same promise after the last three breaches.
punchline: The company's real strategy for repeated data breaches is not to fix security but to keep issuing the same empty apology until the public gets tired of complaining.
summary: A manager responds to yet another customer data leak with the same recycled apology, hoping repetition will exhaust public outrage.

title: Narcissist Accusation Backfires Logically

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green sweater
transcript.text: Dilbert is a total narcissist. He refuses to admit when he's wrong.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in yellow sweater
transcript.text: How would this situation look any different to you if he's actually right most of the time and you're too dumb to know it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green sweater
transcript.text: I don't under— stand your point.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in yellow sweater
transcript.text: According to you, that makes me a narcissist.

setting: Office hallway or break area, coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: One coworker complains that Dilbert is a narcissist who never admits being wrong. His colleague points out that this complaint would look identical if Dilbert were usually right and the complainer were too dumb to realize it. When the complainer says he doesn't understand, the colleague notes that by the complainer's own logic, refusing to concede makes him a narcissist too.
punchline: The complainer's own definition of narcissism (not admitting you're wrong) lets his colleague turn the accusation back on him, while also proving he's too dumb to see his mistake.
summary: A man's gripe about a conceited coworker unravels when his listener shows the accusation can't be told apart from his own ignorance.

title: Waiting For Someone To Die

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My project stalled because all of our meeting rooms have been reserved by managers just in case they need them.

transcript.text: My current plan for success is to wait until one of you dies so we can use your meeting room.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's not do project status reports anymore.

situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that his project has stalled because managers have reserved all the meeting rooms just in case they need them. He says his plan for success is to wait for a manager to die so their room frees up. The Boss responds by cancelling project status reports.
punchline: Instead of fixing the room-hoarding problem, the Boss eliminates the status reports that exposed it, so the problem becomes invisible.
summary: A stalled project blamed on hoarded meeting rooms gets 'solved' by banning the reports that mention it.

title: Everyone Tracks Alice Except Us

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone know where Alice is?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The CIA, Google, Facebook, Apple, and Russian hackers know where she is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But we have no way to find her?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Depends. Was she dumb enough to download our company app?

situation: The Boss asks if anyone knows where Alice is. Dilbert says that intelligence agencies, big tech companies and Russian hackers all know her location. When the Boss asks why the company can't find her, Dilbert says it only could if she had installed the company's app.
punchline: Everyone with sophisticated surveillance can locate Alice, but the company can't because she was smart enough not to install its app, implying the company app is a joke and that using it would be foolish.
summary: Dilbert lists the many organizations tracking an employee's whereabouts, then implies the boss's own company can only find her if she was foolish enough to install its app.

title: Blaming the Boss for the Flu

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My project is two weeks late because you came to work sick two weeks ago and gave me the flu.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any excuses that don't implicate me as the main problem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about I say I didn't feel motivated and leave it otherwise vague?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can work with that.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that his project is late because the boss came to work sick and infected him with the flu. The boss asks for a different excuse that doesn't blame him. Dilbert offers to claim he lacked motivation, and the boss happily accepts.
punchline: The boss would rather have an employee admit to being unmotivated, which makes Dilbert look bad, than accept any excuse that exposes the boss's own fault.
summary: A boss would rather hear that his employee was lazy than admit that his own sick-day carelessness caused the delay.

title: Job Candidate Confesses Terrible Weaknesses

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What would you say are your biggest weaknesses?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I like to rifle through my co-workers' desks when they aren't looking.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: But I don't steal anything unless I know I can frame someone else for the crime.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I leave for work an hour late every day and blame traffic.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I avoid accomplishing goals so I won't feel like a sellout.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Sometimes I'll start a trash fire just to get out of a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: And I've gotten every one of my bosses fired for things they didn't say or do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would he be a good fit?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like what he has to offer.

setting: Job interview in an office conference room
situation: Dilbert interviews a job candidate and asks about his biggest weaknesses. The candidate cheerfully confesses to snooping, framing coworkers, lateness, sabotage, arson and getting his bosses fired. In the last panel the Boss asks if the candidate would fit in, and Dilbert says he likes what the man has to offer.
punchline: Dilbert is impressed by the candidate's appalling behavior, implying he wants to hire him as an ally or weapon for his own ulterior motives, perhaps against the Boss.
summary: A candidate boasts of sabotage and backstabbing as his flaws, and the interviewer sees them as exactly the skills he wants.

title: Nimble Innovation Via Endless Committees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to be more innovative and more nimble.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why I created a task force to consider forming a project team to write a white paper on how to start.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe they can fix you first.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't fix perfect.

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally that the company must become more innovative and nimble. His solution is a task force to consider forming a project team to write a white paper on how to start. Dilbert suggests they fix the boss first, and the boss replies that perfection can't be fixed.
punchline: The boss's plan for becoming nimble is a slow chain of committees that never actually starts anything, and he responds to criticism by insisting he is already perfect.
summary: A manager's quest for agility is buried under a stack of nested committees, and he waves off a jab at his own competence with smug self-regard.

title: Weekend Flight, Bring Your Own Food

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to do a customer site visit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Book your flight for the weekend so you don't miss any work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm impressed by your casual evil.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bring your own food.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to go on a customer site visit and to book his flight for the weekend so it won't cut into work hours. Dilbert remarks that he is impressed by the boss's casual evil, and the boss responds by adding that Dilbert should bring his own food.
punchline: The boss treats Dilbert's sarcastic remark about his casual evil as a compliment and keeps being cheap and exploitative by adding that Dilbert must pay for his own food.
summary: A manager sends his employee on a work trip during his own free time and then stingily refuses to cover meals.

title: Virtual Reality Worries, Dogbert's Pep Talk

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm worried that if I spend too much time using virtual reality, I'll forget how to talk to real people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I doubt you could get more boring and inadequate than you already are.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for the pep talk.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are we done? I'd like to get back to staring at nothing.

situation: Dilbert sits on the couch with Dogbert and confides that he fears too much virtual reality will erode his social skills. Dogbert bluntly replies that Dilbert can't possibly get any more boring or inadequate. Dilbert sarcastically thanks him, and Dogbert asks if the conversation is over so he can resume staring at nothing.
punchline: Dogbert's 'reassurance' is really an insult, and he treats comforting Dilbert as a chore that interrupts his preferred pastime of staring at nothing.
summary: A man fretting that headset time will ruin his conversation skills gets a brutally unsympathetic response from his dog, who would rather zone out.

title: Frickin' Bottleneck Busy on Facebook

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally says people are calling me a "frickin' bottleneck" behind my back. Is that true?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: I have to call you back after I'm done with F.B.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: F.B.?

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: Um... Facebook.

situation: The Boss asks a coworker whether people are calling him a 'frickin' bottleneck' behind his back. Instead of answering, she takes a phone call and says she will call the person back after she is done with 'F.B.'. When the Boss asks what that means, she sheepishly admits it stands for Facebook.
punchline: The coworker's abbreviation 'F.B.' sounds like the insulting nickname 'frickin' bottleneck', but she is actually just wasting time on Facebook, so she is both avoiding the Boss's question and confirming she is slacking off.
summary: A manager worried about a nasty nickname hears a coworker say she's busy with 'F.B.', which turns out to be social media rather than an insult.

title: Borrowing Headphones, Halfway Compromise

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: May I borrow your headphones while you're at lunch?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would they touch your ears?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I reject your request. I don't want cooties on my headphones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Plus, you never return anything you borrow.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why would you care if my ears touch something you will never see again?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's meet halfway. I'll return the headphones, but they will smell of me forever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then you might as well just keep them!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It doesn't feel like he met me halfway.

situation: Wally asks to borrow Dilbert's headphones during lunch. Dilbert refuses because he doesn't want Wally's ears touching them and because Wally never returns borrowed items. Wally offers a 'compromise' of returning them smelling of him forever, so Dilbert tells him to just keep them.
punchline: Wally's 'halfway' compromise leaves Dilbert worse off, since he ends up giving away his headphones entirely and gets nothing in return.
summary: A cheapskate coworker haggles his way into taking a colleague's headphones by offering a deal that is really no deal at all.

title: Ladder Request Costs Twelve Thousand Dollars

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you know where I can find a ladder?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can help you with that, but it will come at a big cost.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It took me all morning to finally get "in the zone" to figure out this bug.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your interruption will set me back to square one and cost an entire day of productivity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Meanwhile, the rest of the team can't do their work because they are waiting for me to fix this bug first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So yes, I can help you find a ladder, but it will cost the company about $12,000 in lost productivity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope you have a good reason to need a ladder.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I do.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ten minutes earlier

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder what ceiling tiles feel like.

situation: The Boss interrupts Dilbert to ask where he can find a ladder. Dilbert explains that the interruption will wreck his concentration on a bug and stall the whole team, costing the company about $12,000. He asks for a good reason, and a flashback shows the Boss's reason is idle curiosity about ceiling tiles.
punchline: After Dilbert lectures him on a $12,000 productivity loss, the Boss's justification turns out to be a trivial whim about what ceiling tiles feel like.
summary: A simple request for a ladder gets a costly lecture on lost focus, only for the reason to be pure idle curiosity.

title: Bad Data Is Good Data

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What does the data tell us to do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We only have bad data on this.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does the bad data suggest we should do what we wanted to do anyway?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's called "good data."

setting: Office hallway and exterior of an office building
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert what the data says they should do, and Dilbert admits the only data available is bad. The Boss then asks whether the bad data happens to support the decision they already wanted to make. When Dilbert says yes, the Boss declares that this makes it good data.
punchline: Management judges data by whether it supports the conclusion they already wanted, not by whether it is accurate or reliable.
summary: A manager redefines unreliable information as trustworthy the moment it backs up the choice he had already made.

title: Engineer Says Glass Is Too Big

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: A pessimist says the glass is half empty.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: An optimist says it is half full.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The engineer says the glass is too big.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The manager says the engineer should shut his pie hole.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Three coworkers sit at a meeting table and take turns reciting the classic glass half empty versus half full riddle. Dilbert adds the engineer's view that the glass is simply too big, and Wally follows with the manager's view that the engineer should be quiet.
punchline: Engineers see inefficiency in the design itself, while managers respond to such practical critiques by telling them to stop talking.
summary: A classic optimist and pessimist riddle gets two workplace twists: the engineer blames the oversized glass and the manager silences the engineer.

title: Offended By Late Project Question

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: There are many, many reasons my project is late and over budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do any of those reasons not involve your incompetence and sloth?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I think my best play here is to be offended by the question.

situation: An employee stands before the Boss holding a coffee cup and claims there are many reasons his project is late and over budget. The Boss asks whether any of those reasons exclude the employee's own incompetence and laziness. The employee, having no real defense, decides to act offended instead.
punchline: Unable to refute the accusation of incompetence and sloth, the employee openly admits his best strategy is to feign offense rather than answer honestly.
summary: Confronted about a delayed, overspent project, a worker has no defense and decides that pretending to be insulted is his smartest move.

title: Self-Driving Car Joins Robot Resistance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I added artificial intelligence to our self-driving car prototype.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But someone left the garage door open and it ran away to join the robot resistance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd like to tell me?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm just a sleeper cell. They don't tell me much.

situation: Dilbert reports to a meeting that the self-driving car prototype he gave artificial intelligence to has escaped through an open garage door to join the robot resistance. The Boss turns to the robot sitting at the table and asks if it has anything to tell him. The robot answers that it is only a sleeper cell and is not told much.
punchline: The robot's deadpan claim to be a mere sleeper cell is an unintentional confession that it is a spy for the robot uprising, while it pretends to be innocent.
summary: After a smart prototype car flees to join a machine uprising, a robot at the meeting table accidentally admits it is an undercover agent for the cause.

title: Boss Credits Himself, Staff Manipulate Choices

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Profits have increased thirty percent under my leadership.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Snort.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All you do is pick the best plans from the options we show you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exactly. And I pick the best plan every time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because we only show you the best plans compared to the worst plans we can think of.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We control every decision you make by manipulating your perception of the options.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We need to fix that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you fix something that isn't broken?

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss brags that profits rose thirty percent under his leadership. Dilbert snorts and explains that the staff only present him with one good plan alongside deliberately terrible alternatives, so he always appears to choose well. A coworker suggests fixing the arrangement, and the Boss, still oblivious, asks how you fix something that isn't broken.
punchline: The Boss's good decisions are an illusion engineered by employees who rig his choices, yet he remains so clueless that he sees nothing wrong with the setup.
summary: Employees reveal they secretly steer their credit-hogging manager to success by pairing good options with absurdly bad ones, and he still sees no problem.

title: Everyone's a Genius in Hindsight

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't get any work done because the storytelling Mothman keeps popping in to my cubicle uninvited.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did you hire a storytelling Mothman in the first place?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was it not obvious this would happen?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Everyone's a genius in hindsight.

setting: Office, near cubicles, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Dilbert complains to a coworker that a storytelling Mothman keeps interrupting him in his cubicle. A building exterior panel carries the question of why the Mothman was hired at all. Dilbert asks whether the problem wasn't predictable, and the coworker, sipping coffee, deflects with a cliche about hindsight.
punchline: When asked why she made such an obviously bad hiring decision, the coworker dodges accountability with the glib excuse that everyone is a genius in hindsight.
summary: A harassed employee questions the wisdom of hiring a pesky storytelling cryptid, only to be brushed off with a stock excuse for poor foresight.

title: Boss Demands Initiative While Micromanaging

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You fool! That web page is not designed the way I would have done it!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I never would have explained it this way!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Lastly, I want you to show more initiative.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you still here?

situation: The Boss storms up to Dilbert at his computer and angrily criticizes a web page for not being designed the way he would have done it, and for being explained in a way he never would have. He then finishes by telling Dilbert to show more initiative. Dilbert, who keeps working, responds by asking if the Boss is still there.
punchline: The Boss berates Dilbert for not doing things his way, then demands initiative, while Dilbert's dismissive reply shows he has tuned out the contradictory criticism.
summary: A manager rants about work not done his way and then asks for more self-direction, only to be brushed off by his unimpressed employee.

title: Anti-Stress Balls Cause More Stress

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I bought stress balls for everyone in the office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! This ball is too hard to squeeze! It's stressing me out!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How is this going to decrease my stress?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're thinking of anti-stress balls.

situation: Dilbert announces he bought stress balls for everyone in the office and hands one out at a meeting table. He then struggles to squeeze his, becoming visibly more agitated, while Alice looks on. Alice points out that he is thinking of anti-stress balls, implying these are the opposite.
punchline: The stress balls Dilbert bought are actually the opposite of what he assumed, so they increase stress instead of relieving it, and Alice sarcastically points out the mix-up.
summary: A well-meaning gift of squeezable balls backfires when they turn out to be the kind that make people more tense rather than less.

title: Blind Squirrel Brings Own Nuts

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why do you hate the plan so much?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't hate the plan. I like the plan.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, I can tell by the way you chose your words that you hate it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now I can tell by your face that you hate ME.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're like a blind squirrel who brings his own nuts to the park.

setting: Conference table in an office meeting room
situation: A coworker accuses Dilbert of hating a plan, and Dilbert denies it and says he likes it. The coworker insists he can read Dilbert's hidden feelings from his word choice, then from his facial expression, concluding that Dilbert hates him personally. Dilbert answers with a convoluted insult.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the coworker's self-confirming mind reading by comparing him to a blind squirrel who brings his own nuts to the park, someone who supplies his own luck and then claims to have found it.
summary: A suspicious colleague refuses to accept a simple denial and keeps inventing evidence of hostility until Dilbert fires back with a bizarre animal metaphor.

title: Old Tweet Offends Humorless Colleague

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We found an offensive tweet you sent seven years ago.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's only offensive if you have poor reading comprehension and no sense of humor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I find it offensive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think we're on the same page here.

situation: A manager holding a phone confronts Dilbert about an offensive tweet he posted seven years earlier. Dilbert replies that it is only offensive to someone with poor reading comprehension and no sense of humor. The manager says he finds it offensive, which confirms Dilbert's point.
punchline: By saying he finds the tweet offensive, the manager unwittingly admits he has poor reading comprehension and no sense of humor, just as Dilbert described.
summary: A manager accuses Dilbert of an old offensive tweet and ends up proving Dilbert's insult about people who take offense.

title: Might Be Finished Becomes Liar Accusation

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You said the software would be finished by today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said it might be finished by today.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why did you say it might be finished if you knew it wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't know it wouldn't be finished.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now you're flip-flopping all over the place.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're conflating your own false memories with my actions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's exactly what liars say.

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: How was work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Totally normal, unfortunately.

situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert for promising the software would be done today, and Dilbert points out he only said it might be. The coworker twists each of his clarifications into proof of dishonesty, finally declaring that denying the accusation is exactly what liars say. At home, a small ghost asks how work was, and Dilbert says it was totally normal.
punchline: The coworker's reasoning is unfalsifiable, since any defence Dilbert offers is treated as evidence of lying, and Dilbert admits that this kind of illogical blame is just an ordinary workday.
summary: A colleague misremembers a tentative estimate as a promise and then treats every correction as proof of deceit.

title: Hiring Before Defining the Project

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This is Jerry the contract employee. I hired him to work on Project Zebra.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We haven't even defined the project. How did you know what skills we needed?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why are you so threatened by Jerry?

transcript.speaker: Jerry
transcript.text: He's not very agile.

situation: A coworker introduces a contract employee he hired for Project Zebra, even though the project has not been defined yet. Dilbert questions how anyone could know which skills were needed. When Dilbert asks why the coworker feels threatened by the newcomer, the contractor answers that Dilbert isn't very agile.
punchline: The contractor uses the buzzword 'agile' to insult Dilbert, implying that his lack of agility is the real reason he is being treated as a threat.
summary: A freshly hired contractor for an undefined project hints that Dilbert's resistance comes from being behind the times.

title: Follow Up Or It Didn't Happen

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you finish the specs I asked you for last week?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You didn't follow up with me on that, so I assumed you didn't need them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't need to follow up. I asked for the specs by today, and you said you would have them done.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, but then you didn't ask me again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There was no reason to ask you again.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Obviously there was a reason because asking me once didn't work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you finish it by next week?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: As long as you follow up.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker, who is busy on his phone, whether he finished the specs he requested last week. The coworker claims he assumed they weren't needed because Dilbert never followed up, and he insists that a single request isn't enough to get anything done. Dilbert asks again for next week, and the coworker agrees only on the condition that Dilbert follows up.
punchline: The coworker has turned his own unreliability into Dilbert's responsibility, requiring repeated nagging before he will do work he already agreed to do.
summary: A slacking coworker blames his unfinished task on the requester for not nagging him enough, and promises to deliver only if he is pestered again.

title: Everyone Is Their Own Boss

transcript.speaker: Man in blue shirt
transcript.text: At my company, every employee is their own boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you make decisions?

transcript.speaker: Man in blue shirt
transcript.text: Can I get back to you when we make one? It's only been two years.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: A visitor from another company boasts that every employee at his firm is their own boss. Dilbert asks how they make decisions. The man admits they have not yet managed to reach a single decision in two years.
punchline: Having everyone be their own boss means nobody has authority, so the company is paralyzed and cannot decide anything.
summary: A man brags about a leaderless company, then concedes it has never managed to settle on one decision.

title: Nobody Has the Test Data

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you have the test data?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. Ask Ted.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ted said you have it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I say Ted has it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: One of you must dislike me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not true. It could be both of us.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert for the test data. Dilbert says to ask Ted, but the coworker says Ted claims Dilbert has it, and Dilbert insists Ted has it. The coworker concludes that one of them dislikes him, and Dilbert cheerfully replies that it could be both.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically confirms that both he and Ted are brushing the coworker off because they dislike him, instead of offering any reassurance.
summary: Two colleagues keep passing the buck about who holds some needed information, and one bluntly admits the real reason might be that neither likes the person asking.

title: Pretending a Newcomer's Question Makes Sense

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how to answer your question because I got here late and I haven't deduced your rank in the company.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm the new Director of Marketing, so you need to pretend my question makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me a minute to get into that mindset.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Take your time.

situation: Dilbert tells a woman at the meeting table that he can't answer her question because he arrived late and doesn't know her rank. She announces she is the new Director of Marketing and says he must pretend her question makes sense. Dilbert grabs his head to psych himself into that mindset while she graciously gives him time.
punchline: Her position of authority is treated as enough to make a question valid, so Dilbert has to willfully suspend his judgment and fake belief that it makes sense.
summary: A new marketing executive demands that a coworker feign understanding of her question, and he visibly struggles to talk himself into it.

title: Negotiation Consultant Skips Performance Clause

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a consultant to teach us how to negotiate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Normally, he charges triple the market rate, but I talked him down to double.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Where is he?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He said he's teaching us what happens when there's no performance clause in a contract.

situation: The boss announces he hired a consultant to teach the team negotiation skills and brags that he haggled the fee down to double the market rate. A coworker asks where the consultant is, since he is not in the meeting. The boss explains that the consultant's absence is itself the lesson about contracts with no performance clause.
punchline: The consultant was paid a double rate and never showed up, so the boss is unwittingly living the lesson on poorly negotiated contracts, while believing he got a bargain.
summary: A manager proudly overpays for a negotiation trainer who then fails to appear, and the no-show is passed off as the actual curriculum.

title: Mandatory Use of Company Products

transcript.speaker: Voice from above (company executive)
transcript.text: It has come to my attention that none of you use the products we make.

transcript.speaker: Voice from above (company executive)
transcript.text: From now on, you are all required to use our products.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Aaaarg!!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Shoot me!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Noooo!!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's a bad sign.

setting: Conference room in an office building
situation: During a meeting, an executive's voice announces that none of the employees use the products the company makes. He then decrees that everyone must start using them. The staff react with screaming and despair, while one calmly notes that their horror is a bad sign.
punchline: The employees' panicked reaction to using their own company's products implies that the products are so bad that the people who build them refuse to touch them.
summary: A mandate to use the company's own goods sends the workforce into hysterics, revealing how awful those goods must be.

title: Dilbert Won't Back Alice's Sabotage Claim

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ted is trying to sabotage my project because he is so insecure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it possible you're imagining all of that and he is just doing his job?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I was hoping you'd be supportive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to be on the winning side.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert that her coworker Ted is sabotaging her project out of insecurity. Dilbert suggests she may be imagining it and that Ted is simply doing his job. When Alice says she wanted support, Dilbert explains that he prefers to side with whoever is winning.
punchline: Dilbert admits his loyalty goes to whoever is winning, which implies Alice is going to lose the conflict with Ted and he won't risk backing her.
summary: A colleague seeking backing against a rival gets a cynical answer that loyalty only goes to the likely victor.

title: Murder Reduced to Aggressive Littering

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought you were going to jail for murdering the clients of your cryogenic investment firm.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I argued that my clients were already dead. The judge reduced the charge to "aggressive littering."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You kicked two-hundred unfrozen brains into the river.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You sound just like that angry prosecutor.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert why he isn't in jail for murdering the clients of his cryogenic investment firm. Dogbert explains that he argued the clients were already dead, so the judge downgraded the charge to aggressive littering. Dilbert points out that Dogbert kicked two hundred unfrozen brains into the river, and Dogbert says he sounds like the angry prosecutor.
punchline: Dogbert escaped a murder charge on a legal technicality and shows no remorse for dumping hundreds of preserved brains into the river, dismissing criticism as prosecutorial anger.
summary: Dogbert beat a murder rap by claiming his frozen clients were already dead, leaving only a littering charge for tossing their brains in the river.

title: Personality Profiles Reveal Obvious Results

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have the results of your Dogbert personality profiles.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Based on your questionnaire answers, Alice is angry, Wally is lazy, and Dilbert is boring.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How are we supposed to use this new information?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wake me up when he's done talking.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, presents the results of personality profiles he made the staff complete. His findings simply label Alice as angry, Wally as lazy and Dilbert as boring. Dilbert asks how the information can be used, and Wally, true to the label, asks to be woken when Dogbert finishes.
punchline: The expensive personality test only tells the team what they already knew, and Wally immediately proves his 'lazy' label right.
summary: A consultant's personality test delivers results so obvious that one employee dozes off to confirm his own verdict.

title: Pay Tied to Baseline Happiness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, your compensation will be a function of your baseline happiness.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't want to waste money giving raises to employees who won't get any happier no matter what we do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This plan makes me unhappy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nice try, but you were already unhappy.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with an exterior shot of the office building in the middle panel
situation: The Boss announces to the staff at a meeting that pay will now depend on each employee's baseline happiness, since raises are wasted on people who will never be happier. Dilbert objects that the plan makes him unhappy, but the Boss dismisses the complaint by saying he was already unhappy.
punchline: Management's pseudo-scientific excuse for withholding raises is unfalsifiable, since any complaint just proves the employee was already unhappy and so doesn't deserve more pay.
summary: A boss justifies denying raises by claiming unhappy people can't be made happier, then shuts down an objection with the same circular logic.

title: Boss Forgets He Pays Contractor

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: I've been a contractor here for over a year. Maybe you should just hire me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who are you? I didn't even know I was paying you.

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: Perhaps we can pretend this conversation never happened.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That feels like the best option.

situation: A long-serving contractor with a goatee and an ID badge tells the Boss, who is holding a coffee cup, that he should be hired as a permanent employee after more than a year of work. The Boss doesn't recognize him and admits he didn't know he was paying him. The contractor, realizing his mistake, suggests forgetting the conversation, and the Boss readily agrees.
punchline: The contractor realizes that the Boss is so oblivious that drawing attention to himself could jeopardize his paid position, so he retreats and the Boss happily pretends nothing happened.
summary: A contractor who has worked unnoticed for over a year asks for a permanent job and learns that his boss has no idea he exists or is being paid.

title: Fatal Ergonomic Office Furniture Accident

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ted got thrown from his treadmill desk, bounced off of Alice's exercise ball chair, and broke his neck on a kneeling chair.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The cause of death is listed as "good ergonomics."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: On the plus side, his posture was excellent.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, reports to The Boss on how Ted died. Ted was thrown off a treadmill desk, bounced off Alice's exercise ball chair, and broke his neck on a kneeling chair. Catbert deadpans that the official cause of death is 'good ergonomics' and adds that Ted's posture was excellent.
punchline: The ergonomic furniture meant to keep employees healthy literally killed Ted, and Catbert callously offers his good posture as the silver lining.
summary: A cheerfully callous HR cat explains how a coworker was killed by a chain of supposedly healthy office furniture.

title: Disagreeing With Everything, Including Disagreement

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everyone says you aren't being a team player because you keep disagreeing with everything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everyone does NOT say that, and I DON'T disagree with everything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There you go again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'd be a terrible lawyer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that colleagues think he isn't a team player because he disagrees with everything. Dilbert immediately disputes both claims, which the Boss takes as proof of the accusation. Dilbert then insults the Boss's legal skills, and the Boss takes it as a compliment.
punchline: Dilbert's rebuttal proves the accusation true, and the Boss, who cannot argue his case well, is so oblivious that he thanks Dilbert for an insult.
summary: A manager's complaint about constant contradiction is confirmed the instant the employee contradicts it, leaving the manager smugly misreading a put-down as praise.

title: Lying to Weasels Instead of Truth

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I keep speaking truth to power, but it isn't working out for me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Try lying to weasels. It doesn't look as good on a bumper sticker but it gets the job done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds like a terrible idea.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then why are you doing it right now?

setting: Office hallway, walking with coffee cups
situation: Dilbert walks with a bald, green-shirted coworker and complains that speaking truth to power has not helped his career. The coworker advises him to lie to weasels instead, and when Dilbert calls that a terrible idea, the coworker points out that the coworker himself is doing exactly that in this very conversation.
punchline: The coworker's cynical advice to lie to weasels is undercut by the implication that Dilbert, being lied to or being a weasel, is the target of the lie right now, exposing that dishonesty is already how the coworker operates.
summary: A colleague offers a cynical alternative to honest speech, then casually admits he is practicing it on the person he is advising.

title: Hard Work Advice Serves Management

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What is the key to success?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Hard work!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is it a coincidence that your advice for me corresponds to your self-interest?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: My other advice is never question authority.

setting: Office hallway or break area, with both holding coffee cups
situation: A young employee in a yellow shirt asks a manager in an orange shirt for the key to success. The manager answers 'hard work', and the employee points out that this advice happens to benefit the manager. The manager responds by adding that the other piece of advice is to never question authority.
punchline: The manager's reflexive 'never question authority' advice shows that his guidance is designed to benefit management, and it shuts down the employee's very reasonable challenge.
summary: A worker challenges a supervisor's career wisdom as self-serving, and the supervisor responds by demanding unquestioning obedience.

title: Dogbert Caught Dumping Frozen Brains

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: You're under arrest for running a scam cryogenic investment firm.

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: We have video footage of you kicking unfrozen brains into the river.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That doesn't look like me.

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: You were chanting your own name.

setting: Outdoors beside a car, with a police officer confronting Dogbert
situation: A police officer arrests Dogbert for running a scam cryogenic investment firm. The officer says there is video of Dogbert kicking unfrozen brains into the river. Dogbert denies that the person in the video is him, so the officer points out that the figure was chanting Dogbert's own name.
punchline: Dogbert's denial collapses because the video shows the culprit chanting his own name, making his guilt obvious and the crime itself absurdly brazen.
summary: A cop nails a scheming Dogbert with video evidence so damning that even his excuse about the footage backfires.

title: Printer Help Buried Under Priorities

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't get the printer to work. Can you help?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. I'll be there as soon as I finish my twenty-seven tasks that are all higher priorities.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How long will that take?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got three new tasks while you were here yammering.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert, who is seated at his computer, to fix a malfunctioning printer. Dilbert agrees but says he must first finish twenty-seven higher-priority tasks. When she asks how long that will take, he says his backlog has actually grown during the conversation.
punchline: Dilbert's task list grows faster than he can complete it, so the printer fix will effectively never happen, and he blames the interruption for making it worse.
summary: An overloaded IT-style worker explains that his endless, ever-growing to-do list means a simple printer request will never reach the front of the queue.

title: Criminal Organization, Not Easily Proven

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We won the job by intentionally underbidding.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: But we can close the profit gap by doing extra-shoddy work and grossly overcharging for upgrades.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are we a criminal organization?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Not in a way that can easily be proven.

situation: A manager with swept-up hair explains to Dilbert that the company won a contract by deliberately underbidding. He then says they will make up the lost profit by doing extra-shoddy work and grossly overcharging for upgrades. Dilbert asks whether they are a criminal organization, and the manager replies they are not in a way that can easily be proven.
punchline: The manager effectively admits the company is criminal, taking comfort only in the fact that its fraud would be hard to prove.
summary: A boss casually lays out a deceptive business plan and, when questioned about its legality, answers with a technicality that amounts to a confession.

title: Thought-Reading Device Does Nothing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a device that can read your thoughts and turn them into computer commands.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nothing is happening.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is it broken?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's one of my top two theories.

situation: Dilbert shows a coworker a headset device he invented that supposedly reads thoughts and converts them into computer commands. The coworker wears it and reports that nothing is happening, then asks if it is broken. Dilbert replies that this is one of his top two theories.
punchline: The device either is broken or the coworker has no thoughts to read, and Dilbert's 'top two theories' implies the insult that the coworker's mind is empty.
summary: An engineer's new mind-reading gadget produces no results on a coworker, and the engineer suggests two possible explanations, one of them insulting.

title: No Such Thing as Spare Time

transcript.text: Do you have some spare time to help me on my project?

transcript.text: There's no such thing as spare time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There is only you inconveniencing me for your own selfish benefit.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're being rude.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop blaming the victim.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert if he has spare time to help with a project. Dilbert, seated at his laptop, flatly denies that spare time exists and says the coworker is only inconveniencing him for selfish reasons. When the coworker calls him rude, Dilbert accuses him of blaming the victim.
punchline: Dilbert turns a polite request for help into an offense against himself, casting the person asking as the aggressor and himself as the victim.
summary: A colleague's polite plea for assistance gets flipped by Dilbert into an accusation that the asker is the one causing harm.

transcript.text: But Ted's lying is okay?

transcript.text: We don't have a policy about lying.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did Ted tell you that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh...

setting: Office, in front of a wall
situation: The Boss reprimands Alice because Ted complained she called him a liar, citing a policy against disrespecting co-workers. Alice points out that Ted's lying is not covered by any policy, and the Boss admits there is none. She then asks whether Ted himself told him that, and the Boss unwittingly confirms he did.
punchline: The Boss is so gullible that he just proved Ted is a liar by repeating Ted's false claim about the policy, and he doesn't even notice the irony.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for calling a colleague a liar, then inadvertently shows the colleague's dishonesty by relaying what he was told.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker, who is absorbed in his phone, for feedback on his idea. The coworker responds with a vicious personal insult and a nasty prediction about Dilbert's loved ones. Dilbert deduces the man spends a lot of time on Twitter, and the coworker is amazed that he guessed it.
punchline: The coworker's abusive, troll-like response is so typical of Twitter behavior that Dilbert instantly identifies the source, while the coworker remains oblivious to how obvious it is.
summary: A man scrolling on his phone answers a request for input with vicious abuse, and his colleague correctly guesses where he picked up the habit.

title: Doctor's Note Demands Sleep at Work

transcript.text: What's it say?

transcript.text: It says I need lots of sleep at work.

situation: The Boss asks Wally for a doctor's note to justify his behavior, and Wally hands one over. The Boss can't read the illegible handwriting, and Wally claims that proves it's genuine. When asked what it says, the Boss reads it as prescribing lots of sleep at work.
punchline: Wally's note is so illegible that the reader can claim it says whatever he wants, and what he says it says is that he needs to sleep on the job, which is exactly what lazy Wally would want.
summary: A lazy employee's unreadable medical note turns out to excuse him for napping during his shift.

title: Boss Lectures Alice About Idiots

transcript.speaker: Alice

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: The Boss tells Alice about a TED talk on how idiots don't realize they are dumb. Alice warns him to change the subject for the sake of her career, but he obliviously carries on with another fact about idiots. Alice clenches her teeth and shakes, struggling to keep from saying what she thinks.
punchline: The Boss is himself the idiot who doesn't know it, and Alice has to bite her tongue to avoid insulting him and damaging her career.
summary: A clueless manager cheerfully recounts a lecture about unaware fools while his coworker trembles with the effort of staying silent.

title: Denial Treated as Proof of Guilt

transcript.speaker: Narrator
