transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That didn't happen. She's nuts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha! You wouldn't be so angry if it weren't true.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's exactly what guilty people say.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that Alice has accused them of deleting her files on the server. The coworker denies it and calls Alice nuts, and Dilbert interprets the anger as proof of guilt. When the coworker objects that this makes no sense, Dilbert says that is exactly what guilty people say.
punchline: Dilbert's reasoning is unfalsifiable: any reaction from the accused, whether anger or protest, gets treated as evidence of guilt, which is exactly how conspiracy theories sustain themselves.
summary: A coworker's every denial gets twisted into confirmation of guilt, showing how conspiracy thinking works.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you like the prototype so far?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Office hallway with coffee cups, ending in a cubicle
situation: Asok proudly announces he finished his project, and Dilbert hushes him because finishing leads to either more work or being fired for lack of work. Dilbert and Wally explain that employees avoid completion by getting the boss to keep adding features. In the last panel Dilbert demonstrates by asking the boss for a red button and cooling fins on the prototype.
punchline: Employees keep their jobs safe by exploiting the boss's tendency to add pointless features, so nothing ever gets finished, and the boss makes it easy.
summary: Veteran engineers teach a newcomer that completing work is dangerous, so they keep projects alive by coaxing their boss into endless feature requests.

He then explains the plan is to relax workplace safety standards and let nature take its course. Screams and cries of pain are heard from elsewhere, and he advises the staff to keep their headphones on for a week.
punchline: The Boss's 'attrition' is a euphemism for deliberately letting employees get injured or killed by removing safety protections, and he cheerfully suggests ignoring the screams.
summary: A manager reveals that his plan to shrink the workforce painlessly on paper actually means making the workplace dangerous enough that employees get hurt.

He then asks whether Dilbert, who wrote the car's operating system, could remotely kill the boss with it. Dilbert, uneasy, says they shouldn't be discussing this. The strip is marked 'Continued'.
punchline: Dilbert's refusal to deny it, and his claim that they shouldn't talk about it, implies he could in fact kill the boss remotely through the car's software.
summary: A coworker idly wonders whether the programmer behind a driverless car's software could use it to eliminate their boss, and the programmer nervously declines to discuss it.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, tells Dilbert he followed up on every intern he has mentored. He casually reports that most died from self-inflicted injuries, and when Dilbert asks about the rest, Wally says other people killed them.
punchline: Wally deadpans that his mentoring left every intern dead, either by their own hand or someone else's, without showing any concern or responsibility.
summary: A nonchalant mentor reveals that every intern he ever guided has since met a violent or tragic end.

He demonstrates by asking the new hire questions, and the hire gives canned answers, including that he is too busy to help and that management is dumb. Wally, who has bonded with the new hire, is told he'll get used to it quickly.
punchline: The new hire's canned responses are exactly what real employees say (too busy, management is dumb), implying that actual workers already behave like scripted NPCs and that people quickly accept it.
summary: A manager shows off a scripted video-game-style hire whose pat answers about being busy and disliking management sound just like those of ordinary employees.

She screams, her hair on fire, as she is overwhelmed by the vitriol. Dilbert asks how her first day went, and she is dazed and says she's already addicted.
punchline: Despite being horrified by the toxic, hellish content on Twitter, Alice is instantly hooked, suggesting the platform's nastiness is exactly what makes it addictive.
summary: A new social media user is traumatized by the torrent of vicious replies to her first post yet immediately can't stay away.

situation: In a recurring 'Dogbert's Life Advice' strip, Dogbert reviews a client's file and recommends a bizarre plan: live unhealthily, die young, and hope for reincarnation. When the client asks whether reincarnation is real, Dogbert admits he doesn't know, only that the dead are easier to please than the client.
punchline: Dogbert gives no real answer about reincarnation and instead insults the client by saying corpses are less fussy than he is.
summary: A consultant dog tells his picky client to hasten his own demise and then deflects the follow-up question with a jab at his complaining nature.

title: Government Back Door Makes Traitors

transcript.text: Traitor.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he is uneasy about giving the government a back door into the company's self-driving car software. The Boss brushes off the worry, saying it will only be used to kill terrorists and traitors. Dilbert then muses that he might secretly disable it, and the Boss silently labels him a traitor.
punchline: By reassuring Dilbert that the back door only targets traitors, the Boss makes Dilbert's plan to quietly disable it exactly the kind of act that would get him classified as a traitor and killed.
summary: A reassurance about who the government will target backfires the moment the engineer considers quietly sabotaging the surveillance feature.

title: Blank Time Management Book

transcript.text: I just saved you three hours.

situation: Dogbert offers Dilbert a copy of his book on time management, and Dilbert agrees to read it. He opens it and discovers every page is blank. Dogbert points out that by giving him nothing to read, he has saved Dilbert the hours the book would have taken.
punchline: Dogbert's blank book on time management technically delivers on its promise by saving the reader time, mocking the self-help genre as padded and low in real value.
summary: A scheming dog hands over an empty self-help volume and claims credit for freeing up the reader's afternoon.
